Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
- Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark 
  - Published7 June
- Antonelli says he still has questions to answer 
  - Published11 June
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Logitech is facing a proposed class action lawsuit for not giving customers tariff refunds.
In April 2025, Logitech raised the prices on 51 percent of its portfolio, with some prices increasing by as much as 25 percent.
The complaint seeks to “recover monies that Logitech extracted from American consumers as offset for import tariffs that the United States Supreme Court has since declared unlawful, tariffs for which Logitech now stands to be reimbursed by the federal government. This is all while Logitech retained every dollar of the corresponding price increases it charged its customers due to the illegal tariffs.”
A construction and residential housing builder in California, SJK Development, and California resident Ala Awadalla filed the complaint in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, San Jose Division on Tuesday. Per the complaint, both parties bought Logitech mice at higher prices.
“Had Logitech not inflated its prices in the name of the unlawful IEEPA [International Emergency Economic Powers Act] tariffs, Plaintiff[s] would have paid less for the same product. Plaintiff[s] has received no refund, credit, or other compensation from Logitech corresponding to the tariff component of the price Plaintiff[s] paid,” the complaint reads.
Logitech didn’t make a public announcement about the price hikes, which are still implemented. The complaint highlights multiple times that Logitech executives told investors that the price increases would or had offset the financial impact of the tariffs. This includes a call in May when Matteo Anversa, Logitech’s CFO, said, “The positive impact of the US price actions and favorable foreign exchange more than offset the impact of tariffs and higher promotions.” Anversa was discussing Logitech’s fiscal Q4 2026, which he noted was “the highest level of profitability in the history of the company outside of the COVID peak.”

A video (here & here) showing a group of people raising slogans against Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is being shared on social media, with the claim that the incident occurred at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station in Delhi during Independence Day, i.e., on 15 August 2026. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of a crowd raising anti-Modi slogans at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station in Delhi on 15 August 2026.
Fact: The video is from 20 July 2026, capturing protestors raising anti-Modi slogans during NEET protests at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search of the video’s keyframes revealed that the same clip (here, here & here) has been online since at least 20 July 2026. These posts indicated that the video shows NEET protesters at the Rajiv Chowk metro station in July 2026.
Further research led us to similar videos (here & here) published by media outlets showing the protests at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station. According to reports (here & here), on 20 July 2026, several protesters entered the station, caused chaos, and raised anti-Modi slogans while demanding the resignation of then Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan during the ‘Chalo Sansad’ march. This indicates that the viral video predates August 15 and shows the earlier NEET protests. Moreover, we couldn’t find any credible media reports of anti-Modi slogans being raised on 15 August 2026 at the Rajiv Chowk Metro station.
To sum it up, the viral video showing anti-Modi slogans at Rajiv Chowk Metro station is not from August 15. It is an older clip from the NEET protests held in July 2026.

It was just after dawn in Sevastopol when a powerful explosion tore through a quiet square in a residential district of the Russian-occupied Crimean port city.
Hidden inside a rubbish bin, a bomb containing the equivalent of about 500g of TNT detonated on 13 August as Robert Shageev, the deputy commander of a Russian Black Sea fleet submarine brigade, walked past in naval uniform. He was killed on the spot.
Within hours, investigators had a suspect. Police detained Margarita Reutt, a 32-year-old resident of Sochi, the Russian resort city about 300 miles across the Black Sea from Sevastopol.
During a search, investigators said they had found a remote control they believed was used to detonate the bomb that killed Shageev, a former commander of Ukraine’s only submarine who switched allegiance to Russia in 2014 when Moscow annexed Crimea.
According to the security service, she confessed to the attack and said that a handler linked to Ukrainian intelligence had promised her a large payment in cryptocurrency and documents that would allow her to leave Russia afterwards.
The FSB also said Reutt showed no remorse.
Those assertions could not be independently verified, and Russian security agencies have previously publicised purported confessions from detainees before their cases have reached court. But several people previously accused by Russia of carrying out similar attacks against military figures were later found by reporters to have been involved in the operations Moscow had accused them of conducting.
What exactly drove Reutt to allegedly embark on such an audacious mission remains unclear. As with other cases involving accused Ukrainian intelligence operations, her trial is likely to take place behind closed doors, offering little opportunity for her to give her own account publicly.
But interviews with a dozen friends and acquaintances, combined with an examination of years of her social media activity, offer a portrait of a determined and adventurous woman whose attitude towards her country appears to have hardened gradually, with signs of a more striking change emerging in the months leading up to the attack.
“Rita believed that the country was going in the wrong direction,” said a longtime friend, using the diminutive form of her name. “But I am still shocked she went so far,” the friend added.
Russia quickly accused Reutt of carrying out the attack on the orders of Ukrainian intelligence. Kyiv has not commented on the bombing or Reutt’s alleged role in it.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have been linked to a string of assassinations and attempted killings of senior Russian military officers whom Kyiv has accused of involvement in the invasion. Ukrainian officials have occasionally acknowledged involvement in such operations, but more often have remained silent.
The attacks have involved an array of methods and recruits, from committed anti-Kremlin saboteurs to Russians promised large sums of money. In other cases, unsuspecting couriers and delivery workers have effectively been used as mules.
Usually, little is known about those accused of carrying out such attacks or how they prepared for them. Some have managed to escape, or were never publicly identified by Russian authorities, while others were killed carrying out their operations.
The swift capture and naming of Reutt, however, offers a rare opportunity to examine the journey of a Russian citizen accused of turning against her own country.
Reutt, born Margarita Yakovleva, grew up in Yaroslavl, a city north-east of Moscow, where she took the surname of the grandmother who largely raised her after her parents divorced. Friends recalled a largely unremarkable childhood, remembering her as warm and sociable, but also unusually drawn to adventure and risk.
“Margarita was fearless. She would climb trees, jump off cars, do things most boys were scared of,” recalled one friend from her childhood.
That streak followed her to Novosibirsk, thousands of miles to the east, where she studied management and threw herself into university life. Reutt became a regular at a local parachuting club, with photographs showing her jumping from Soviet-era aircraft, often the only woman among groups of men in camouflage gear.
She also won prizes in amateur go-karting competitions and took up water polo, becoming goalkeeper for the university team and quickly distinguishing herself despite being new to the sport. “Margarita was so talented and never afraid of the ball,” recalled her water polo coach at the time.
There was little then to suggest hostility towards the Kremlin. In Novosibirsk, Reutt became a well-liked member of a patriotic volunteer group that searched for the remains of Soviet soldiers killed during the second world war, part of a nationwide movement dedicated to recovering and reburying the war dead.
After graduating, Reutt moved south to Sochi, the Black Sea resort that became her home. She briefly tried her hand at running a travel agency before joining Vitauct in the early 2020s, an alternative medicine company specialising in longevity.
“She was the most ordinary person,” said Gennadiy Garbuzov, the company’s founder, who struggled to reconcile the woman he knew with the allegations now facing her. “There was nothing to indicate she would do this. She must have fallen under someone’s influence.”
On the surface, her online life was similarly unremarkable. She posted frequently about health and animal rights and took to Telegram forums to discuss alternative medicine.
Reutt also travelled widely. Leaked records from travel databases seen by the Guardian and photographs posted online show frequent trips abroad, including to Turkey, Thailand and Sri Lanka, where she often shared photographs of herself in bikinis at beach resorts.
“Margarita just seemed to be living her life and had lots of plans for the future,” said another colleague at Vitauct.
“She was good-looking and popular,” the colleague added.
In October 2025, Reutt travelled to Minsk for her sister’s wedding. Photographs from the celebration show her smiling among relatives and catching the bridal bouquet. To one friend she painted an idyllic picture of her life in Sochi, traversing mountains, waterfalls and canyons. “You can explore endlessly here, everything is lush and green,” she wrote to the friend.
But beneath that outwardly happy life, another side of Reutt was becoming visible. She increasingly expressed concerns about environmental problems plaguing Sochi, and started to become involved in local volunteer initiatives, friends said.
After a large oil spill in the Black Sea in December 2024, when two Russian tankers were wrecked in a storm, Reutt travelled to Anapa to join volunteers cleaning mazut, a heavy fuel oil, from contaminated beaches.
Exactly when dissatisfaction with her surroundings hardened into something more political is difficult to establish. Friends described a growing estrangement from Russia that deepened after the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“The war came as a shock,” said one friend, who recalled Reutt becoming increasingly outspoken in public about the fighting in Ukraine. “I told her once to keep quiet, otherwise she would get us both into trouble,” the friend said.
By July 2025, her anti-war feelings had spilt into public view. While travelling on a Samara-Adler train, Reutt was fined under Russia’s sweeping law against “discrediting” the armed forces after reportedly shouting “Serves you right, Russians!” when news broke of a Ukrainian drone strike on a railway station in the Rostov region.
The following February, Reutt posted the results of a genetic test showing she was 98% Russian, adding a hashtag declaring that she was “ashamed to be Russian”.
Yet to friends and acquaintances, Reutt appeared to carry on much as before. She picked up occasional jobs, appeared in video clips made by friends and continued to travel. As recently as March, photographs from a trip to Cuba showed her drinking from a coconut.
It was only in late spring, several people who knew her said, that her behaviour began to change in ways they struggled to understand at the time. “She became more withdrawn,” recalled one friend.
Around the same time, a group of friends began planning a trip together for the autumn. Reutt declined to join them without much explanation – an unusual response from someone friends said could be counted on to say yes to a new adventure.
Another friend remembered Reutt suddenly acquiring a second phone. “She bought this second phone in the spring. She explained that she needed it for work, but it didn’t really make sense to me at the time.”
“Margarita was hiding something,” the friend added. “I thought maybe she had a new boyfriend.”
By the summer, Reutt had begun spending more time in Crimea, the place where she would eventually be arrested. One acquaintance said she explained the trips to Crimea by saying she was scouting possible locations for video shoots, having recently begun appearing more frequently in music clips.
What she was actually doing in Crimea – and when, if at all, she came into contact with Ukrainian intelligence – remains unknown.
If Russia’s allegations that she was recruited by Ukraine are true, Reutt would join a growing group of Russian citizens accused of being enlisted by Ukrainian intelligence to carry out sabotage and assassinations deep behind the frontlines.
Such recruits offer obvious advantages: they can move around Russia more freely, and attract less scrutiny than Ukrainian operatives, and they can reach targets far from the frontline without putting trained agents at risk. Women have featured prominently in several of the most high-profile operations, potentially attracting even less suspicion.
For those close to Reutt, there is no easy explanation for how the woman they remember ended up accused of carrying out an assassination. But a friend of two decades recalled a stubborn determination to follow through on whatever she decided to do.
“If she had a plan in mind, she would do it,” the friend said. “Even if it was something like this.”

A man who abandoned his seven-year-old son on Mount Fuji in Japan after the boy complained of feeling tired while on a family hike has been reprimanded by local police.
A worker on Japan’s highest mountain discovered the child sitting alone on a bench near the sixth station of the Fujinomiya trail at an altitude of more than 2,000 metres (6,500 feet) on Thursday.
After inviting the boy to take shelter at the station, the worker called the police, who took the child into protective custody.
It emerged that he had told his father he was too tired to continue while they were hiking up the trail in the early hours of the morning.
The man, who was from Japan’s fourth-largest city, Nagoya, gave his son some snacks and a soft drink.
He then told him to wait for him before continuing his five-hour ascent to the summit with the child’s older brother, who had already gone on ahead. It would have taken him about eight hours to return, according to local reports.
By the time police officers managed to contact the boy’s father, he had ascended to the eighth station, a three-hour hike from where he had left his son.
They told him to turn back, and after reuniting him with his son reprimanded him for leaving the child alone on an active volcano.
“Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable,” officers said, according to Japan Today.
Weather on the mountain, which has its own microclimate, is unpredictable and can change rapidly. Hypothermia poses a serious risk for hikers even in the summer.
The father is said to have apologised to the police, saying: “I made a rash decision, and I deeply regret it.”
Local police are urging hikers to consider the abilities and stamina of everyone in their group when planning an ascent on Mount Fuji, and to adjust their pace accordingly.

Conservative MP urges government to release 'full details' of U.S. trade deal that was on the table
Shuvaloy Majumdar says releasing the details will let Canadians 'debate and discuss the way forward'
The Conservative Party is urging Prime Minister Mark Carney's government to release "the full details" of the proposed Canada-U.S. trade deal that was on the table before negotiations collapsed late on Friday.
Conservative MP Shuvaloy Majumdar, the party's shadow minister for Canada-U.S. relations, said in a letter to Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc on Sunday that the Conservatives aren't asking for "negotiating secrets."
But the party is seeking information that Ottawa and Washington already know, Majumdar said. "This information will allow Canadians to debate and discuss the way forward as a country."
Fifty per cent U.S. tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect early on Saturday after extended trade negotiations between the two countries fell apart.
- ListenThe fallout from failed Canada-U.S. trade talks
- Trump says Canada 'wants the benefits' of being a U.S. state 'without being one' as trade dispute deepens
Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters on Saturday that Canadian negotiators decided to walk away from the talks after the United States had made what he said were unacceptable demands.
That included "efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals," Carney said.
"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or to undermine our key industries," he said, adding that his government would impose "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods, starting Sept. 8.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the talks failed after "new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada."
The U.S. "offer would have led to supply chain co-ordination on aerospace, complementary actions to address unfair trade practices, critical minerals co-operation, increased enforcement against imports produced with forced labour and the announcement of formal U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement negotiations," he said in a statement early Saturday.
Greer also told the New York Times in an interview on Saturday that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration offered, in part, to cut 10 per cent tariffs on softwood lumber and lower steel tariffs from 50 to 25 per cent.
Exact details not yet released
But neither government has released the exact details of the deal that was being negotiated.
Despite that, Carney's decision to walk away from the talks appears to have garnered widespread support in Canada, including from provincial leaders like Ontario Premier Doug Ford and B.C. Premier David Eby.
Many also have backed Carney's plans to impose reciprocal tariffs on the U.S. next month.
There is "anxiety" among Canadians for what the escalating trade dispute means for the economy and their daily lives, said David Coletto, founder and CEO of the Abacus Data polling firm.
But there is also a sense that "we're not going to let Donald Trump bully us," Coletto told CBC News in an interview Sunday. "And I think most Canadians still feel good about what the prime minister said yesterday and now are going to wait to see what comes next."
Opposition party leaders have also said Canada should remain united in the face of Trump's tariffs.
"Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal. Instead, we must continue the fight for tariff-free trade," Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a social media post Saturday morning.
Poilievre said he would seek a call with Carney "to discuss what we can do to fight for our workers, businesses and economy."
Asked by reporters on Saturday if he would brief opposition leaders on the trade situation, Carney said that would likely happen Monday afternoon or Tuesday morning.

Former Liberian vice president charged in drug-trafficking probe

Liberia has charged former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor with drug trafficking, money laundering and a range of other offences, the country's Justice Ministry announced.
Howard-Taylor, who served as vice president for six years to 2024, was detained before boarding a flight to leave Liberia at Roberts International Airport in the capital, Monrovia.
She was taken to national police headquarters, and has yet to make any public comments about the charges.
The West African country has launched a major crackdown of transnational drug trades, particularly cocaine trafficking, in recent years.
Howard-Taylor is accused of illegally importing, selling and transporting controlled drugs, as well as helping to facilitate drug trafficking.
Police have charged three foreign nationals – two Croatians and one Ukrainian – in absentia as part of their investigation. They are accused of being part of the same network as Howard-Taylor.
Liberian authorities say they are determined to apprehend the foreign nationals, and that they are targeting all parts of the drug-trafficking network: organisers, facilitators and financiers.
In recent months, officials have conducted multiple drug trafficking seizures, with some of them among the largest in the country's history.
She held a senior role in former President George Weah's administration, whose six years in power from 2018 to 2024 was plagued with allegations of corruption and financial mismanagement.
When President Joseph Boakai took over, he pledged to crack down on corruption.
He has also said that he does not want Liberia to turn into a haven for drug trafficking. West Africa is increasingly a major transit route for cocaine trading from South America to Europe.

Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
- Published
Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction.
A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive.
A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box.
It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades.
For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states.
But the 2015 federal election was a seismic shock.
The PDP lost the presidential vote to Muhammadu Buhari and the newly formed All Progressives Congress (APC) - a coalition of opposition parties and disgruntled former members.
Thrust into the political wilderness the party's national leaders were bewildered - familiar with the trappings of federal power they had to work out what to do in opposition.
This was the beginning of the end, according to political analyst Ishaq Buhari.
"They were a party that was so used to power, being in opposition was a new challenge they struggled with from the start," he told the BBC.
If 2015 was a major blow, 2025 was the year the party's foundations were left in ruins.
It was marked by a dizzying wave of defections and bitter internal conflicts.
A group of state governors switched party allegiance, which had a particularly devastating effect.
At the start of that year, the PDP still held eight states. But by December, five state governors - from Delta, Akwa Ibom, Enugu, Bayelsa and Rivers - had gone over to the ruling APC.
They cited the PDP's declining viability and a desire for better co-operation with the federal government as reasons for their departure.
Early this year, the PDP held three states but that is now down to zero - with the Oyo governorship slipping from the party's hands just last month.
Internal power struggles, factionalism, insistence that power rotates through the regions and disciplinary measures have all added to the sense of disillusionment within the party.
The PDP has been robbed of high-profile figures and talent, including the loss of former Vice-President Atiku Aubakar last year.
The crisis was intensified by a debilitating leadership tussle.
In November 2025, a faction of the party, which observers say represented the majority of members, held a contentious national convention in Ibadan, Oyo state, despite court orders attempting to stop it.
The convention expelled Nyesom Wike, a prominent PDP member who is serving in President Bola Tinubu's APC-led government.
Wike, who helped found the party, heads a rival faction creating a political stand-off that has paralysed the PDP.
He had controversially helped the APC win Rivers state in the last presidential election leading to accusations that he had betrayed the PDP.
But in the eyes of the law the faction that he heads is the legitimate party.
This means that it has been able to submit its slate of presidential and parliamentary candidates to the electoral commission leaving the rival faction without any representatives on the ballot.
Despite the chaos, some die-hard loyalists remain optimistic.
Politician and staunch PDP member Aminu Adamu, part of the anti-Wike faction, believes a return to its former glory is possible.
He cites examples from Thailand and Argentina, where parties have bounced back after years in the wilderness.
"We have seen it happen before," he tells the BBC. "All we need to do is put our house in order and start to build from there.
"If we make all the necessary corrections, by 2032 I really think PDP can be a major force again."
Others point out that the party still has a grassroots network - essential to win and sustain power - with offices, activists, supporters and local leaders. But by 2032 it may be too late.
With the party in such disarray and candidates backed by Wike on the ballot - voters are unlikely to trust them.
Analyst Deji Olarenwaju believes the only thing that could save the once-mighty party is an alliance with the African Democratic Congress - now seen as the biggest opposition group or Peter Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
"Because on their own they are going nowhere," he says.

For a generation of Indian students preparing for competitive exams, "Hello bacchon…" became more than a classroom greeting. It became a recognisable greeting from Alakh Pandey's PhysicsWallah lessons on YouTube. Pandey began tutoring students by uploading videos on YouTube for free. What began with no-charge JEE and NEET lectures has now grown into a multi-channel education business spanning paid online courses, hybrid learning, offline coaching centres and a widening portfolio of education offerings. PhysicsWallah, a mere name on YouTube not five years ago, became India's first new-age edtech startup to hit the public market last year and is now generating quarterly revenue of more than ₹1,000 Cr. After its maiden round of $100 Mn in 2022, which took the company to the unicorn club, PW entered offline education, expanded its course catalogue beyond its original JEE and NEET focus and acquired businesses across test preparation, upskilling and other education categories. Physics Wallah managed to expand revenue streams while racing away from the tides that have consumed the rest of the edtech industry in a post-pandemic world. BYJU'S collapsed, while Unacademy found a home within upGrad. Vedantu has not managed to push its scale as expected, given its unicorn status, despite reaching break-even as per its founder. PW, meanwhile, has grown in profile, in scale and in terms of what it is building — a full-stack education model that increasingly blends digital with offline learning. Its online business brought scale and reach, while offline centres gave it a higher-value channel to monetise students. Acquisitions further widened its presence across categories and geographies. That evolution is now reflected in the numbers. In Q1 FY27, PhysicsWallah reported a total revenue of ₹1,162.8 Cr, with online, offline and other businesses contributing to the topline. But topline growth alone does not explain the PW story. The more interesting question is how the money flows through its education ecosystem. And as the company has expanded from a YouTube-led teaching platform into a multi-channel education company, the ways in which it earns from that student have multiplied too. Inside PW’s Hybrid Model The PW business model starts well before a student buys a course. Its free YouTube content acts as the entry point, helping the company build a large learner base and funnel students towards paid offerings. While we keep calling it free, let's not forget the advertising revenue coming from YouTube. From there, students can move into paid online batches and, increasingly, into physical learning formats such as Pathshala and Vidyapeeth. In Q1 FY27, this translated into ₹1,054 Cr in revenue from operations, up more than 24% YoY. Online education contributed ₹549 Cr, while offline education generated ₹490 Cr, with the remaining revenue coming from other businesses. PW's original monetisation engine remains its online education business. Students can access free lectures and other educational content, but the revenue from the service comes when students enrol in paid programmes across categories such as JEE, NEET, K-12, government examinations, CA/CS/ACCA/CFA, skills and other courses. This segment is standalone profitable and recorded an operating profit of ₹75.9 Cr in the June quarter of FY27. The second major revenue engine is offline education, where PW monetises students through its Vidyapeeth and Pathshala centres. In 2021, PW rolled out Pathshala, which serves as a more hybrid format combining online teaching with physical support, while Vidyapeeth is its full-fledged offline classroom coaching format, launched in 2022. The offline segment collectively contributed a revenue of ₹490 Cr in the quarter under review, up 14% YoY. However, unlike online, it remained loss-making at the segment level, with an operating loss of ₹27 Cr in the quarter. The company’s shareholders’ letter reflects this loss to be ₹54 Cr after allocation of unallocated corporate costs, as per the revised allocation by the company. It is to be noted that PW has reported segment-wise financials for the first time this quarter, with the Q1 FY26 numbers presented on the revised allocation basis for comparison. Beyond these two core engines, the company also earns from its B2B business of supporting K-12 schools and other education offerings such as the sale of hardware devices and student financing solutions — reported under PW's "Others" category. This segment contributed an operating revenue of ₹15.3 Cr in Q1 FY27. But having multiple ways to earn from a learner also makes the revenue story more complicated. The next question is not just how much PW collects — but how those collections translate into reported revenue, and how much of that revenue the company actually gets to keep. PhysicsWallah Revenue Report Card The growth in PW's revenue does not tell the entire story. The amount the company collects from students, the revenue it recognises and the economics of serving those students can vary significantly across its businesses. That makes the quality and timing of revenue just as important as the topline itself. Both online and offline segments monetise students differently. PW uses ACPU (average collection per user) for its online business, which captures the average amount collected from transacting users. Offline education is measured through ARPU (average revenue per user), reflecting revenue recognised per enrolled student. During its Q1 FY27 earnings call, the company's management explained that "collections" are more relevant for online because students generally pay their fees upfront for the entire year. In contrast, ARPU is the more appropriate metric for offline because it captures the "revenue" recognised from enrolled students over the year. For the June quarter, online ACPU increased 10% YoY to ₹4,312, while ARPU for the offline segment made a 7% YoY uptick to ₹12,633. Management did address the relatively modest movement in both metrics. PW's vice president Vikram Bhardwaj attributed the muted growth to the shift in the NEET cycle by around five to seven weeks, affecting collections and enrolments. The impact was largely a timing issue, and collections picked up strongly after the NEET results were announced in July, he said. The point to be noted here is that PhysicsWallah's revenue growth is not relying only on the fee collection from each student, as ACPU's growth is much slower than the online segment's overall revenue jump of 33%. Management itself cautioned against looking at ACPU and enrolments as rigid metrics. Rather, the company is working on acquiring more students and expanding into newer categories to strengthen the pillar for revenue growth. The second point is the relevance of the academic calendar for PhysicsWallah. "We did see an impact on our collections and enrolments across our core business and our subsidiary Xylem. We do believe that while the NEET UG calendar shifted by five to seven weeks this year, our collections post the results announcement on July 16 have been encouraging and we've seen almost 50% growth as compared to last year," the management said. That means quarterly numbers can move depending on when exams take place, when results arrive and when students eventually enrol. Management therefore repeatedly pointed investors towards looking at the business over the full year rather than reading too much into a single quarter. Where Physics Wallah Is Spending PW is effectively running several businesses under one roof, and they do not make money in the same way or at the same rate. Its mature online categories such as JEE, NEET, CA, MBA and Commerce are highly profitable, while newer bets such as NEET PG, Skills, Curious Junior and vernacular education are still in investment mode. Offline is an even bigger contrast — it generates revenue, nearly as much as online, but remains loss-making at the segment level. This difference in category economics shapes PW's expansion strategy. The company is using its established, profitable businesses to invest in newer categories and a more capital-intensive offline network. While this can widen its addressable market and increase a student's lifetime value, it also risks diluting margins if these newer bets take longer to mature. Each new business also brings its own costs. The bigger question is whether PW can build enough scale in these new businesses before the cost of expansion starts to weigh on its consolidated business. The company’s cost structure is also showing signs of operating leverage. During the earnings’ call, the management said employee costs excluding ESOP expenses were down 2.6% YoY in Q1 FY27, while marketing spends rose to ₹128 Cr from ₹117 Cr a year earlier. But the bigger challenge sits offline. Unlike online courses, every offline expansion brings a heavier fixed-cost burden. Centre rentals, faculty, infrastructure and other operating costs have to be absorbed before a new centre reaches maturity. The company earmarked ₹1,008.9 Cr of its IPO proceeds for offline and hybrid centre expansion and leases. As of June 30, 2026, ₹874 Cr of this amount remained unutilised, with ₹134.9 Cr spent so far. However, offline profitability completely depends on centres maturing. During the earnings call, PW said that mature Vidyapeeth centres can deliver 13–15% steady-state margins. In simple terms, a centre generating ₹10 Cr in revenue could eventually generate ₹1.3–₹1.5 Cr in operating profit once it reaches its normal scale and utilisation. But PW has to absorb the costs of setting up and running a centre while enrolments strengthen. Besides, the company is also seeing higher ARPU and better student results as two key levers to achieve steady margins for offline centres. For ARPU, the company might look at increasing fees, which could hurt the enrolment count. Hence, the quality of its offline solutions can only justify the cost and keep the students coming. This becomes particularly important as the company moves beyond its earlier affordability-led positioning and looks to make offline a profitable growth engine. Beyond JEE And NEET: Into The Full Stack With PhysicsWallah having moved beyond competing for just the JEE and NEET student, its next phase of growth is focused on owning multiple steps of the learner's journey — starting from school education and competitive exams to higher education and skilling. PW is now trying to move the starting point of this monetisation journey much earlier. The company has been building its K-12 and early-learning business to bring students into the PW ecosystem before they reach the traditional JEE and NEET preparation stage. In Q1 FY27, this business grew 88% YoY to ₹105 Cr in revenue, while enrolments rose 41% to 7.8 Lakh, according to management. The expansion spans foundation, pre-foundation, Curious Junior, commerce, school boards and other offerings. The company is also expanding its state board offerings to 14 boards, from seven before. In addition, PhysicsWallah is developing newer categories such as NEET PG, skills and vernacular education as future growth levers. In addition to that, PW is adding new categories to its business through acquisitions. Saarthi IAS adds more strength to PhysicsWallah in the UPSC preparation space, whereas Xylem Learning and Utkarsh Classes enable PW to expand its presence across competitive examinations and offline business. The company has launched new products such as PW Books, Earners for short-term skilling, and AI-based products such as Ask AI, AI Companion and AI Tutor. All of this comes with logical reasoning behind the move. The earlier PW enters a learner's journey, the longer the relationship it can potentially build. Management has described K-12 as a growth opportunity, arguing that students acquired early could remain with PW as they progress to competitive exams, higher education and skills. But this is also where the competitive challenge becomes harder. PW is moving into markets where it faces different competitors, different customer expectations and different economics. The bigger question is whether PW can turn this breadth into an advantage rather than a collection of unrelated businesses.

Every morning, many of us drink one or two cups of coffee and feel good, refreshed, and ready for the day. Some of us drink one or two more cups at work before lunchtime. Some use pure coffee while others add chicory to it. We prepare the powder using a filter, add milk and sugar, and take a swig.
While many Indians have a fondness for coffee, almost everyone in the U.S. and Europe drinks coffee, and more of it, every day.
Now, what are the effects of drinking coffee? How many cups per day? Should it be black coffee or can it include milk and sugar? And how does this affect our health? These are some questions that have been on our minds — and for which research has offered contradictory answers in the past. Fortunately, a new publication, titled ‘Caffeine and Cardiovascular Disease: A Scientific Statement from the American Heart Association’, may clear some doubts. The authors of the statement analysed several studies that examined the effects of caffeine, the active molecule in coffee that stimulates the brain and the central nervous system and encourages the body to produce and use more energy.
The statement reported that moderate caffeine intake, especially through coffee, may lower the risks of type-2 diabetes, stroke, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation. However, high doses, especially from energy drinks, may harm cardiovascular health, and unfiltered coffee can also raise LDL cholesterol levels.
Data from the Nurses Health Study at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Harvard Medical School and an analysis of 3 lakh people from the U.K. Biobank and Health Canada have indicated that drinking four cups a day may lower the risk of developing cancer, type-2 diabetes, heart diseases, and age-related disorders like dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. However, analyses also suggest that it would be prudent for pregnant and lactating women to limit their coffee intake to three cups a day.
Drinking hot black coffee is recommended, with little or no additives like sugar or milk. However, a group from Copenhagen, Denmark, pointed out in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Science in 2023 that adding milk to black coffee can be good as milk contains antioxidants, minerals, and vitamins and allays the bitter taste.
Chicory-blended coffee
Many people in South India prefer to have pure coffee, i.e. with no additives like chicory, which comes from a perennial herbal plant with coloured flowers. This herb contains no caffeine but a polysaccharide called inulin, which supports digestion and can help control blood sugar.
The benefits of a coffee and chicory blend and their implications for nutrition and health implications were discussed in a recent review paper by a group led by Pushpa S. Murthy at the Central Food Technology and Research Institute, Mysuru, published in the Journal of Food Science and Technology. Chicory contains several compounds that help protect the liver from inflammation, shield the stomach from damage, and may help defend against cancer. Adding chicory to coffee also improves coffee’s fragrance and taste.
The optimal blend of coffee and chicory was suggested to be 70:30 or 60:40, coffee to chicory, to strike a balance between taste and benefits. In fact, most coffee sellers across India have these ratios, unless of course a customer asks for ‘pure’ coffee. This writer himself used to prefer pure coffee until he read the review article by the Mysuru group!

I’ve never used Apple's built-in Shortcuts app before, despite owning an iPhone for years. While automating tedious tasks sounded nice, the necessary scripting to trigger actions and thread them together felt overwhelming when I first opened the app. But my experience with the iOS 27 beta has completely changed my perspective on Shortcuts. What was previously clunky and forgotten now feels streamlined and essential.
When iOS 27 lands this fall, Siri AI might be the most tangible change for many users, with its improved capabilities and stand-alone app. Even so, Apple Intelligence integration into the Shortcuts app has me humming “Zero to Hero” from Disney’s Hercules.
Called “Describe a Short,” it lets you say what you want it to do conversationally, then the app generates an automation flow. You can also tweak it by sending a follow-up prompt in the app; the manual scripting option remains available for power users. Since I was testing this app through the iOS 27 beta, I experienced a couple of glitches where the automations didn’t generate perfectly. Even so, this new Shortcuts feature was incredibly fun to tinker with. After a few tries, I generated automations that actually feel useful as part of my daily smartphone habits.
Here are a few basic shortcut ideas worth trying once you download and install iOS 27. My examples only scratch the surface of what you can automate with the app, but hopefully it will spark ideas for your needs.
Habit Breaking
This might be the most basic automation I’ve set up, but it's already my favorite. I spend so much time mindlessly scrolling on my phone that when I close social media apps, like Instagram, to focus on something else, I sometimes reopen them almost immediately out of habit.
I asked the app to generate a shortcut that triggers whenever I open Instagram. Now I get a notification asking: “Do you really want to use this app?” If I choose yes, then the pop-up goes away. But if I pick no, the phone automatically closes out of Instagram and locks the screen. It’s not exactly transformational, and there are other options for reducing screen time, but this little nudge feels helpful for breaking my repetitive habits.
Quality Checking
Since I live in California, I often check the air quality in my neighborhood on my way out of the apartment to gauge whether I should pack a mask. Rather than manually checking the air quality index each day, I wanted to automate the process. So, I set up a shortcut that runs every morning at 6:40 am. It checks the current weather, looks at the air quality index, and then sends me a notification. If the air quality index is above a certain threshold, I get an alert; if it’s below, it sends me the all-clear.
Battery Saving
Shortcuts can also be triggered based on your location. Whenever I leave my apartment, no matter the time of day, I want my phone to be charged, or I have to grab a battery pack just to be safe. To help with this, I generated a shortcut that triggers when I leave home and checks my device’s current battery level. If it’s below 50 percent when it runs, I get a friendly notification that reminds me to bring that power bank. (A quick trip back inside to grab it is better than being miles from home with no way to communicate.)
Plant Watering
These next two automations are a good example of how you can build shortcuts on your home screen and tie shortcuts together. While plenty of apps log plant watering, I wanted to see if Shortcuts could do it for me. First, I created a shortcut that, whenever I run it, grabs the current date and time and adds that to a dedicated plant watering note to keep a consistent log. I then tapped on the drop-down menu at the top of the app and clicked Add to Home Screen. Now, each time I do the chore, I can tap that app icon to log it.
That alone could have been helpful, but I wanted to push the automation a little further. I created another shortcut that, every morning at 9:00 am, finds the plant watering log and sees if it was modified within the last week. If no changes have been added within the last week, it sends me a notification reminder to check on the plants.
Screenshot Extracting
Although this automation is a little more niche, I use it fairly often as someone who’s chronically online and often taking screenshots. Now, whenever I take a screenshot, my phone automatically extracts any text in the images and copies it to my clipboard. This simplifies my previous process of saving screenshots, manually opening the Photos app, then copying the text from the images.
Plane Landing
This one isn’t very complicated, but it makes my life just a little bit easier. I often travel without my partner and can be negligent in sending updates. So I asked the Shortcuts app to generate an automation that sends a “just landed” text to my partner every time I turn off airplane mode. Simple. During setup, the app asked me to select which iPhone contact was my partner. It's an easy automation that solves the issue of me being incredibly distracted when deplaning.
Sound Recognizing
While this shortcut requires you to adjust your accessibility settings, the extra hassle seems worth it for the payoff. I’m almost always wearing headphones when working from home, with the music turned up quite loud. I’m also anxious about not hearing someone knocking on my door or ringing the bell. There's a fix! Start by going into your Accessibility settings, then find Sound & Name Recognition. Here you can enable sound recognition for everything from glass breaking to babies crying; I picked Door Bell and Door Knock.
Since I don’t always have my phone on me while wearing headphones, the basic notification wouldn’t be that helpful. So I beefed it up by building a shortcut so that when my iPhone recognizes either sound, it pauses whatever is playing. Now I can blast my podcasts without worrying about missing a package delivery.

Jane Schoenbrun’s latest film, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, is making a splash in theaters right now. So it seems like the perfect time to revisit their first film, We’re All Going to the World’s Fair. I fell in love with this film when I first saw it at Sundance in 2021.
We’re All Going to the World’s Fair is an intimate coming-of-age horror film
With Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma out in theaters, now is the perfect time to revisit Jane Schoenbrun’s first film.
We are immediately introduced to our protagonist, Casey, as she engages in the World’s Fair Challenge, a sort of ARG creepypasta meets ice bucket challenge. There’s a creepy mantra, some bloodletting, and a mysterious video — basically a speedrun of horror movie tropes. But having them all delivered by this young girl alone in her room who just stares directly into her webcam the whole time is unsettling. And I actually physically recoiled when she jabbed herself repeatedly with a pin to draw blood.
The idea is that people perform the ritual and then they’re supposed to change in some sort of nebulous way. It’s set up as some sort of “game” where people are supposed to report their symptoms, as they turn into plastic or their guts and become Tetris pieces.
Ultimately, World’s Fair is a coming-of-age story about a lonely young girl. She’s never shown talking to kids her own age. Her father is never seen, only heard, and does nothing but yell. She desperately attempts to connect with others by uploading videos documenting the changes she experiences after performing the challenge.
Importantly, unlike many other coming-of-age films, World’s Fair isn’t about Casey’s sexual awakening and avoids sexualizing her entirely. Instead, it’s about her search for belonging in an extremely online world.
Basically the only other character to get any screen time is JLB, a lonely middle-aged man who claims Casey is in danger. The relationship between JLB and Casey adds another layer of unease to the film, which already blends horror elements with uncomfortably intimate glimpses into the life of a young girl. The whole thing has a voyeuristic quality. It’s never explicitly stated, but it certainly seems like JLB is attempting to groom the vulnerable Casey.
The movie stews in its uncomfortable ambiguity. And that’s part of what makes it great. It may not reach the surreal or campy heights of I Saw the TV Glow or Camp Miasma, but it’s a rare indie cinema original that uses body horror tropes in new and interesting ways.
We’re All Going to the World’s Fair is available to stream on Criterion Channel, Kanopy, and Hoopla.

Nostalgia, like ecstasy, is a hell of a drug and Kieron J. Walsh’s warm-hearted, hot-headed “Skintown” is buzzing on both. A more polite brother to the “Kneecap” boys and a more cautious cousin to those “Derry Girls” still, the Fermanagh-set friendship comedy sends fizzy, sweetly chemical energy coursing through a rave-romanticizing riff on the coming-of-age formula. The story may not be exactly new, but its bittersweet life lessons are delivered with such retroactive affection and such eagerness by the appealing cast, that if you’re of a mind to complain, well, in the parlance of the movie, would you ever give over, catch yourself on and wise up.
It is 1994, in Enniskillen, unflatteringly dubbed “Skintown” by its denizens and famous for “a lake, an old castle and an IRA bomb that killed 11 civilians in 1987.” Vinny (Jack Rowan) wants nothing more than to get the hell out. Partly, that’s due to the omnipresent dangers of an intractable conflict that has been ongoing since before he was born. (Vinny is 23, though his characterization here skews younger.) But really his disillusion with Skintown is an independence struggle of a more personal kind — one recognisable to anybody who remembers their jaundiced familiarity with their childhood hometown starting to curdle into contempt as adulthood beckoned. When Vinny strikes up an unlikely friendship with Wilson (Hope Ipoku Jr.) a Black squaddie from Manchester who’s been deployed to serve in the universally despised British military patrols, they bond when he realises that for Wilson, joining the army was his escape from the place he grew up in.
Popular on Variety
Still, as soon as Vinny gets the money together, he’s resolved to leave, although there are things he’ll miss: his supportive, hardworking paramedic mum (Roisin Gallagher); his peppy unrequited crush Eileen (Jamie Lee O’Donnell); and most of all, his best mate Jonty (Chris Walley), a shell-suited, high-spirited raver just out to have a good time. Vinny and Jonty are as thick as the thieves they eventually, inadvertently become when they’re pressganged into a caper involving a load of ecstasy stolen from the UVF (a loyalist paramilitary group).
On the bright side, though — and DP Ruairi O’Brien’s pleasant images make most everything bright even when, among sparse crowds and street scenes that feel rigidly dressed to the camera, the limits of the budget show — if they manage to sell the drugs and survive, they stand to make quite a bit of cash. More, anyway, than they could hope to score from their part-time jobs at the neighborhood pizzeria, whose oleaginous owner, splendidly named Tony Pepperoni (Michael Smiley), insists on serving his pizzas with a side of Peking ribs because, he contends, “the Irish aren’t ready for pizza on its own. They need a wee side of ribs to wean them off the Chinese.”
That kind of authentically eccentric observation feels lifted directly from experience, and the pacy screenplay, adapted by Enniskillen native Ciarán McMenamin from his 2018 novel, abounds in such flourishes. As a ritual, the whole pub greets the TV newsreader (modelled on BBC institution Moira Stuart) like an old friend every time she begins her report with “Good evening.” “Body of Christ,” blasphemes Jonty benignly, handing out pills at a rave like they’re communion wafers. And, it being marching season, everyone is used to maneuvering around the Orangemen who take to parading down the main street at the drop of a bowler hat. “They’d want to get a move on if they’re planning on stopping outside every Catholic pub,” sighs barmaid Chalky (Tara Lynn O’Neill) resignedly.
Ah yes, the Catholics. The Protestants. The Republicans. The Unionists. The IRA, the UVF, the UDA, the INLA, the RUC, the Brits and the Battle of the Boyne — Vinny’s rather unnecessary voiceover namechecks them all, with more or less equal disparagement. While he and his mates are from a Catholic/Republican background, “Skintown” is careful not to overtly assign blame to one side and virtue to the other. Instead, most of its rancor is directed without sectarian bias, at the politician class. The brief, incredulous euphoria that follows the fateful announcement of an IRA ceasefire, is immediately dampened by one barfly (Belfast-born icon Lalor Roddy) observing drily, “If there’s any conceivable way to fuck this up, those politicians will find it.”
This careful avoidance of any alienating perspective, and its streak of sentimentality make “Skintown” a more timid proposition than, say, “Kneecap,” even as it ramps up to an inevitable tragedy to undercut the bursts of MDMA-infused idealism elsewhere. But it also serves up a gently pointed reminder that for all the region was internationally synonymous with terrorism, reprisal and violent death, most of its inhabitants were ordinary people just going about the humdrum business of everyday life. And being Northern Irish, they did it with an indomitable sense of humor. So don’t come to “Skintown” for trenchant political commentary; come for the slangy jokes, the ’90s kitsch and the precise evocation of the love/hate relationship so many of us Irish have with the place that, however begrudgingly, we call home.

'We're not going to run from it': Sydney Marathon laughs off medal error
- Published
The organisers of Sydney Marathon have laughed off a mistake which saw a German stadium etched on to medals for participants, saying "we're not going to run from it".
Questions arose after the event's official social media account unveiled the design of this year's medal earlier in the week, which had mistakenly etched Allianz Arena, based in the German city of Munich, instead of Sydney's Allianz Stadium.
A spokesperson for the Sydney Marathon told the BBC: "A little too much international flavour has found its way onto the back of the finishers medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium."
It was "an unfortunate error," they added.
Recognisable Sydney landmarks feature on the double-sided medal, including the Opera House and Harbour Bridge, which are part of the 42.2km (26.2 mile) course.
Users on social media noticed the shape of the stadium engraved on the medal appeared to be carved in the wrong likeness.
Munich's Allianz Arena is sculpted by thousands of diamond-shaped inflatable cushions, while Sydney's similarly named Allianz Stadium has a flatter facade smoothed with long bronze fins.
Sydney Marathon confirmed runners would receive the medal depicting the incorrect city's stadium, noting: "It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."
"It's certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humour."
Germany's Allianz Arena also poked fun at the mistake, writing on Instagram: "Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!"
"Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena -- Sydney Opera -- Unique Architecture -- Both are worth a visit!"
The reverse side of the Sydney Marathon medal shows a gold and indigo pattern designed by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian, widely commended for its ornate pattern.
He confirmed to the BBC that he was not involved in designing the other face of the medal engraved with the wrong stadium.
Some 40,000 runners will take part in the event on 30 August, following more than 120,000 ballot entries.
Organisers praised record participation and fundraising for this year's event.
