The fates of 22 crew members aboard a Panama-flagged bulk carrier that sank in the Bay of Bengal off Odisha remained unknown even after 24 hours of intensive search and rescue operations by the Indian Navy and the Indian Coast Guard (ICG) on Sunday (August 23, 2026).
According to the latest reports from the Navy and the ICG, two Chinese crew members of the ill-fated M.V. Ocean Winner, which was carrying iron ore from Odisha, were rescued, even as Navy ships and aircraft continued to search for the remaining crew.
Ocean Winner (IMO 9145530), with 24 (20 Chinese, three Myanmarese, and one Bangladeshi) crew onboard, had left Paradip Port late on August 20.
The ICG said that 36 hours after the ship’s departure, the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) received information that communication with the vessel was lost. It also received a request for a search and rescue operation.
The Eastern Naval Command said on X that it responded to the distress alert by deploying the P8I surveillance aircraft in coordination with MRCC, Sri Vijaya Puram. “The Indian Navy aircraft located a geographically dispersed liferaft in the area and soon coordinated with MT Aisopos, which was transiting nearby, with a request for the merchant vessel to render assistance. By late evening on August 22, MT Aisopos had rescued two of the 24 crew members from the liferafts,” the Navy said.
The Navy said it continues to coordinate with the ICG in the operation to find the remaining crew.
“Sustained monitoring and focused aerial search by Indian Navy P8I MR aircraft led to the successful detection of two floating liferafts and oil slick near the reported position,” the Navy posted on X.
According to Equasis, a global merchant shipping database, Ocean Winner was a 28-year-old vessel that could carry around 73,000 tonnes of cargo. Built in 1998, it was 225 metres long and 32.26 metres wide, and was in its end-of-life period. Periodic inspections by national authorities uncovered several deficiencies. The last inspection by Bangladesh authorities in Chittagong this June reported three deficiencies, including in the ship’s magnetic compass.
Ocean Winner was covered by Protection and Indemnity insurance that would compensate for the loss of life. The insurance is up-to-date, starting from August 1, 2026. The ship has changed hands many times, starting with Greek ownership. The current owner is located in Fujian, China.

Victim of sword attack at Swedish school was a 17-year-old girl
Police in Sweden say the victim of a deadly sword attack at a school was a 17-year-old girl
STOCKHOLM -- The victim of a deadly sword attack at a school in central Sweden was a 17-year-old girl, police said Saturday.
An 18-year-old man armed with a sword carried out the attack at the Brinell School in Fagersta, northwest of Stockholm, while classes were in session on Friday. One person was killed and three others were wounded, two of them severely.
Police said the suspect had been arrested and that the case was being investigated as murder and attempted murder. The police said they have no reason to believe there were more perpetrators.
Vastmanland County, where the town is located, said that the two seriously injured boys were ages 12 and 17. A third person, also under 18, was slightly injured and has been discharged from a hospital, Swedish news agency TT reported.
On Saturday morning, around 70 people gathered at the memorial site that the municipality prepared, carrying flowers and lighting candles, TT reported.
There was no official information on the attacker’s possible motive.
Sweden’s national police said that investigators have already carried out two house searches in connection with the suspect. Many witnesses were expected to be interviewed as part of the investigation.
The region went into a state of emergency on Friday, but it had ended by Saturday.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, in an earlier X post, lamented the violence in Fagersta “right after the summer break.”
“We do not yet know what lies behind the act, but we know that the police are working very intensively,” he said. “Our thoughts are with all those affected.”
Sweden has seen a series of violent school attacks over the years.
Last year, 11 people, including the gunman, died after an attack at an education center in Örebro in central Sweden, leading the government to propose tougher gun laws. It's considered to be the worst mass shooting in the country's history.
In 2022, an 18-year-old man attacked two female teachers with a knife and an ax in a school in Malmo, killing them.
In 2015, a 21-year-old local man rampaged through a school in the southern industrial city of Trollhattan, stabbing three people to death before being fatally shot by police. Authorities called it a racist hate crime, saying he methodically selected dark-skinned victims at Trollhattan’s Kronan school, where most students are foreign-born.

UBE, YAMAGUCHI PREF. – A Japanese civic group is leading efforts to collect the remains of those who died in the 1942 flooding accident at the Chosei undersea coal mine in Ube, Yamaguchi Prefecture.
The Japanese and South Korean governments have begun DNA analysis of remains collected from the site after the group requested such research.
“We’ve managed to reach the stage of DNA analysis through the efforts of citizens,” said Yoko Inoue, 76, who represents the group to record the coal mine accident.
“We want the Japanese government to make a decision to lead the searches and recovery of remains from now on,” she added.
The Chosei coal mine, which opened in 1914, was submerged after an abnormal inflow of water about 1 kilometer from the entrance Feb. 3, 1942, during World War II. The accident killed 183 people, including 136 from the Korean Peninsula.
Its entrance was closed with the bodies of the victims left inside.
The civic group, established in 1991, has conducted underwater investigations as the government failed to meet its request for probes inside the mine on grounds that remains could not be located.
The group collected funds mainly online and conducted its investigations, cooperating with divers.
In August 2025, divers who went underwater from an exhaust and drainage shaft successfully collected bones including a skull. The civic group requested the government to conduct joint DNA analysis with South Korea.
In a summit in January this year, the two countries’ leaders agreed to cooperate in identifying the remains. They also agreed to advance related procedures in May.
Members of the Japanese Foreign Ministry and a South Korean expert organization visited Yamaguchi to bring back samples of the remains and are conducting analysis.
But the group halted its investigations after a Taiwanese diver died in an underwater probe during a memorial ceremony in Ube in February. The group decided not to discuss restarting its investigations until the next memorial ceremony, scheduled for late January 2027.
The group is planning to fix the shaft as part of a project to build a peace park around the site of the former coal mine.
“We want to preserve (the site) as a cultural property and make it a historical place,” Inoue said.

September 11, 2001, will be remembered as one of the darkest days in American history. As the 25th anniversary approaches, National Geographic, in collaboration with the 9/11 Memorial and Museum, is marking the occasion with a new documentary miniseries: 9/11: Reunited. The three-episode series revisits the personal stories of several survivors of the terrorist attacks, with a twist: It reunites people whose paths crossed at that time to celebrate the bonds they formed 25 years ago.
Director Julian Jones was a producer on NatGeo’s Emmy-winning 2021 documentary miniseries 9/11: One Day in America. The experience inspired him to return to direct 9/11: Reunited. “What emerged for me [while making the 2021 documentary] was a sense of people showing up for each other, a selflessness and everyday heroism,” Jones told Ars. As the 25th anniversary of the attacks approached, he and National Geographic decided to commemorate the milestone with a documentary series focused on that aspect.
“We wanted to bring people together to offer gratitude to each other, to answer unanswered questions, to talk about things that maybe they weren’t ready to talk about until now, and also to remember their fallen comrades or friends,” said Jones. “After 25 years, who do they want to meet? What questions have they got? I think we also wanted to tell the story of what many in the 9/11 community call 9/12, that’s the rest of your lives—the journey, and in many cases, the psychological and physical struggles.”
“The challenge was not to impose a story onto anything,” said Jones. “It was to let the story emerge organically in a way that would feel meaningful to our participants. Our job was to really listen to our participants and be guided by what they wanted.”
Jones and his team had vast amounts of archival footage at their disposal, and selecting which footage to use—and how much of the often gruesome details to include—proved to be a delicate balance. There is no footage of the desperate people jumping to their deaths from the burning North Tower, for instance.
“You can’t sanitize history,” said Jones. “You can’t sanitize what happened. But at the same time, you have to be sensitive. The horrible images we all remember of people falling or jumping—those people are someone’s husband, wife, child, or parent, and we have a duty to be sensitive to that. We tried to choose archival material that reflected the experiences our participants were having at that moment.”

Among those featured in 9/11: Reunited are John Paczkowski, George Phoenix, and Jan Demczur. Paczkowski worked on the 67th floor of the North Tower; Phoenix worked on the 74th floor. They had just entered the elevator to get to work that morning when Demczur, a janitor, jumped in at the last minute with his gear. The first plane hit the North Tower as the elevator approached the 65th floor; the car plummeted 15 floors before the emergency brake kicked in.
Trapped in the elevator with smoke pouring in, they managed to pry open the doors only to be faced with a wall. Undaunted, Demczur used his squeegee blade to carve a hole in the plaster so the men could kick through the wall to escape—a process Demczur re-enacts for the series. They ended up in the 50th-floor men’s room and managed to evacuate down the stairwell with other survivors before the North Tower collapsed.
Debbie St. John was taking the subway to work that morning, unaware that the North Tower had been hit. She disembarked to find police officers directing passengers to the street exits. She was walking down the street when the second plane hit the South Tower. So was Stefan Herlacher, a bond trader who worked nearby. He spotted a large piece of wreckage falling toward him and thought he would be hit; the wreckage hit St. John instead.
Herlacher braved the falling debris and panicked people running through the streets to help her and was horrified to find the fragment had cut through her back. He waved down a passing ambulance driver who transported St. John to a hospital. She was the first 9/11 patient admitted and the last to be discharged 18 months later after 50 surgeries. St. John spent years working on her rehabilitation, marrying her fiancé, and having children, but she never forgot the man who saved her life.
“I remember speaking to Debbie on the phone and she said, ‘I’d love to meet Stefan,’” Jones recalled. “I asked, ‘Well, what would you like to do?’ And she said, ‘I want to take him horseback riding.’ Because she had such terrible injuries and couldn’t walk. She just said, ‘I want to show him how far I’ve come thanks to him.’ So we did that.”
Cmdr. Craig Powell was working at the Pentagon when the third plane hit, as was Lt. Col. Marilyn Wills. Wills had been in a meeting and recalled a fireball flying past and singeing her bangs. Trapped in the burning wreckage, Wills led a group of survivors down the corridor, crawling, because she knew there was a window there. The window was bomb-proof and initially wouldn’t open, but Wills and her commanding officer kicked until it popped open. They were on the second floor, so Powell and others on the ground below formed a fireman’s catch as people jumped, one by one.
“You get a second chance, live life.”

It was Powell who caught Wills, one of the last to jump to safety. He initially thought Wills was dead when he passed her off to a teammate for CPR. “In that situation, giving a person CPR [on site], I didn’t hold out much hope,” Powell told Ars, although he later learned she had lived. As for her second-story jump, “That takes a lot of courage,” he added, since it was the equivalent of a fourth-story jump from a regular building. He remembers being in considerable pain the following day—“catching all those people is not easy on your body, and I was inside the room when the ceiling came down”—as well as needing a shower. “I stunk, and it wasn’t BO,” he said. “When the shit hits the fan, so to speak, your body dumps all these endorphins; it’s literally the smell of fear.”
Powell admitted to some apprehension about reuniting with Wills, mostly because of the cameras, but Wills took control of the situation and helped him through it. “I wanted to participate to close the loop,” said Powell. Despite his experiences with active combat, the events of 9/11 hit differently. “It was an attack on American soil,” he said. “It really hit close to home and made me very concerned about the safety of my family.” He was diagnosed with leukemia in 2015, related to his rescue work at the Pentagon that day, but the treatment worked, and he was able to walk his daughter down the aisle for her wedding. “My greatest appreciation is that my kids are alive and I got to watch them grow up,” he said.
Kevin Shea had just joined the FDNY’s Ladder 35 unit, and his shift was ending when the first tower was hit. He volunteered to stay on, and his supervisor agreed, but there was no room for him on the trucks. Shea planned to find his own way to the site and meet up with the team there. But when he reached the staging area, he couldn’t find Ladder 35. His crewmates were filmed walking into the South Tower several minutes before it collapsed—the last time any were seen alive. Shea was standing just outside when the tower collapsed. It’s the last thing he remembers.
Paramedic Al Kim was working triage in the South Tower Marriott lobby and survived the collapse. He recalled hearing beeping alarms sounding in the wreckage—motion sensors worn by all the firefighters that trigger alarms when the wearer stops moving for a prolonged time. Kim started combing through the wreckage looking for survivors when he came across an unconscious and badly injured Shea, and he salvaged medical supplies from one of the burning ambulances to stabilize the firefighter.
When the North Tower started to buckle, he moved Shea to the safety of an underground parking garage nearby, leaving him in the care of another physician who had taken shelter there. Kim never saw Shea after that—until they were reunited for the documentary—and found no other survivors. Shea spent several weeks in the hospital. He had broken his neck in three places and credits Kim’s on-site care not just with saving his life, but with preventing him from becoming quadriplegic.

Bill Spade of FDNY Rescue 5 on Staten Island was on site helping evacuate people from the North Tower when he met John D’Allara of NYPD’s Emergency Services Unit coming down the stairs. They ended up chatting for about 25 minutes about their respective wives and sons; Spade recalled that it was almost as if they were writing their own obituaries. Then everything went eerily quiet, and an evacuation order came through due to fears that the North Tower might collapse. D’Allara was hurrying others through the exit door when it fell. Spade curled up in a ball under falling debris, having lost sight of D’Allara, who was later confirmed dead.
Spade was only one of two Rescue 5 members to survive, but he never forgot D’Allara and contacted his widow, Carol D’Allara, a few years later. But D’Allara’s sons were still too young. Spade, who volunteers at the 9/11 museum in Manhattan, thought the 25th anniversary was the right time to reconnect with the family and let the sons know their father “was thinking of them right to the very end.” D’Allara saved 20 lives that day; his son Nicholas also joined the NYPD and even carries his father’s old badge.
Perhaps the most well-known story—depicted in Oliver Stone’s 2006 film, World Trade Center—is the rescue of Port Authority Police sergeant John McLoughlin. McLoughlin and colleagues William Jimeno and Dominick Pezzulo were on the main concourse between the two towers when the South Tower collapsed, trapping them in the rubble 30 feet underground. Pezzulo was attempting to lift debris off his comrades when the North Tower collapsed 30 minutes later and he was buried by falling debris. McLoughlin was buried up to his elbows, slowly being crushed under the weight, and recalled hearing Pezzulo take his last breath—but not before firing a single shot into the air to alert any rescuers to their location.
Meanwhile, above ground, Scott Fox had joined the rescue effort, despite having retired nine months earlier from Rescue 5, as the FDNY formed makeshift companies out of surviving firefighters. So did John Busching of the NYPD’s Emergency Services Unit. They risked their lives navigating increasingly unstable debris to help dig out first Jimeno (after 13 hours), then McLoughlin (after 22 hours)—a small victory in the midst of tragedy.
McLoughlin was gravely injured and spent six weeks in an induced coma, underwent 27 surgeries during his three weeks in the hospital, and then went through rehabilitation. He still walks with a slight limp. But thanks to Fox, Busching, and several others, “I got to see my kids grow up and meet my grandchildren. How do I thank you for that?”
These are harrowing stories, and it almost seems cruel to ask the survivors to relive that trauma yet again. Per Jones, it helped that there were pre-existing relationships with many of the survivors because of the earlier documentary, which helped establish trust.
“It’s a big deal to ask someone to share the story of the worst day of their lives,” said Jones. “It is emotional, and it is hard for them, but I was astonished by the bravery of the people who participated. They wanted so badly to meet the person who saved them, or the person they saved. In those fleeting moments, amidst all that chaos and horror, these incredible bonds were formed that can never be broken. Many survivors also have a real sense of gratitude and of a duty to keep telling their stories, to remember that day and all the people who didn’t survive.”
Fair warning: 9/11: Reunited is an undeniably powerful documentary series—how could it not be, given the subject matter?—and exquisitely well done. But it’s not an easy watch, and for many who lived through that day, even 25 years might feel a bit too soon to relive those painful memories. (As a former New Yorker who had just moved to DC four months before the attacks, I couldn’t bear to watch more than one episode at a time, and felt pretty wrecked by the end. But nonetheless, I’m glad I persevered.)
“It’s a tough watch, and it is emotional,” said Jones. “But I hope what comes out of the series is a sense that, out of all this tragedy, this was a day when people turned up for each other. There was a human instinct to help each other regardless of what you look like or believe in. People just wanted to help. Personally, I found that incredibly moving.”
9/11: Reunited premieres August 21 on National Geographic. It will be available for streaming on Disney+ and Hulu the following day.

Vieira named new Senegal head coach
- Published
Former Arsenal and France captain Patrick Vieira has been appointed as the new head coach of the Senegal men's national team.
The 50‑year‑old replaces Pape Thiaw, who was sacked in the wake of the country's last‑32 exit at the 2026 Fifa World Cup.
Born in Senegal's capital Dakar, Vieira will now manage the country of his birth, having moved to France aged eight before later winning over 100 caps for Les Bleus and lifting the World Cup in 1998 and the European Championship in 2000.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) said the appointment reflects its "desire to strengthen its high-level technical staff" and is "perfectly aligned" with the nation's sporting ambitions.
Details of Vieria's contract and his starting date in the role are still being discussed.
His first matches in charge of the Teranga Lions are expected to come next month in qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
Vieira joins the West Africans after he left his role as Genoa head coach by mutual consent last November, with the team bottom of Serie A.
He won eight and drew nine of his 26 games during the 2024-25 season to guide the Italian club to safety and a 13th-place finish.
However, he left the club after managing just two wins in 25-26, with both of those victories coming in the Coppa Italia.
During his playing career, midfielder Vieira won three Premier League titles and four FA Cups at Arsenal, as well as silverware with AC Milan, Inter Milan and Manchester City.
He retired in 2011 and became the manager of New York City in 2016 before returning to Europe with Nice and leading them to seventh in Ligue 1 in his first season.
Vieira was sacked in December 2020 and became Crystal Palace manager the following year, guiding the Eagles to 12th in the Premier League and the FA Cup semi-finals in 2021-22.
He was dismissed in March 2023 after a 12-game winless run, before joining RC Strasbourg as their first appointment following a takeover by BlueCo, the company which owns Chelsea. He left Strasbourg by mutual consent in July 2024.
His predecessor Thiaw was at the centre of controversy in January when he ushered his Senegal team off the field when Morocco were awarded a stoppage-time penalty in the 2025 Afcon final.
The players eventually returned after a delay of about 17 minutes before Brahim Diaz's penalty was saved and Pape Gueye scored an extra-time winner.
However, Morocco were declared the winners of the tournament in March when the a Confederation of African Football appeals board overturned the result of the final following Senegal's walk-off.
Senegal have lodged an appeal against that decision with the Court of Arbitration for Sport - with the case due to be heard on 8 October.

NEW DELHI: Former diplomat Navdeep Suri on Sunday said he was facing "trouble establishing his citizenship" during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Punjab, despite having represented India in three countries.In a post on X, Suri shared his experience with the voter roll revision and said he was asked to provide "unspecified documents" to establish that he was an Indian citizen."Sharing my experience with #SIR in Punjab. Went to BLO, submitted Voter ID and Aadhaar card, was assured that everything is in order. Got a message today from a volunteer saying some details don’t match with SIR in 2003!" Suri said.
He said that after speaking to the booth-level officer (BLO), he was asked to collect a notice and return with documents proving his citizenship."Spoke with BLO, was told that I should come and collect the notice. And then come again with unspecified documents that show I am an Indian citizen. Replied that I was not in India in 2003, so they’ve asked for passport as proof," he added.Suri said he had documents apart from his voter ID and Aadhaar, but questioned what the process would mean for ordinary citizens."I happen to have documents other than voter ID and Aadhaar card.
But can’t help asking: If I have trouble establishing my citizenship after representing India in three countries, what’s the fate of the common citizen? Ease of Living, I presume!" he said.Former ambassador Navdeep Sur has served as India's high commissioner to Australia and ambassador to UAE and Egypt.The SIR was first launched in Bihar in June 2025. Following the exercise, more than 60 lakh names, including those of deceased voters, were removed from the electoral rolls. In West Bengal, around 90 lakh voters were deleted from the rolls ahead of the assembly elections.Under the SIR process, voters who were not included in the 2002 or 2003 electoral rolls are required to submit documents linking them to people included in those legacy rolls. The Election Commission of India (ECI) had initially listed 11 acceptable documents, excluding Aadhaar.
Following proceedings in the Supreme Court, the poll panel expanded the list to include Aadhaar as an acceptable document.The Supreme Court has also made observations on the broader constitutional implications of the exercise, stressing that while the ECI has the power to revise electoral rolls, those powers cannot be "untrammelled" and must comply with principles of transparency and natural justice.

While the photo is authentic and shows Trump in Moscow, it is from a visit he took to the Russian capital in 1996, when he was 50. Dubinin was not the nation's ambassador to the U.S. at that time.
Over the years, people have shared an image allegedly showing a 41-year-old Donald Trump during his first visit to Moscow in July 1987. Users' posts claimed Yuri Dubinin, the Soviet Union's ambassador to the U.S., invited Trump to the event. The posts promoted the long-standing claim that the future U.S. president has secret ties with Russia.
The black-and-white picture features Trump standing at a gathering of men in a large room, wearing a tie and overcoat, holding a drink glass and surveying a buffet table.
For example, on Aug. 18, 2026, a Reddit user posted (archived) the image with the caption, "Future reality tv show host, Don Trump, 41 years old, in Moscow at the invitation of Soviet Ambassador to the U.S., Yuri Dubinin. July 1987."
(SteveNtheseagulls accessed via Reddit)
Other users have shared the picture and rumor on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), LinkedIn (archived) and X (archived). Some posts featured additional claims about Trump's plans for a Moscow hotel and his 1988 purchase of the Plaza Hotel in New York, as well as the claim that officials for the KGB — the former Russian secret police and intelligence agency — recruited him as an asset.
Trump's 1987 book "The Art of the Deal" says a Dubinin invitation did take the 41-year-old future president to Moscow for the first time in July 1987, in part to survey sites for potential Trump hotel properties.
Beyond the claim's age and year inaccuracies, no available evidence has credibly and conclusively confirmed Russia secretly recruited Trump as an asset. We previously reported the facts about a former Soviet and Kazakh security official claiming the KGB recruited Trump in 1987, finding no solid proof for the claims.
The Associated Press credited photographer Igor Tabakov with taking the picture in question on Nov. 5, 1996. The AP's caption read, in part, "In this Nov. 5, 1996, file photo, American real estate mogul Donald Trump, left, visits a reception, as he checks out sites in Moscow, Russia, for luxury residential towers."
The rumors presented alongside the photo follow the trail of other Trump and Russia claims, in particular Russian involvement in the 2016 U.S. presidential election. A Republican-led Senate Intelligence Committee report published in 2020 detailed findings on that matter, telling of a "grave counterintelligence threat" and that Trump associates expected to benefit from the Kremlin's help.
This article documents some of the information known about the other claims that have appeared with the picture on social media.
Trump's first visit to Russia in July 1987
In Trump's "The Art of the Deal," the author describes Trump meeting Dubinin at a luncheon, apparently in 1986. The book describes Dubinin's daughter as being familiar with Trump Tower:
A prominent businessman who does a lot of business with the Soviet Union calls to keep me posted on a construction project I'm interested in undertaking in Moscow. The idea got off the ground after I sat next to the Soviet ambassador, Yuri Dubinin, at a luncheon held by Leonard Lauder, a great businessman who is the son of Estee Lauder. Dubinin's daughter, it turned out, had read about Trump Tower and knew all about it. One thing led to another, and now I'm talking about building a large luxury hotel, across the street from the Kremlin, in partnership with the Soviet government. They have asked me to go to Moscow in July.
Later in the book, the author continues, saying Trump flew with his first wife, Ivana Trump, to Moscow on July 4, 1987:
In January 1987, I got a letter from Yuri Dubinin, the Soviet ambassador to the United States, that began: "It is a pleasure for me to relay some good news from Moscow." It went on to say that the leading Soviet state agency for international tourism, Goscomintourist, had expressed interest in pursuing a joint venture to construct and manage a hotel in Moscow. On July 4, I flew with Ivana, her assistant Lisa Calandra, and Norma to Moscow. It was an extraordinary experience. We toured a half dozen potential sites for a hotel, including several near Red Square. We stayed in Lenin's suite at the National Hotel, and I was impressed with the ambition of the Soviet officials to make a deal.
Later that July, Trump reportedly (archived) told the Press of Atlantic City, a New Jersey-based newspaper, that the Moscow trip did not go well, saying he had given up hopes of building a hotel after Russian officials offered only a joint venture with Trump having a minority control of the property.
A Reddit user posted a photo allegedly showing Donald and Ivana Trump standing in Moscow during the July 1987 visit. That post got the city wrong; the photo was taken at St. Petersburg's Palace Square. A Washington Post article captioned the photo as, "Donald Trump and his then-wife, Ivana Trump, visit St. Petersburg in 1987."
(chennai94, accessed via Reddit)
The Plaza Hotel
Users who shared the black-and-white Trump photo captured in 1996 (not 1987, as they claimed) presented the timing of Trump's Plaza Hotel purchase as suspicious.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) alleged, in part, that during Trump's 1987 visit to Russia he received loans from 16 banks and purchased the Plaza Hotel for $407.5 million.
Research in newspaper archives via Newspapers.com located past reporting on that matter.
In 1988, The Business World, a New York Times Magazine publication, reported Trump received a $425 million loan "provided by a consortium of banks led by Citicorp," as well as that he allocated $407.5 million of the total to his purchase of the hotel and 22 Central Park South.
At the time, Trump spokesperson Howard Rubenstein reportedly credited (archived) Trump's interest in purchasing the Plaza Hotel with Trump admiring the property from his office window. "He keeps looking out and seeing things. That's how he got involved in the [Wollman] skating rink, and now this."
In 1995, The New York Times published news of Trump selling the Plaza Hotel to a Saudi Arabian prince and one of Singapore's leading entrepreneurs. According to the article, banks in the U.S. originally lent money to Trump for his 1988 purchase, with banks in Japan holding a mortgage on the property. The story did not mention Moscow or Russia.
Trump's November 1996 Moscow trip
On Nov. 7, 1996, USA Today reported (archived) Trump as telling The Moscow Times about his trip to Russia, "We're looking at building a super-luxury residential tower, which I think Moscow desperately wants and needs."
The newspaper printed the article two days after Tabakov captured the black-and-white photo of Trump and nearly a decade after his first visit to Moscow.
Voice of America and The Washington Post published further reporting providing more details of Trump's past pursuits to expand his real estate empire in Russia.

Hamilton later caught Russell in the closing stages of the race but ran out of time to pass him, his attempts hindered by a late virtual safety car.
McLaren's Lando Norris won the race.
Hamilton, who is 59 points behind championship leader Antonelli, said the race was "definitely frustrating".

India is home to more than 1.4 billion people, thousands of communities, hundreds of languages, and five major language families. Many communities have historically practised endogamy and in some regions, consanguineous marriage. This is both a social and a biological fact with medical consequences. India is not one genetic population. Indians carry a layered inheritance shaped by ancient migration, mixing, isolation, ecology, language, culture and marriage patterns.
Our political map shows States and districts. Our genetic map often shows boundaries shaped by communities that lived near each other but did not always marry into each other. This matters, because genes influence inherited diseases, drug response, disease risk prediction, and the success of screening programmes.
Ancient layers
There is no single Indian genome. The oldest layer of Indian ancestry goes back to early modern humans who reached South Asia tens of thousands of years ago. This ancient ancestry forms the deep foundation of the subcontinent’s population history. Later came other ancestry layers linked to populations associated with the Iranian plateau, the Indus Valley world, Steppe pastoralists, and Tibeto-Burman-speaking groups. These movements were not like a single flood covering the whole land evenly. They came through different doors, at different times, and settled into different social worlds. That is why a Punjabi agrarian group, a Tamil caste group, a tribal population in Central India, a North-Eastern community, and an indigenous island community from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands cannot be treated as genetically identical. Some remote island populations preserve deeply distinctive ancestral lineages because of long isolation. But even here, caution is needed. No living community is a fossil.
Genetics can complicate community pride. A community may have a strong language, faith, identity, regional history, or story of origin. These identities matter. They give people belonging. But genes do not always obey the neat boundaries of culture. A group may preserve a language or ritual for centuries while carrying ancestry from multiple ancient sources. Two neighbouring communities may share a landscape but remain genetically distinct because they did not intermarry. Another two groups may speak different languages but share some older ancestry. Cultural continuity does not require genetic purity. It is a story of movement, mixture, separation, adaptation, and memory.
Marriage and disease patterns
After ancient mixing, many Indian communities became socially closed. Endogamy–marriage within a social group, and consanguinity–marriage between biological relatives, became the norm. Both can increase the chance that two parents carry the same rare recessive disease variant. We inherit two copies of most genes, one from the mother and one from the father, and in recessive diseases, a person with one altered copy remains healthy (called a carrier), while persons with two altered copies get the disease. If two carriers of the same disease-causing variant have a child, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of producing an affected child. This is why a child can be born with a serious genetic disease even when both parents are healthy. The family may have no known disease history, but the risk gene may have travelled silently through generations.
When a small community remains genetically closed for centuries, a rare variant present in an ancestor can become more common among descendants. This is called the ‘founder effect’. This is central to India’s public health future. Sickle cell disease is more common among several tribal populations in Central, Western, and Southern India. This pattern reflects old malaria pressure, population structures, and local history. Thalassaemia and other haemoglobin disorders also show region-specific and community-specific patterns. Some metabolic disorders, neuromuscular conditions, inherited hearing disorders, and rare recessive conditions may cluster in particular groups.
The correct message is that specific populations may carry specific risks, and knowing those risks can prevent suffering. Genetics should not be used to label communities; it should be used to guide screening, counselling, diagnosis, and care.
Testing and counselling
Genetic testing without counselling can do harm. A carrier may wrongly think that they are diseased. A family may blame the mother. A marriage proposal may be rejected because a test result is misunderstood. A whole community may feel stigmatised. This is why genetic counselling is not an ornamental part of modern medicine. It is the ethical bridge between a laboratory report and a family decision. Good counselling explains risk without panic. It tells people that being a carrier is common and usually harmless. It helps couples understand reproductive choices. It protects autonomy. It avoids coercion. Carrier screening, when voluntary and confidential, can help couples know their risks before the birth of an affected child. Newborn screening can identify treatable disorders early. Better rare disease diagnosis can end the long and exhausting journey that many families face, moving from one hospital to another without an answer.
Data gap
India does not yet have a large, deeply characterised, health-linked biobank comparable to resources such as the U.K. Biobank. Such a resource would not merely store DNA. It would connect genetic data with health records, laboratory results, imaging, drug response, and long-term outcomes. It would include India’s internal diversity, not only convenient urban samples. It would also require trust, consent, privacy protection, community engagement, and strong ethical governance.
Large population datasets can help identify new disease mechanisms and molecular targets for new medicines. This gap matters. A genetic risk score for diabetes or heart disease developed mainly in European populations may not work accurately in Indian populations. A drug-response marker common in one ancestry group may be uncommon in another. A rare disease variant important in one Indian community may be missed if reference databases are dominated by non-Indian genomes. Precision medicine will remain imprecise if the populations behind it are mismatched.
Mapping medical futures
India’s genetic mosaic is not merely an ancestry story, but a medical map. It can help prevent inherited diseases, improve newborn screening, guide safer prescribing, diagnose rare disorders earlier, and support drug discovery. But the map must be read carefully. Genetics should not be used to make claims of purity, rank communities, or frighten families. Its value lies in the responsibility to turn knowledge into care.
The Indian genome is not a single national portrait. It is a mosaic made of many tiles some ancient, some recent, some widely shared, and some found in small communities and still barely studied. Medicine now has the tools to read this mosaic. Our task is to read it responsibly, without cultural arrogance, without stigma, and without delay.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com; Dr Veera Rajagopal is a physician-scientist and chief scientific officer at Wellytics, a health and wellness solutions company. veera.scientist@gmail.com)

A senior Madhya Pradesh police officer has become untraceable after being booked over an alleged coercive land deal in Katni district. She has meanwhile approached a local court for anticipatory bail.
Neha Pachisia, who serves as Katni’s City Superintendent of Police, was booked along with Kshitij Raj Barapatre and Maroof Ahmed Hanfi. The case concerns the sale of 2.15 hectares of land belonging to the family of Akash Lodhi, an accused in a murder case.
Pachisia, a former air hostess who later joined the police force, was attending a departmental training programme in Bhopal from August 18 to 20 when the FIR was registered. She allegedly left after learning about the case and has not been traced since.
Barapatre and Hanfi are also untraceable. Police have sealed Pachisia’s office and are searching for the three accused. A Special Investigation Team is likely to be formed.
The Madhya Pradesh government has suspended Pachisia on the directions of Chief Minister Mohan Yadav.
LAND DEAL LINKED TO MURDER CASE
The allegations surfaced after Lodhi secured default bail because police allegedly failed to file a chargesheet in the murder case within the mandatory 90-day period.
After his release, Lodhi complained that his family had been pressured into selling its land while he was in jail. The complaint reached the Chief Minister’s Helpline, prompting senior officers to examine the whole case.
According to the complaint, Lodhi’s father, Ramesh Lodhi, was allegedly made to stay at a house for two days under pressure from Pachisia. He was then taken in a government vehicle to Kanhwara, where the land was registered.
The deal was allegedly finalised for Rs 1.07 crore. The family claimed it received only a cheque for Rs 15 lakh at the time of registration and was promised the remaining Rs 92 lakh within seven days. The balance was allegedly never paid.
The inquiry found that the land was valued at about Rs 82.86 lakh under the government guideline rate. The registration documents reportedly recorded a payment of only Rs 18.20 lakh.
Investigators are also examining an alleged transfer of Rs 15 lakh from Barapatre’s bank account to Hanfi’s. The complaint described Barapatre as Pachisia’s alleged partner and close associate.
PREVIOUS EXTORTION ALLEGATION
Pachisia was already facing separate inquiries over an alleged extortion attempt during a vehicle inspection.
Transport operator Mahendra Jain accused her of demanding Rs 30,000 after one of his trucks was stopped during an inspection on July 21.
Jain alleged that Rs 25,000 was collected in cash at the spot and that the remaining Rs 5,000 was to be paid through the driver the next day. He claimed he was threatened that the truck would be impounded if he refused to pay.
Katni Superintendent of Police Abhinay Vishwakarma ordered a preliminary inquiry after Jain submitted a complaint and supporting evidence.
Pachisia’s driver, constable Keshav Singh, was suspended, and the probe was handed over to Additional Superintendent of Police Kamal Maurya. Three police stations were also removed from Pachisia’s jurisdiction and assigned to another officer.

US military newspaper editor voices censorship fears after being fired
- Published
The editor-in-chief of US military newspaper Stars and Stripes has told the BBC of his concern over censorship a day after being dismissed by the US Department of Defense (DoD) for "insubordination".
"This is a time when we really need to hear what's happening," Erik Slavin said, adding that Pentagon officials appeared to be "less and less inclined to speak on the record".
Slavin says he believes he was fired for having stated in an interview that "in a hypothetical situation, censorship would be a red line". A reporter and the paper's publisher were also sacked.
The Pentagon told the BBC it would not comment. But the sackings come amid tension between the Trump administration and the US media.
Even though partially funded by the Pentagon, Stars and Stripes has been editorially independent - through a congressional mandate and DoD rules.
The newspaper's Middle East reporter Lara Korte said she had also been told she was fired.
Both Slavin and Korte say their dismissals - both for insubordination - relate to an interview they gave to CBS's Sunday Morning programme last month, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
Stars and Stripes reported that publisher Max Lederer was also fired.
He had announced his retirement on Tuesday, saying his understanding of the paper's value and mission differed in "fundamental ways" from the Pentagon's plans for the publication.
Slavin, who has worked for the paper for 21 years, told the PM programme that he had not been given an official explanation for his dismissal - and was considering his response even though he was not allowed to appeal.
He said he did not know if it had to do with his paper's original reporting of conditions aboard USS Abraham Lincoln - the warship which has been deployed in the Gulf for months as the US-Israeli war with Iran continues.
The vessel has spent a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days and family members of sailors aboard have expressed concern about their mental health, with some sailors having reportedly attempted to jump overboard.
But Slavin said his dismissal came in a climate where the Pentagon had not had a press conference since May, and where journalists had refused attempts to interfere with their reporting.
For her part, Korte wrote on X: "It's a shame for the institution and service members, who swore to defend the Constitution and deserve the right to a free and independent press."
The president of the National Press Club, Mark Schoeff Jr, described Slavin's firing as "another brazen attempt by the Pentagon to dictate coverage of the military and should be immediately reversed".
An average of 1.4 million people consume Stars and Stripes's content daily, mostly online, according to CBS.
The paper is still printed outside the US for members of the military in places with unreliable internet access.
In October, leading US news outlets rejected a new policy which barred journalists from entering the building unless they only reported information officially authorised by the DoD.
At the time, the New York Times, Washington Post, CNN and the BBC were among the major outlets which said they would not agree to the new rules.
The Trump administration argued that the changes were needed to protect national security.
In April 2025, a US judge ordered the administration to restore the Associated Press's access to presidential events after it was blocked in a dispute over the term "Gulf of America".
A few months prior, the White House broke with tradition and took control of the press pool which covers the US presidency.

UK, Canada and Australia condemn Israel for refusing criminal probe into aid worker killings in Gaza
- Published
The UK, Canada and Australia have described as "shameful" Israel's decision not to launch a criminal investigation into strikes on a World Central Kitchen (WCK) convoy in Gaza in 2024, which killed seven humanitarian workers.
The victims were three British nationals, a Pole, an Australian, a Canadian and a dual US-Canadian citizen.
A joint statement by the three foreign ministries said: "The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf."
Earlier, Israel's ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, defended the decision, saying "there was no criminal intention" and therefore "no criminal responsibility".
The statement said that on 1 April 2024, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) fired on the WCK convoy as it was delivering food to civilians in Gaza.
"In the more than two years since, we have been pressing for Israel to swiftly and thoroughly consider the case and hold those responsible to account," it said.
The three countries said the fact that Israel's announcement came on World Humanitarian Day, "while the world honoured the courage and sacrifice of humanitarians, was particularly egregious".
It also said the WCK attack was only "one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability", as Gaza remains "the deadliest place to deliver aid", with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025.
It urged Israel to comply with its obligations under international humanitarian law and do more to ensure that humanitarian staff can carry out their work safely.
'Serious failures'
In its statement on Wednesday, the IDF said the presence of an armed guard with the convoy had not been flagged to it before the convoy set off, and that he was falsely identified as a Hamas fighter. It also accused the convoy of deviating from the route co-ordinated with the military.
Notwithstanding "serious failures" in the process that led to the killings, "the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct," the IDF said.
Prior to the statement by the three countries, Australia summoned Hillel Newman. Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said her country was "outraged" by the Israeli government's decision.
She also said there were still many "unanswered questions" about the strikes, including why, if the first strike on the convoy was "a catastrophic error", two further strikes followed just minutes apart.
Poland's foreign ministry also said on Thursday that it was "very disappointed" and had summoned Israel's ambassador in Warsaw.
The founder of World Central Kitchen, Jose Andres, described the decision as "wrong" and "painful for all of us", demanding an independent commission to investigate.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has not publicly responded to the latest statement from the UK, Australia and Canada, but he previously said that the military had "unintentionally" killed the volunteers.
The statement came after a harsh exchange of words between UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar over Israel's plans to open tenders for the construction of about 1,200 settlement homes in a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank.
Israeli settlements are illegal under international law and plans to build in the so-called E1 area - east of Jerusalem - have long been internationally condemned.
Miliband condemned the publication of the tender as "an unacceptable and destructive act", and called on Israel to "halt E1 plans immediately, retract the tender and stop all settlement expansion".
In response, Saar said on social media that he rejected "outright" Miliband's statement.
"The Jewish people have the right to live throughout the Land of Israel, just as the British have the right to live in London and throughout the United Kingdom," he wrote.
While the IDF had decided not to launch a criminal investigation into the strikes on the WCK convoy, it announced in the same statement that it would carry out a criminal investigation into the killing by Israeli forces of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab and six of her relatives in Gaza in 2024.
It also said it would similarly investigate the killing of 15 Palestinians, including medics and a UN worker, in March 2025. Their bodies were found buried in shallow graves a week later next to crushed vehicles.

As USS Lincoln heads home, mental health experts tally the stressors of life at sea
The USS Abraham Lincoln — which has been participating in U.S. military operations in the war with Iran — is now on its way home. The roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard that ship have spent a grueling nine months at sea with little relief.
Reports have emerged of deteriorating conditions — and of deteriorating mental health, including apparent attempts by crewmembers to jump overboard. The Navy has not confirmed those reports and NPR has not independently verified them. "A small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life," Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said in a statement last week.
Experts say while the physical circumstances are difficult, a lack of careful and consistent messaging from leadership at the highest levels also contributed to the crews' mental distress.
The USS Lincoln is like a small city, according to Armen Kurdian, a retired U.S. Navy captain who served aboard the aircraft carrier in 2005. The labor aboard the carrier, he says, can be uniquely physical and difficult.
" It takes a toll on your body," says Kurdian. "The plane captains are out there on the flight deck — you know, these 18-, 19-, 20-year-olds lugging these 100-pound chains on their backs in 120-degree weather."
He describes dehydration and exhaustion as pilots have to take off and land on the carriers, sometimes at night and in bad weather, and "then just being mentally prepared to go fly because lives are at stake."
In the off-hours, Kurdian says there is little to no privacy, with people sleeping in crowded quarters.
While difficult, these conditions can be bearable, he adds. But experts say once uncertainty is thrown into this equation, it can push people to their mental brink.
Jack Stuster is a retired behavioral scientist who spent decades studying human performance.
"In conditions of isolation and confinement," says Stuster, "one of the worst things that you could do to the person is to tell them they're gonna come home at a certain time, and then you say, 'No. It's gonna be delayed.'"
Return is overdue
The Abraham Lincoln's deployment was originally scheduled to end in May.
In addition to the Navy, Stuster worked with NASA and scientists operating in small groups in places like Greenland, where return flights home were often canceled at the very last moment — even after their would-be passengers had dragged their duffle bags right up to the flight line.
" People have described to me going out there for the third time … only to be told that it wasn't gonna happen," says Stuster, which caused them "to break down in tears."
Then there's the issue of duration. A three-month deployment is ideal, says Stuster, or even six. At nine months, he says, things start to become untenable.
Dr. Phillip Hunt was for years a Navy physician who deployed on several submarine missions. His background is in emergency medicine, but Hunt says in the Navy much of what he treated was mental health. " I was kind of the father confessor, psychologist, what have you," says Hunt.
With a crew of 5,000 people on a ship, Hunt says it's inevitable that some people will struggle with mental health — even in the best of deployment conditions. "You'd have guys getting anxious. You'd have guys getting depressed."
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says reports of poor conditions aboard the Lincoln are overstated. President Trump recently called the deployment "not nearly long enough."
Hunt says a lack of certainty or reassurance from leadership at the highest levels can trickle down to impact everyone's mental well-being. "Denial of this unit's deteriorating operational conditions is highly detrimental to the crew's morale," says Hunt. "The result can include anger, anxiety, or eventually mental exhaustion and depression."
Hunt says he blames leadership at the highest levels for the lack of recognition of this hardship.
" I just, I feel so badly for that crew. It's just tragic," says Hunt. "Just thinking about them almost brings me to tears."
If you or someone you know is struggling with their mental health, please call or text the number 9-8-8 to connect with a counselor.

This affordable fix may be all you need to improve earbud sound quality
Improved noise canceling and punchier bass? Yes, please.
Apple's courageous decision to drop the 3.5mm headphone jack in 2016 seems to have worked in the company's favor. The AirPods are by far the most popular truly wireless earbuds globally. Competition has also caught up in terms of sound quality and features, and it's generally pretty difficult to end up with a bad pair of wireless earbuds these days. With most higher-end offerings touting active noise cancellation, lossless audio codecs and customizable EQ settings, the purchase decision often comes down to comfort and ecosystem benefits.
Most truly wireless earbuds ship with ear tips that are made of silicone. It's a material that's cheap to manufacture and flexible enough to accommodate a wide range of ear shapes. Manufacturers often throw in two more pairs of ear tips in different sizes to maximize the chances of users finding a fit that works. Unfortunately, human ears come in a vast range of shapes and sizes. In fact, a multi-ethnic study involving more than 1,400 people found that the human ear is a reliable biometric identifier, not unlike a fingerprint.
Besides not providing a secure and comfortable fit, the wrong set of ear tips can also negatively impact sound quality. Unlike over-ear headphones that create a wider seal around your ears, earbuds rely almost entirely on the ear tips to form a proper seal. If it's not a good fit, sound can leak out, and outside noise can get in. This results in weaker bass and noticeably poorer noise cancellation performance.
Foam ear tips are the solution
Silicone ear tips are easier to clean and can last virtually as long as the actual earbuds do, but they shouldn't be your first choice if you're looking for the best comfort. There are a handful of renowned third-party manufacturers that sell foam ear tips. If you use memory foam pillows or insoles, you know what I'm getting at. Unlike silicone ear tips that come in a few preset sizes at best, foam tips expand to match the shape of your ear canal and create a much better seal.
I'm one among the lucky souls who don't have a problem with how most earbuds fit. When I picked up a pair of AirPods Pro 2, though, I decided to go all out and replace the stock silicone ear tips with a set of memory foam alternatives. The first thing I noticed was how much of a better fit they provided. I was no longer adjusting my AirPods every few minutes to keep them in place. The bigger difference, however, was how much more punchy the bass felt.
Now, switching over to foam tips won't magically make your earbuds sound better, but by minimizing sound leakage, they can help music sound fuller and more impactful without you having to crank the volume all the way up. Since foam ear tips create a tighter seal, they dramatically improve passive noise isolation. Not only does this help improve the performance of active noise cancellation when you turn it on, but it also makes it so you don't have to rely on ANC as much in the first place.
How to pick the right earbud tips
Comply and Sonicfoam are two reputable brands you can shop from, but make sure you check compatibility with your earbuds first. For instance, AirPods feature a proprietary snap-fit mechanism that requires a specific type of ear tip. Though Engadget has not formally tested them, I can personally vouch for the quality of the memory foam ear tips that Sonicfoam sells — I've been using them for over two years now.
Foam ear tips have their fair share of downsides, though. For starters, they wear out rather quickly. If you use your wireless earbuds every day, you can expect your foam ear tips to last around two to three months, although they start losing their ability to fully expand well before that. They also tend to get dirty and attract dust more easily than silicone tips.
Pricing can range from $10 to $40, depending on the brand and the number of ear tips included in the package. Once you've found a pair of foam ear tips that work well for you, it's worth checking if the brand sells refill packs that contain only your preferred size. This way, you don't spend money on smaller or larger ear tips that you'll never use.
Foam ear tips also make it quite clear when it's time for a replacement. If you pinch them and they don't expand as well, they're not going to create the same tight seal in your ear canal. Ideally, you'd also replace them when you notice any visible deformation or damage. A final helpful tip: It's best if you clean them regularly. I've made it a habit to give mine a quick wipe before each use since any buildup of earwax or skin oils can leave them smelling less than pleasant over time.

- The claim that U.S. President Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp is a cancer survivor cannot be independently verified by Snopes. Because Snopes looks for primary sourcing and evidence to rate our claims, we are leaving this claim unrated.
- The rumor stems from social media posts criticizing a senator for referencing Harp while mocking Trump in August 2026. These posts said Harp was a cancer survivor, while other posts argued there's no proof of that claim.
- The claim that Harp had cancer is based on her own accounts of her experience battling a rare bone cancer, which she wrote and spoke about in 2019 and 2020. In Harp's account, she was told she'd have to wait for certain treatment options to be approved before she could continue treatment after failing two chemotherapies and being rejected from a clinical trial for an investigational drug. Harp credits Trump's right-to-try law, signed during his first term, for enabling her to be treated with an FDA-approved immunotherapy drug that wasn't approved for use in treating her cancer.
- Based on the available evidence, much of Harp's experience, as told by her, is realistic and believable. Bone cancers in general are rare and often resistant to chemotherapies. Immunotherapy drugs, which are still relatively new and frequently researched, are a promising possible treatment for many bone cancers. Many such treatments are not yet approved for use for treating bone cancers because the cancers are rare and difficult to treat.
- However, there are a few details, largely in her descriptions of cause and effect, that could potentially be inaccurate, based on our research. For example, she credits Trump's right-to-try law for saving her life, when her description of the drug that finally made a difference for her better aligns with a drug that she would've been able to access through an FDA system that has existed for decades.
- Snopes reached out to the White House by email to ask if it could share details about Harp's history with cancer that could potentially be verifiable, such as the name of the drug used in her treatment. The White House did not answer our questions.
In August 2026, news reporting about one of U.S. President Donald Trump's aides, Natalie Harp, intensified, particularly after Sen. Jon Ossoff , D-Ga., referenced her in criticism of Trump, drawing increased attention to the once little-known aide.
Many conservative figures then criticized Ossoff for referencing Harp, who they said was a cancer survivor, in his attacks on Trump. For example, one X post (archived) said, "Harp is a 35-year-old cancer survivor who works in the White House. Ossoff chose to make her part of an anti-Trump attack because he thought it would score points with the Democrat base and generate attention."
The claim surfaced elsewhere on X (archived) and Facebook (archived). Other social media posts (archived) cast doubt on whether Harp ever really had cancer. Some Snopes readers searched the site or sent emails asking whether it was true that Harp was a cancer survivor.
Harp first rose to fame by sharing her account of suffering from Stage 2 bone cancer and how a Trump-signed "right-to-try" law apparently saved her life. Snopes cannot independently verify Harp's account and medical history, so we're unable to rate this claim true or false.
However, we can compare the details of Harp's account with the current medical research available to get a sense of which details, if any, may sound unrealistic in her story.
Harp's account
Harp's claims about her history with bone cancer came from a LinkedIn blog post she wrote and an interview with Fox News in June 2019, as well as a speech she gave at the Republican National Convention in August 2020.
The LinkedIn post, her earliest public description of her experience with cancer, didn't give any details about the specific cancer she was diagnosed with except that it was rare.
She shared slightly more detail two days later in her appearance on Fox News. Brian Kilmeade, co-host of "Fox & Friends," opened the interview (0:04) by saying Harp had Stage 2 cancer. Harp went on to say her illness was terminal (2:10), Kilmeade Said Harp had Stage 2 of a rare bone cancer (2:18) and Harp confirmed she was "the youngest person in this rare bone cancer" she had (2:52).
The cancer diagnosis is not where Harp has begun any of her accounts, however; instead, she has frequently highlighted a medical error she suffered before that.
"On November 9, 2015 — a year to the day Donald Trump would win the presidency — a nurse mixed up my IV with the deadly substance of sterile water leaving me housebound and searching for care," Harp wrote on LinkedIn. She said her physicians offered her medications for managing pain and even Death With Dignity instead of diagnosing her condition.
On Fox News, she said it took two years for doctors to figure out what was wrong with her. Harp also said in that interview that this medical error is one that "no one has survived" (0:52). At the Republican National Convention, Harp said (0:38) she was a victim of a "notoriously deadly medical error," but survived "only to be diagnosed with a rare and terminal bone cancer." Harp then presented the care she was offered afterwards, which is in contrast to her other accounts in which she described receiving these offerings prior to diagnosis of the cancer.
Notably, the web article Fox News published alongside the video of the interview said Harp "has battled stage 2 bone cancer for most of her life," even though the above descriptions make it sound like her struggles with the cancer developed in the several years prior to that interview.
In all of her accounts, Harp described the available chemotherapies failing to address her cancer and being denied participation in clinical trials. At the Republican National Convention, she claimed (1:22) that no one wanted her in their clinical trials because she'd "make them look bad" after failing the chemotherapies.
Harp said her doctor told her she'd have to suffer through symptoms for either several more months (LinkedIn) or more than a year (Fox News interview, 2:43) for the next round of FDA approvals for the clinical trial drugs she was denied.
She wrote that her doctor did not tell her she had other options, so she went to another doctor who was willing to try a different approach: prescribing an FDA-approved immunotherapy drug for an unapproved use. She credits that experimental treatment for her recovery, and Trump's Right to Try Act for that treatment even though she acknowledged that some may argue it was repetitive of existing law.
Snopes emailed the White House to ask if it could share more verifiable details about Harp's experience, such as which unapproved drug was used in her treatment, but 
Right-to-try law
The right-to-try law Harp credits for saving her life essentially allows patients to access drugs without FDA approval for treatment in specific circumstances. According to the law's text, an eligible patient can consent to the use of an "eligible investigational drug" that has completed a Phase 1 clinical trial and "has not been approved or licensed for any use." The drug manufacturer is allowed to decide it won't permit the patient to access the unapproved drug.
A contradiction between the law and Harp's story immediately jumps out. The right-to-try law applies specifically to drugs that have not been approved for any use, but Harp claimed her lifesaving treatment was an FDA-approved immunotherapy drug being used for an unapproved use.
Such a drug could still theoretically be used to treat Harp's condition under a different process that existed prior to the Right to Try Act: expanded access. Expanded access also allows patients who have exhausted all other treatment options for a serious or life-threatening condition to use an investigational drug instead. Investigational drugs eligible for use in expanded access have not been approved by the FDA "for their specific use."
FDA researchers wrote that the agency has been facilitating access to investigational drugs since the 1970s, and regulations describing the pathways to accessing these unapproved drugs have existed since 1987.
A chart by Triage Cancer, a nonprofit organization focused on practical and legal issues that may affect cancer patients, both expanded access and right-to-try require a physician and the drug manufacturer to approve a request to use an unapproved drug. Expanded access also requires approval from the Institutional Review Board and the FDA, which right to try does not.
FDA data says that between fiscal years 2019 and 2023, the FDA approved anywhere between 97.1% to 100% of expanded access requests, depending on the year and the type of request.
Harp's description of events suggests that her physician, and potentially drug manufacturers, would not approve her request for expanded access. Such obstacles would also to be an issue for Harp under the right-to-try law; based on her story, it sounds like Harp became able to use an unapproved drug treatment because she got a new doctor, not because of the new law.
Comparing Harp's story to actual research
While Harp's story may be vague on specifics such as names and dates, it does have enough details to compare it to reality.
In 2008, the Pennsylvania Patient Safety Authority reported that bags of sterile water were being mistaken for IV solutions because of similar appearance, and that these mistakes were capable of causing serious harm to patients, sometimes even killing them.
It's unclear whether Harp suggested that such a medical error led to the development of her cancer, but in any case, Snopes could find no evidence that such a mistake could cause cancer. According to the Pennsylvania Patient Safety Authority, the IV error is dangerous is because sterile water can cause red blood cells to break down too soon.
Based on the report's description of a patient who survived the sterile water injection, others have survived the medical error that Harp claimed no one else had survived. The less-extreme version of Harp's claim, in which she calls the error "notoriously deadly," is accurate.
Bone cancers are rare in general, and there are many different specific kinds of bone cancers. The American Cancer Society even suggests seeking out clinical trials because these cancers are rare and difficult to treat.
In fact, the University College London wrote that bone cancers are frequently resistant to chemotherapy. The American Cancer Society says that "in recent years" researchers have developed non-chemo drugs, including immunotherapy drugs, to help treat some bone cancers.
The Cancer Research Institute says that while surgery is often the main treatment method for early-stage bone cancers, immunotherapies may be used in treating more advanced or far-reaching forms of the cancer.
The FDA first approved an immune checkpoint inhibitor, the kind of immunotherapy drug often used for treating these cancers, in 2011, according to the Osteosarcoma Institute. (Osteosarcoma is a type of bone cancer.) The institute says no new treatment options for the cancer have been approved in 40 years.
The research above does suggest that much of Harp's story about her battle with cancer is plausible. Bone cancers are rare, so it's expected that whatever kind of bone cancer she'd have would be rare itself. Many bone cancers are resistant to chemotherapy, which would explain why Harp failed such treatments twice.
It also makes sense that the unapproved treatment she and her doctor tried would be an immunotherapy drug. Cancer research organizations point to immunotherapy drugs as a promising avenue for treating some forms of bone cancer. New immunotherapy treatments are still emerging today, and so it wouldn't be surprising if the drug wasn't yet approved 10 years ago.
On top of all of that, the rarity of bone cancers can make it difficult for emerging treatments to be tested with large enough sample sizes in trials to quickly move through the approval process.

Kalyan: Barely days after an alleged assault on a doctor and nurse at Shastrinagar Hospital in Dombivli another incident of violence against a medical professional has been reported from the Bhanu Jyot Hospital in Kalyan East, triggering concern among doctors and hospital staff over their safety.
Relative of patient accused of assault
According to information available, a doctor was allegedly assaulted inside his cabin by a relative accompanying a patient. The incident was captured on CCTV, and the Kolsewadi police have registered a case and initiated an investigation.
The incident occurred when a patient visited Bhanu Jyot Hospital accompanied by a relative. Dr Yogendra Jaiswal was reportedly explaining the patient's condition and the proposed treatment when the relative allegedly became agitated and entered into an argument with the doctor.
CCTV captures alleged assault
As the situation began to escalate, the patient reportedly intervened and asked the relative to leave the cabin. However, according to the complaint, the same person returned to the doctor's cabin a short while later and allegedly assaulted Dr Jaiswal.
The sudden altercation created panic inside the hospital. Hospital staff intervened and managed to bring the situation under control. The entire incident was reportedly captured on CCTV cameras installed inside the hospital.
The Kolsewadi police have taken cognisance of the incident and begun investigating the circumstances leading to the alleged assault. Police are also examining the CCTV footage as part of the probe.
Rising concern among medical fraternity
The latest incident has once again brought the issue of security in hospitals into focus. The alleged assault comes at a time when doctors and healthcare workers in the Kalyan-Dombivli region are already expressing concern over incidents of violence at medical facilities.
Doctors say that confrontations over treatment, waiting time and other issues can escalate rapidly, leaving medical professionals vulnerable to physical attacks while performing their duties.
The latest incident has also renewed demands from the medical fraternity for stronger security arrangements at hospitals and prompt action against those who attack healthcare workers.
With repeated incidents being reported from hospitals, doctors are now questioning whether they can focus entirely on treating patients without having to worry about their own safety.
The incident has added to the growing debate over whether hospitals, particularly those handling patients and their relatives round the clock, have adequate security mechanisms in place to protect doctors and other medical staff.

University dean’s cautionary words come as Beijing is increasingly on guard about historical views at odds with the official line
China’s secondary school students are dropping history as an exam subject, a trend that could leave the public more vulnerable to distorted narratives in the future, an academic at a top university has warned.
“History education in secondary schools is an important means of preserving historical, cultural, ethnic and national identity,” said Liu Linhai, dean of the school of history at Beijing Normal University, in a commentary in the state-backed China Teacher Paper.
“Its current weakening and even marginalisation should be a matter of urgent concern for policymakers, who should take coordinated and effective measures to address the structural problems affecting the subject,” Liu wrote.
Authorities in China have become increasingly alert to challenges to the orthodox view of the country’s history.
On Thursday, a newspaper published by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences ran two front-page pieces framing pseudo-history as a “new variant” of historical nihilism.

Only four in 10 healthcare facilities worldwide meet basic sanitation standards for accessible and usable toilets, the United Nations said on Tuesday (August 18, 2026), while 11% have no sanitation services at all.
In a report, the UN’s health and children’s agencies said only 40% of healthcare facilities last year had toilets that adequately met the needs of patients and staff, including people with limited mobility.
The report from the World Health Organization and UNICEF for the first time provided global estimates of basic sanitation services in healthcare settings.
Its 2025 estimate found significant gaps in access to basic sanitation standards, which it said required usable facilities including at least one toilet dedicated to staff, at least one sex-separated toilet with menstrual hygiene facilities and at least one toilet accessible for people with limited mobility.
Relying on data from 70 countries, the report showed that sanitation levels in healthcare facilities varied widely between regions, with only 23% of facilities in sub-Saharan Africa providing basic services, compared to 55% in central and southern Asia.
It found there was no sanitation service at more than one in 10 health facilities globally, serving 936 million people.
In addition to sanitation, the report estimated access in healthcare facilities to water, hygiene, environmental cleaning and waste management.
It found that an estimated 85% of facilities last year had basic water services, 72% had basic hygiene services and 71% basic healthcare waste management services.
Only 59% of facilities meanwhile met basic so-called environmental cleaning standards, which require both cleaning protocols and trained cleaning staff and is core to infection prevention and control.
A full 18% of facilities, serving around 1.5 billion people, met neither of the environmental cleaning requirements, said the report, which for this category relied on data from 54 countries.
The situation is particularly dire in poorer countries.
The environmental cleaning standard was met by just 24% of facilities in the world’s least-developed nations.
