What About the New Kindle Scribes?
Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There's now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.
All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, slightly slimmer form factor, and updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.
Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities, but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.
Accessories for Easier Reading
If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.
Cases and Covers
Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs.
Looking for more accessory ideas? Check out my guide to all of the best Kindle accessories. Also, don't forget that if the Kids' editions come with cases, so if you're buying one of those, you won't need a case.
About Those Older Kindles
Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.
Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.
Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.
Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.
Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less.
Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.
Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.
FAQs
Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?
As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon's services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.
The following Kindle devices are impacted:
- Kindle 1st Generation
- Kindle 2nd Generation
- Kindle DX
- Kindle DX Graphite
- Kindle Keyboard (3rd Generation)
- Kindle 4
- Kindle Touch
- Kindle 5
- Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation
What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?
Have an old Kindle lying around? Are you looking at a used one for sale? If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.
Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation.
How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?
If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.
If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines.
If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:
- Get a library card for your local branch.
- Check your branch's website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
- Download directly to your Kindle library. They'll automatically be removed when they're due back.
If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned.
What Else Can a Kindle Do?
Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.
Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations, and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.
While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too.
When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.
Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.
There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches.
How Do You Update a Kindle?
When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when it's connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you're on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it's not on the latest software version, you'll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.
What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?
Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.
Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?
The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days.
You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price.
Are Kindles Good for Students?
Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.

De Zerbi learns cash alone cannot fix Spurs' losing mentality
- Published
Roberto De Zerbi may have spent close to £400m by the time his Tottenham Hotspur rebuild is complete – but it took just his side's first Premier League game of the season to prove all the money in the world is no guaranteed cure for a losing mentality.
De Zerbi, by his own admission, confirmed his role was more psychologist than coach when he was given seven games to keep Spurs in the top-flight following his appointment in March.
He achieved that feat, but only just as Spurs survived with victory against Everton on the final day.
The Italian has been handed vast funds for a host of new players to ensure Spurs do not suffer a repeat of the nightmare campaign.
This dreadful defeat was not the start he or the Spurs power brokers envisaged.
For all the change in transfer strategy and personnel, the manner in which Spurs capitulated at the first sign of pressure as they were run ragged by Brentford provided gruesome evidence that you need more than a huge transfer fund to give a team mental strength.
De Zerbi may feel he has addressed some of the ills in a squad that has finished 17th in the Premier League two seasons in succession. However, he will have to turn psychologist once more as the new Spurs looked like the old Spurs as they were dismantled in the west London sunshine.
He pointed to a lack of physical conditioning of players who had been at the World Cup or were newcomers, but this did not excuse the lack of basics, shortage of resilience and the fact Brentford were so superior in every area.
De Zerbi told BBC Sport's Match of the Day: "Bad game. We lost and suffered the difference in the duels. It was the key of this game. We didn't fight in the right way. Maybe credit to them because it's the best quality Brentford have.
"Our physical condition was not in the right level for all players because many came later after the World Cup and there were many new players in the squad and first XI. But we have to analyse this game better because we can't play this way in this type of game."
The day started with Spurs fans bursting with optimism in one corner of The Gtech Community Stadium, welcoming their new recruits raucously. It ended with those same players applauding a large swathe of empty seats, some vacating as early as the 49th minute when Michael Kayode put The Bees 3-0 up.
It could have been even worse had the normally reliable Igor Thiago not struck the post with a penalty, but that was no consolation for Spurs or De Zerbi on what was a chastening day.
Rock superstar Jon Bon Jovi was an interested spectator at The Gtech Stadium - and Spurs gave him enough material for several albums worth of sad power ballads as they started badly and went into rapid decline.
De Zerbi gave debuts to four of his new acquisitions in Andrew Robertson, Marcos Senesi, Jan Paul van Hecke and Sandro Tonali. They will feel the only way is up because they were at rock bottom here. None of them distinguished themselves, although neither did any others.
Italian midfielder Tonali cost £100m from Newcastle United, but was utterly outshone and overpowered by Brentford's record buy Mamadou Sangare, who was the game's outstanding performer.
Tonali's only memorable contribution was a first-half attempt on goal that flew horribly skywards, prompting the inevitable suggestion from Brentford supporters that Spurs had wasted their money.
Matheus Fernades, at £85m from West Ham United, came on as a substitute, while Savinho and possibly Omar Marmoush will add strength, but it was the lack of heart and fight that will be De Zerbi's biggest concern.
From the first minute, Spurs' brave new world hauntingly resembled the old one as they cracked under the first sign of pressure, Brentford sensing their weakness as they hunted down a side they clearly felt could be exposed.
And how Spurs were exposed.
Brentford should have been ahead before Keane Lewis-Potter broke the deadlock after 12 minutes, the contest effectively over when Vitaly Janelt doubled their lead before half-time.
De Zerbi cut a frustrated, animated figure as he tried to enliven Spurs, but heads were down, physical challenges lost, desperation their trademark, with not the slightest indication of any self-belief that they might recover the situation.
Conor Gallagher and Lucas Bergvall did not return after the half-time interval, although they might justifiably point out others could have accompanied them.
De Zerbi somehow needs to get into the heads of these Spurs players to give them strength and steel. That is not something that can be achieved with a wave of the chequebook.
For context, this is Spurs' first game of the Premier League season and many teams with aspiration and ambition have had nightmare starts.
This, however, looked like the worrying continuation of a pattern of defeat and despair.
That pattern has cast a cloud over Spurs' recent seasons, along with De Zerbi's predecessors Ange Postecoglou, who at least won the Europa League, then Thomas Frank and – in his "blink and you'll miss it" reign – Igor Tudor.
De Zerbi added: "I am surprised for the result and performance. I knew we were not in the right condition. We can't find an excuse. I am sorry for the result and performance. We are starting a new project and we couldn't find the principle.
"Marcos Senesi, Jan Paul van Hecke and Sandro Tonali are not in the best physical condition. We knew that before the game. We have to improve on that and many other things like organisation and pressing."
More signings may be on the way, but De Zerbi said: "I don't want the excuse that the first XI was not enough to compete and get a result. Brentford's spirit on the pitch was great, it has to be the right example for us."
New faces are all very well, but this loss showed Spurs problems run deeper than fresh personnel. De Zerbi must banish the ghosts of two seasons littered with losses. And quickly.
He must not change his squad. He must change a culture in which defeats like this have become commonplace.

Penguin bird flu vaccination drive passes 1,000-dose milestone on Phillip Island
In short:
About 1,000 little penguins on Phillip Island have now received a dose of the H5N1 bird flu vaccine.
Authorities are planning to vaccinate 5,000 of the island's 40,000-bird population.
The birds require two shots of the vaccine several weeks apart.
The rush to protect Victoria's little penguin population against bird flu continues, with about 1,000 birds having received their first doses of a H5N1 vaccine.
Authorities plan to vaccinate 5,000 little penguins at Phillip Island and St Kilda, with hundreds of the birds being rounded up and given a shot each night for the past week.
Last night, a team at the Phillip Island Nature Park, south-east of Melbourne, vaccinated their 1,000th bird, on the same day as the deadly strain that has killed hundreds of birds was detected in a long-nosed fur seal in South Australia, the first time it's been confirmed as crossing over to Australia's mammal population.
Phillip Island is home to about 40,000 little penguins, making it the world's largest colony.
Worst-case modelling suggests a major bird flu outbreak could kill between 8,000 and 16,000 of the birds.
About 10,000 doses of the vaccine are needed for the two-shot program.
Environment Minister Jaclyn Symes says little penguins that feature in Phillip Island's nightly "parade" will have now had their first dose, with the team to recapture the birds to deliver the second dose in three to four weeks.
"We know that bird flu is here, we know we can't stop it but we want to put the penguin colony in the best possible place to ensure that they are protected as much as possible," Ms Symes said ahead of last night's effort.
Ms Symes said the vaccine would increase the antibodies each bird had but it remained unknown whether it would stop them from catching the flu.
"It will provide a level of protection but importantly, it may provide a level of ability to recover from the disease if it does catch it,"
Vaccination program thought to be world first
Phillip Island Nature Parks reserve manager Ben Thomas said the team had been out late each night over the past week, starting at the quieter end of the penguin parade ground before focusing on the busier western end of the parade on Sunday night.
He said as the penguins came up the beach, the team trapped them in an enclosure, then moved them to smaller pens to deliver the vaccine.
"They are feisty little animals; you do go home with a few bites and scratches," he said.
"We're trying to process them as quickly as we can but as gentle and safe as we can to make sure these penguins are happy and healthy."
Despite taking time to ensure careful handling, Mr Thomas said there was a sense of urgency among the team.
"[The penguins] do live shoulder to shoulder so once [the flu] arrives, it may spread quite quickly through the colony."
Phillip Island Nature Parks CEO Catherine Basterfield said it was the first time the team had attempted anything like this.
She said she also believed it was the first mass vaccination program of this scale in the world.
"It is really tricky and penguins are difficult to handle," Ms Basterfield said.
"Our team took some time earlier in the week in testing, planning, trialling different methods of being able to roll out this vaccination program."
But she said the team was being helped by the habitual characteristics of the little penguins, which return to the same beach most nights, mostly waddle up the same pathway, return to the same burrow every night, and are used to human interaction.
Ms Basterfield said the team was confident they would be able to re-capture the same birds in three weeks' time to deliver the crucial follow-up dose.
"This is the world's largest little penguin colony so in terms of the species it's an amazing opportunity to really protect this stronghold."

The oldest iPhone model you can trade-in with Apple is older than you'd think
Even old Apple devices you haven’t touched in years could still get you some credit towards a new phone.
If you've ever bought an iPhone directly from Apple, you've likely seen the option to trade in an older device. By sending the company your previous phone, you get credit towards your purchase. If you don't have plans to use your old phone, this is a good way to reduce the cost of an upgrade.
The trade-in value Apple offers varies by how new the device is, as you'd expect. However, you might be surprised at how old of a phone you can trade in and still get some credit. Spend a few minutes digging out that old phone sitting in a drawer, as it could have some value. Vintage phones won't be a ton, but with how expensive iPhones are nowadays, any little bit is appreciated.
It's a good idea to learn how the official iPhone trade-in program works in case you've never used it before, as well as knowing the other options you have to get cash from an old gadget.
The oldest iPhone you can trade in with Apple
Apple's Trade In page is where you check the trade-in value of various devices. For iPhones, the oldest model you can trade in and still get credit for is the iPhone 8, which came out in 2017. Upon picking a phone from the list, you'll need to indicate if the phone is in Good or Damaged condition. Your phone is still considered as Good even with minor scratches or dents. In this shape, Apple offers a mere $35 for the iPhone 8.
If you choose the latter option, you'll be asked several more questions about what is specifically wrong with the phone. But even if you indicate that a damaged iPhone is functional and its body/display are in good shape, you may not get anything for an older model.
2017's lineup also included the iPhone 8 Plus and then-premium iPhone X. Those with an iPhone 8 Plus can get $40 of trade-in credit if the device is in good shape, or $10 if it has limited damage. An iPhone X in good shape warrants $60, with no value for a damaged model. Keep in mind that trade-in amounts are estimates — you might get less than quoted if you didn't describe the condition accurately.
Apple's trade-in list goes all the way back to the iPhone 5, but you won't get any credit for these obsolete phones. If your device is too damaged or old to accept, the company will only recycle it.
Other devices you can trade in for Apple credit
Of course, trade-ins are also available for devices newer than an iPhone 8. The maximum currently available is $720 for an iPhone 16 Pro Max, though given this phone cost $1,199 upon release and will still be usable for many years, trading it in now makes little sense. Other phones vary upon their age and condition, so go through the steps to evaluate yours.
Aside from phones, Apple also accepts trade-ins for your old iPad (max of $690), Mac ($2,045 at most), or Apple Watch (up to $305). You're required to enter a serial number to see the value of these trade-ins. Other devices like the HomePod, Apple TV, and AirPods are eligible for recycling but give no cash.
Those considering switching from Android to iPhone aren't left out. Apple also provides trade-in credit for select Android phones; these are currently limited to Samsung Galaxy, Google Pixel, OnePlus, and Huawei models. As you'd expect, these phones don't grant as much value as first-party offerings; you're also asked about the storage capacity, unlike iPhone trade-ins. For example, a 128GB Pixel 9 Pro in good condition is eligible for $255, while a 1TB model in good shape yields $315. Meanwhile, Apple offers $50 for a Pixel 6 Pro in good condition, no matter the storage.
These evaluations for non-Apple devices aren't great, so you're better off selling those on other marketplaces (see below). But if you're desperate to get rid of your old phone with minimal effort, this is better than nothing.
How the Apple Trade In process works
If you're planning to trade in towards a new iPhone (or other Apple device) you buy online, walk through the steps on the company's site to choose the color, storage, and other elements. When you see the Apple Trade In heading, choose Add a trade-in, select your phone, and answer the questions about its condition to get your estimate.
Your purchase method affects how the trade-in credit is applied. When you pay the full cost upfront, the company will credit your payment method once the old unit is received and verified. If you finance the phone through an Apple Card or carrier, or lease through the new Apple Upgrade program, the trade-in amount lowers your monthly payments.
In case you don't want to buy anything new right now, or if you want to trade another type of device towards an iPhone, you can get the value applied to an Apple gift card. To do so, visit the Apple Trade In page, go through the steps to evaluate, and choose Trade in for an Apple Gift Card at the end. You'll need to provide the serial number.
Trading in online vs. in-store
When trading in your iPhone online, the company will mail you a box for securely packing it, along with a prepaid shipping label. Once your new phone arrives, transfer everything from your old device to the fresh one before preparing your old phone for trade-in. The package contains drop-off instructions; you'll usually bring it to a UPS or FedEx location.
If you prefer, you can also trade in your iPhone at an Apple Store. These don't require an appointment, though making one can save you time. For this option, the company advises you unpair your Apple Watch (if applicable), back up your device and sign out of your Apple account before heading to the store. Don't erase it until a representative has evaluated it. Similar to online trade-ins, you can apply the credit to either a new purchase or a gift card.
When trading in your phone, you don't have to include chargers or any other accessories. Apple will recycle these if you want, but there's no point in handing over anything you can still use.
Consider other trade-in options too
Apple Trade In is a convenient option if you don't want to deal with the hassle of selling your device to someone directly. But if you're willing to spend a little more time, you can likely get a better value for your device at one of the many places to sell old gadgets.
For instance, Mac Me An Offer accepts iPhones directly, with no haggling or meeting in person required. And its prices can sometimes be higher than Apple's. At the time of writing, Apple provides $320 for any iPhone 15 in good shape, while Mac Me An Offer goes up to $425 for a 512GB iPhone 15. Sites like SellCell help you compare prices from many outlets. And there's always the option to sell directly to someone on eBay, Facebook Marketplace, or similar.
Selling directly is more of a hassle, but you make more (a company buying your phone has to make a profit reselling it, while an individual doesn't). Another benefit of selling on third-party sites is the option to get paid via a check or services like Zelle, rather than having the value tied up in Apple credit.

Over the past few years, I have seen a steady stream of patients who have never set foot in a gym, yet present with the kinds of injuries I mostly see in weekend athletes. While the increased awareness about the need to stay physically active and fit is welcome, many young people are now relying on YouTube videos or Instagram reels without fully understanding their body’s limitations.
There is no doubt that home workouts are certainly better than no exercise at all. What began as a necessity during the pandemic has, for many, become a long-term habit and that is a positive development in many ways. However, what concerns me is that many people are training without proper guidance on exercise form, load management, nutrition, or recovery. While the motivation to stay active is commendable, exercising without the right knowledge or supervision can sometimes do more harm than good.
Here are the five most common injuries due to home workouts and how to prevent them.
Shoulder Pain - Rotator Cuff Strain: This is probably the most common shoulder complaint I see in patients who work out at home. It is often caused by overhead presses or push up variations performed with poor shoulder positioning, inadequate shoulder blade control, or the elbows flaring out at an awkward angle.
In most cases, the pain doesn’t begin suddenly. It starts as a dull, nagging ache that many people ignore for weeks. Over time, if left unaddressed, it can progress into a sharp, intense pain that makes simple daily activities difficult,such as lifting the arm, getting dressed, reaching overhead, or even combing hair.
Prevention: Keep your elbows at somewhere between a 30–45 degree angle from your body during pressing movements, and don’t start pushing heavy weights before your shoulder mobility can support the range.
Back Pain: Lower Back Strain: Working out with a rounded spine, especially during exercises such as deadlifts, bent over rows, and even certain sit-up variations is one of the most common causes of back strain. When exercising at home, without a mirror or a trainer to monitor and correct your form, it’s easy to unknowingly round the lower back instead of maintaining a neutral spine.
Prevention: Take a deep breath and brace the core before lifting any weights, keep the spine neutral and if you feel you cannot maintain the position through full movement, then reduce the weight. I usually tell patients to first do a workout out without weights, just to get the correct posture and form initially, before starting with weights.
Knee Injury: High Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) has become one of the most popular workout styles today. However, high impact exercises such as jump squats and burpees are also common causes of knee pain, often leading to conditions including patellar tendinitis and ligament strain. This usually happens because people focus on generating maximum height and power during the jump but pay little attention to how they land.
Prevention: A soft, controlled landing is essential to protect your knees during high impact exercises. Ensure your knees track in line with your toes throughout the movement, and increase your jump volume gradually on a week-to-week basis to allow your body time to adapt.
Wrist and Elbow Pain: Exercises such as push-ups, planks, and mountain climbers performed on hard floors with the wrists held in a fully extended position can place excessive strain on the tendons and ligaments around the wrist and elbow. Over time, this repetitive stress can lead to overuse injuries such as tennis elbow, golfer’s elbow, and even wrist ganglion cysts.
Prevention: Use a soft exercise mat and, if needed, a wrist wrap. Make sure the load is distributed evenly across the entire palm. Maintain proper form and listen to your body’s signals. If you experience pain, burning, or increasing discomfort, slow down, or stop rather than pushing through the pain.
Ankle Sprains: Working out on uneven flooring or in confined spaces without adequate clearance can significantly increase the risk of ankle injuries. Poor landing mechanics, awkward foot placement, and repetitive strain on the ankle ligaments are common causes of sprains during home workouts. Even after recovering from an ankle sprain, many people neglect balance and stability training, which is essential to prevent re-injury. Unlike larger joints, the ankle is supported by relatively small muscles and relies heavily on ligament strength, rather than weight training alone
Prevention: Clear a proper flat space before you start, and if your workout involves any lateral movement or jumping, footwear with real ankle support matters more at home than most people assume.
Why this keeps happening
In almost all the patients I see, the root cause isn’t the exercise itself but not following a proper warm-up routine; skipping the basics and starting with advanced variations; ignoring early warning signs of pain because of not being sure how much discomfort is considered normal during exercise.
Pain is one of the body’s most important ways of communicating with you. A little muscle fatigue is normal but a sharp, localised pain that changes how you move is not something that should be ignored.
Preventing long-term complications
- Warm up for at least 5 minutes before any home routine. This should include dynamic stretches and not static ones.
- Work on form before you increase the intensity - a slow, well-controlled rep is better than fast one ending with an injury
- Progress load by not more than 10% a week - this is the common teaching among long-distance runners and the same applies for strength workouts too
- Don’t train through pain - soreness or discomfort is normal but a sharp pain on one side is a sign of concern - if you experience it, then reach out to a medical expert
- Invest in the right mat/shoes
When you work out at home, you are the trainee and you are the coach - so it is you who should watch and correct your form and understand & listen to your body, because an untreated overuse injury can set your fitness journey back by months.
(Dr. Shriram Krishnamoorthy is senior orthopaedic & sports Injury surgeon, Shri Bone & Joint Clinic, Chennai. skshriram@gmail.com)

It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”
Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor to the Migration Story, where this story was first published

“Nasty” Nestor Cortes is a Phillie. But when will his nastiness arrive in Philadelphia?
It could be a couple weeks.
The former All-Star left-hander signed a one-year deal with the Phillies on Friday and get paid $1.5 million if he reaches the big leagues and $250,000 if he stays in the minors.
Cortes’ first stop will be Class A Clearwater, where he’ll continue his rehab. He needed surgery to repair a torn left biceps in October, and it’s been almost a year since his last MLB appearance on Sept. 3, 2025.
Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said Cortes has thrown several extended bullpen sessions, including a live bullpen on Friday. Here’s a sneak-peek at Cortes at work a few days prior to his Phillies signing:
According to Mattingly, Cortes “says he’s ready to roll.” But will he roll as a starter or a reliever? Cortes has primarily been a starting pitcher, having started 94 games in his career.
Earlier this season, Mattingly hinted to deploying a six-man rotation, but that may not be the wisest move at this juncture with the Phils in a playoff race. Plus, Aaron Nola and Andrew Painter both have pitched well of late, solidifying the rotation.
The Phillies greatest need is a bullpen piece – specifically a lefty – and Mattingly has had few lockdown relievers other than Jhoan Duran all season.
Cortes gives Mattingly a flex option – starter or bulk-inning guy or even a specialist – while adding a fresh arm to an dog-tired 'pen.
“I’m not sure the plan is trying to get built to be a starter,” Mattingly told the media on Friday. “That’s kind of a long build. That’s throwing, getting to 75 to 90 pitches, four days in between every one of those. So I think it’s getting going, build him up, at least to a bulk grow, go from there.”
Cortes was 2-4 with a 6.29 ERA in eight starts last year with Milwaukee and San Diego, a season cut short by a left flexor tendon strain that kept him on the IL from April 4 to Aug. 6, and left biceps tendinitis ended his season on Sept. 3.
The 31-year-old spent the previous seven seasons with the Yankees, becoming an All-Star in 2022, and has a 35-25 career record with a 3.94 ERA.

With its wide avenues lined with tall palm trees, its quaint cafes and old-school cantinas, as well as the mix of English and Spanish spoken on the street, the Tabacalera neighborhood in downtown Mexico City has a certain US feel – so much so that it is has become known as Little LA.
The nickname is about more than appearances, however. In recent years, this corner of the metropolis has become a haven for many Mexicans deported from the US, particularly those who spent years or decades living across the border and for whom Mexico feels like a foreign country. In Little LA, they have found a more familiar place to belong.
With the Trump administration embarking on a massive anti-immigrant crackdown, deportations to Mexico are expected to surge. Since taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump has deported roughly 145,500 Mexican nationals.
Christopher Gil Ortíz was one of them. He was on his way to work in Los Angeles in June this year when Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents stopped him, handcuffed him and threw him in detention.
After months of living in constant fear as an undocumented immigrant in Trump’s US, Ortíz said that when the detention finally happened he felt relieved. “At this point I was like, OK, that’s it, I’m going back,” he recalled. “It’s like they took a weight off my shoulders.”
More than 30 years since he had left as a child, Ortíz was sent back to Mexico, leaving behind his wife and two young children. Dumped in the resort town of Tulum, he made his way to Cancún, only to have all his belongings stolen from his hotel room. Eventually, he ended up in Mexico City, where he had family.
“I was nervous,” he said. “Even though I was born here, I have very vague memories of the city itself.”
He was also facing the many challenges of being a deportee: getting his birth certificate, ID and finding a job. His sister sent him a TikTok post from an organization called New Comienzos (New Beginnings). Based in Little LA, it was set up to help returnees reintegrate. When he saw the post, Ortiz decided to check out Little LA for himself.
“Seeing the palm trees, it kind of does make you feel like you’re in LA,” he said, adding that he was grateful to New Comienzos. “There’s a lot of people that are going through what I’m going through and I’m pretty sure there’s going to be more.”
The New Comienzos founder and executive director, Israel Concha, said he was preparing for exactly that. “The atmosphere [in the US] right now is one of humanitarian crisis and panic. People no longer even want to take their children to school,” Concha said. “You’ll probably start seeing mass deportations in a few months.”
Concha founded New Comienzos when he witnessed first-hand how little support the Mexican government was offering recent arrivals. In 2012, he was living in Texas with his pregnant wife and had started a successful private transport business. He had lived in the US for 30 years. “I wanted to try to achieve that American dream, and I think I succeeded,” he said.
Then one day he was caught speeding on his way to pick up a client. While in detention, he fought his case for two years but was deported in 2014. On his first day in Mexico, he was kidnapped by a criminal gang working with local police.
“That was my welcome to my native country,” he said.
After being severely beaten, Concha escaped to Mexico City, where he found a job at a bilingual call centre – one of several starting to pop up in the Tabacalera neighborhood, attracting young returnees who spoke fluent English. Less than a year later, he started New Comienzos to address the challenges faced by people like himself.
“People didn’t just need a job; many of them needed emotional support because they had just lost everything following a deportation,” he said. The organisation offers legal support and free English certification and classes, as well as mentorship for recent arrivals. Little LA remains the organization’s center of operations.
“A community reintegration lab,” said Concha, “that’s what we’ve created there in Little Los Angeles.”
Sergio Aaron Pérez, 36, said the area felt like home. Wearing a Los Angeles Lakers jersey and baseball cap, his face and arms covered in tattoos, Pérez looked as though he had just stepped off the plane from the US. In fact, having lived in the US for more than 30 years, the former California resident was deported in 2011 for doing what he calls “bad things”.
In Little LA, he found work at call centers. “If you speak English there’s a lot of money,” said Pérez. “I love my city. There’s a lot of community.”
Ortíz, for his part, had little interest in a call center job. He has applied for a job at a glass-making factory – work he used to do in the US. Next on his agenda: bringing his wife and children to Mexico.
“My kids are OK with it,” he said. Referencing a local Mexican custom, he added: “My daughter told me that she was already practising drinking soda out of a plastic bag.”

The Latest

- The iconic Canadian rock band's hometown has held numerous events commemorating the event, including tonight's live showing of the rebroadcast in Springer Market Square, where tens of thousands gathered in 2016.

On Aug. 20, 2016, Canadian rock band the Tragically Hip played their final concert, at the K-Rock Centre in their hometown, Kingston, Ont. (And if you needed the passage of time underlined further, that venue is now known as Slush Puppie Place.)
The concert, aired on CBC, was a final goodbye to the band, who announced a 10-city, 15-show tour after lead singer Gord Downie was diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.
In honour of the anniversary, CBC will rebroadcast the recording of the concert tonight.
The Tragically Hip: A National Celebration airs Canada-wide at 7 p.m. across the country on CBC-TV and CBC Gem (8 p.m. AT and 8:30 p.m. NT). We'll be carrying the CBC Ottawa broadcast here in about an hour.The rebroadcast will begin with a short film by Gord Downie's brother Mike called A Beautiful Thing, which includes behind-the-scenes tour footage and notable Canadians sharing what the Hip means to them.
We'll bring you live coverage from Kingston tonight from CBC's Gabrielle Huston. The city is capping a three-day celebration of the band with a public viewing of the concert.
This live page will also act as a second screen of the concert, sharing behind-the-scenes details from the night and explaining the meaning behind Downie's Canadiana-laced lyrics, which helped make the band a national icon.

Tonight people are gathering in the square to watch the concert, as they did a decade ago. We'll have reports from CBC's Gabrielle Huston there.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

The founder of Evergrande, one of China’s largest property developers, has been sentenced to life in prison and had all of his personal property confiscated.
Hui Ka Yan, 67 and once named by Forbes as China’s richest man, with a net worth of $42.5bn (£31.2bn) in 2017, pleaded guilty in April to eight charges.
These included misuse of funds, fundraising fraud, illegally taking public deposits, illegally extending loans, fraudulently issuing securities and bribery.
The company Hui founded, Evergrande Group, was fined 8.8bn yuan (£950m), while its property arm was fined 7bn yuan, according to Chinese state media.
Hui’s convictions relate to a debt crisis at Evergrande, which shook China at a time when the government had been trying to make the world’s second-largest economy less reliant on the real estate sector.
Evergrande, which delisted from the Hong Kong stock exchange last year, has defaulted on most of its $300bn in liabilities.
Shenzhen intermediate people’s court in southern China said in its ruling that between 2016 and 2021, Hui “violated state laws by employing methods such as sustained, large-scale financial fraud to inflate assets and conceal liabilities”.
It said Hui’s actions had “severely disrupted the order of the socialist market economy” and “caused exceptionally heavy economic losses”.
More than 50 individuals linked to Evergrande were also sentenced on Thursday, with prison terms ranging from 20 months to 18 years.
Evergrande’s troubles began in 2020 when the Chinese government introduced regulations limiting the amount of debt that property companies could hold. This torpedoed the debt-fuelled real estate sector, which has traditionally accounted for between one-quarter and one-third of China’s GDP.
Construction stalled on hundreds of property developments as companies scrambled for cash and struggled to pay suppliers amid weak demand during the Covid-19 pandemic. A study published this year estimated that the regulatory crackdown led to about $347bn in sunk costs across the Chinese economy.
Hui’s company was at the centre of this crisis. Evergrande’s implosion has been seen as a symbol for the wider troubles in the property sector, which still weighs heavily on the Chinese economy.
Born to a poor family in rural Henan province, Hui was raised by his grandmother before setting up Evergrande in 1996.
In 2018 he thanked the Chinese Communist party for providing “everything that Evergrande and I have”.

The Trump administration’s crackdown on immigrant truck drivers could remove as many as 200,000 drivers from US roads, potentially worsening the country’s longstanding truck-driver shortage, critics have warned.
Critics argue that the campaign is being driven less by public safety concerns and more by the administration’s broader mass deportation and “America First” agenda.
“This is ‘just an immigration raid by any other name,’” said Cassandra Zimmer-Wong, an immigration policy analyst at More in Common, according to USA Today.
The Trump administration has cited fatal crashes involving immigrant truck drivers to justify tighter enforcement. But Zimmer-Wong said there is no hard evidence that immigrant truck drivers are less safe than American truck drivers.
She pointed to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s own acknowledgement of the lack of such evidence when it introduced new rules restricting most immigrants with temporary work permits from obtaining non-domiciled commercial driver’s licences.
Zimmer-Wong also accused the administration of “manipulating a bureaucratic issue” involving differences between commercial driver's licence and work permit expiration dates.
CDLs can typically remain valid for four to eight years, while federal work permits may last only one to two years. A work permit can therefore expire before a driver's CDL, but that does not necessarily mean the driver is illegally in the US, she said.
The American Immigration Council has cited long delays in work-permit renewals caused by backlogs, stricter background checks and the end of automatic extensions under the Trump administration.
“Do I think that these expiration dates should be standardized? One hundred percent,” Zimmer-Wong said. “But I don't think the answer is taking 200,000 people off of the road when likely the vast majority of them are legally here.”
The crackdown could have consequences beyond immigration enforcement.
The US trucking industry has faced driver shortages for years, and removing a large number of immigrant truckers could put additional pressure on freight transportation and supply chains.
The Trump administration maintains that stricter enforcement is necessary to ensure that only qualified, authorised and safe drivers operate commercial vehicles.
Critics, however, say the policy risks turning administrative issues involving work permits and CDLs into grounds for detention and removal, while disproportionately affecting immigrant communities that have become an important part of the US trucking workforce.
The Trump administration has stepped up enforcement against immigrant truck drivers, citing road safety, English-language proficiency and immigration concerns as reasons for removing some drivers from US highways.
A key part of the crackdown involves non-domiciled commercial driver’s licences (CDLs), which are issued by state motor vehicle departments to eligible drivers who are legally present and authorised to work in the US but do not have a permanent residence or domicile in the state.
The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) began strictly enforcing English-language proficiency requirements in May 2025.
Under the tougher enforcement approach, commercial truck drivers who fail English proficiency tests during roadside inspections can be immediately taken off the road.
Federal officials argue that truck drivers need to understand traffic signs, communicate with law enforcement and safety inspectors, and respond appropriately during inspections. Failure to communicate effectively, they say, can create serious safety risks when operating large commercial vehicles.
The administration has also pointed to several fatal crashes involving noncitizen or immigrant truck drivers while defending the crackdown.
One case cited by officials occurred in August 2025 on Florida's Turnpike near Fort Pierce. According to the Department of Homeland Security, investigators determined that a truck driver from India made an illegal U-turn that blocked all lanes of traffic. The crash killed three people.
The administration has used such incidents to argue that stricter screening and enforcement are necessary to keep potentially dangerous drivers off American roads.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has strongly defended the policy.
"When illegal aliens are behind the wheels of semi-trucks, they are putting American lives in danger," Mullin said on August 4 while announcing the results of an operation targeting immigrant truck drivers.
The administration's position is that immigration status and compliance with commercial driving regulations are closely connected when drivers do not meet federal safety or eligibility requirements.
A non-domiciled CDL allows certain drivers who are legally present and authorised to work in the US but do not have permanent domicile in the issuing state to operate commercial vehicles.
The category has become a major focus of the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts.
Federal authorities are examining drivers who received these licences while holding temporary legal status or work authorisation, including some asylum-seekers and other immigrants with temporary ties to the US.

What does Savinho's £75m move reveal about Man City's multi-club model?
- Published
For the City Football Group (CFG), the soon-to-be-completed sale of Savinho to Tottenham will mark a milestone moment.
The fee of £75m plus £10m in add-ons agreed represents a record sale for Manchester City, the most prominent club in CFG's stable.
Savinho's time with City's ownership group has not been without scrutiny.
He was a record signing for CFG-owned French club Troyes from Atletico Mineiro in 2022. But left two years later having never played for the club.
At 18, he was sent on loan to Dutch side PSV for the 2022-23 season, and then to fellow CFG-owned Spanish club Girona for 23-24, where he built his reputation.
He featured in 37 league matches as Girona secured Champions League qualification for the first time, registering nine goals and eight assists.
City immediately bought him from Troyes for £30.8m in 2024, which raised questions at the time whether that fee was fair market value, after an impressive spell in Spain.
Savinho scored just twice and contributed 12 assists during his two seasons in the Premier League so, although it could be argued he was not a sporting success in Manchester, he has been a financial one.
The fee attached to Savinho - which has caught many by surprise - has represented a huge win for CFG, which has links to 12 clubs worldwide.
In an industry where player trading has become such a vital component of how modern day football is run, the enormous profit generated from the 22-year-old's sale - at almost £70m if all the bonuses linked to his move to north London are met - is significant.
City would argue signing an 18-year-old from South America and selling that player for £75m four years later does also represent sporting success and Tottenham will be encouraged by his loan spell in La Liga which saw Savinho named in the La Liga team of the year.
"Our intention from the moment that we reached the Champions League was to try to get him to stay for another year," Quique Carcel, director of football at Girona, told BBC Sport.
"But logically after making such a big impact, City, Pep and Txiki [Begiristain] were already considering having him in their first-team squad.
"But there was a moment when they were deciding between the two options, because they also knew that Savio having another year at Girona playing in the Champions League was also a very good option.
"But as soon as there was an interest from Pep and Txiki in him being a player that would be able to play in the [City] first team squad, then of course the player didn't have any doubts."
In his first season with City, during which he made 48 appearances under Pep Guardiola, Savinho made 16 goal contributions in all competitions and his eight Premier League assists during that campaign was the highest at the club.
"It's a success story for the group," CFG's managing director of global football Brian Marwood told BBC Sport.
"The idea is always 'can we get them to the pinnacle in our group', which is Manchester City. There might be some along the way that might be good assets for the group.
"And Savinho has clearly been a fantastic asset - because not only has he played for Manchester City but now he is leaving for a considerable amount of money.
"We have created a pathway for the boy but credit to him because he is playing in one of the best leagues in the world."
Nevertheless, there are those who will maintain Tottenham have overpaid for Savinho but what he does on the pitch will answer those questions.
Those at CFG will look on with interest at how Savinho fares away from their nest.
Academy sales a big business
In January, BBC Sport highlighted how Manchester City, as a separate entity, has turned selling players nurtured in their academy into big business.
Morgan Rogers, Douglas Luiz, Cole Palmer, Liam Delap and Oscar Bobb are among the players developed by City to have been sold on and are now playing, or have played, for rival Premier League sides.
City have recouped more than £250m from selling young players over the past five years alone.
"To find a balance between recruiting players for sporting success and ones that could become more of an asset in the future is difficult," explained Marwood.
"One of the hardest bits about signing young players is that you don't know an awful lot about them but some will come in, adapt, work hard, have ambition and aspiration and go on and have fantastic careers.
"Oleksandr Zinchenko is a prime example. Taty Castellanos is another. So is Jack Harrison."
Invariably, CFG is not always on point with its talent identification of young talent. Some will make it, some will not. That's the nature of the player recruitment beast.
The success of Rogers and Palmer, with Aston Villa and Chelsea, has shown that City have sometimes have sold too soon.
Former Aston Villa forward Rogers was sold by Manchester City to Middlesborough in February 2024 for an initial fee of £8m. Last month Chelsea paid £117m for him.
Palmer - sold by City for £40m in 2023 - would demand a similar fee if he were to leave Stamford Bridge.
But as Savinho takes the next step in his career, City are turning their attentions to the future.
There are high hopes for Ryan McAidoo, an 18-year-old at City who has already made his senior debut for the club.
Japan's Shin Miidera, a 16-year-old attacker playing for partner club Yokohama F. Marinos, is another CFG are monitoring very closely.
Then there is 16-year-old American midfielder Cavan Sullivan, who currently plays for MLS club Philadelphia Union, but will join Manchester City when he turns 18.
Vitor Reiss - who spent last season on loan to Girona from City - is tipped to make the grade.
"In an ideal world you would love for them to stay with you from the beginning right through to the very end - but the reality is it's probably not going to happen," added Marwood.
"The challenge is can we produce the next one? OK- Savinho's gone - but where is the next one? That's the fascination of this business, you have to look three and four years ahead.
"It's important we grow this hub of young talent and hopefully find them pathways and produce a conveyor belt of talent and use our network of clubs to aid there development."
The measure of their success will be judged on the pitch and on the books.

GRAMADO, Brazil — “Seduction” (“Sedução”), a feature set in the Amazon Rainforest region and helmed by Zelito Viana and Marcos Palmeira, will have its world premiere on Sept. 11 at the 30th edition of the Inffinito Brazilian Film Festival in Miami.
H2O is also releasing in local theaters Miguel Faria Jr.’s doc, “Tom Jobim – Esse Seu Olhar,” in the week of Jan. 25, which marks the celebration of the 100th birthday of the legendary composer of “The Girl From Ipanema,” who died in 1994, said Jorge Peregrino, member of the board of H2O Films, the distributor of both films.
H2O hosted a panel during the Gramado Film Market at the 2026 edition of the Gramado Film Festival, in Southern Brazil.
Popular on Variety
“Seduction” marks the debut as a helmer of Marcos Palmeira, a major actor who starred in dozens of telenovelas, series and films in Brazil over the past 50 years. He toplines and co-directs the pic along with his father Zelito Viana, a vet producer of Cinema Novo classic films and director of several features, such as “Villa-Lobos: A Life of Passion.”
In the plot, Paulo (Palmeira), a renowned actor, when he learns of his father’s death in the Amazon Rainforest, embarks on a journey to settle his father’s unfinished affairs, faces the rough reality of the region and undergoing a radical transformation.
“In my opinion it is the best film of Zelito Viana, even better than ‘Villa-Lobos: A Life of Passion,’” Peregrino told Variety. “And it is fair to say, and I believe Zelito will agree with me, that Marcos’ direction work brought a freshness to the film.”
Peregrino stressed the high production value of the pic, lensed in Alter do Chão, in the Amazon region, along the Tapajós River. The pics deals with local issues, such as illegal land grabbing.
“Seduction” also features two Brazilian film and television stars: Camila Morgado plays Sara Teixeira and Dira Paes portrays Maria Rita Martins in the film.
The Inffinito Brazilian Film Festival is the largest Brazilian film fest held abroad and a pioneer in the promotion and dissemination of local pics in the international market. It takes place in several cities, such as Miami, NYC, London, Vancouver, Rome, Milan, Madrid, Barcelona, Buenos Aires and Shanghai.
“Tom Jobim – Esse Seu Olhar” marks the new documentary by Faria Jr, recognized as a top Brazilian director of feature-length docs about music composers. He has helmed the critically acclaimed “Vinicius” (2005), about Vinicius de Moraes, which had a strong box office performance, and “Chico: Artista Brasileiro” (2015), about Chico Buarque, another legend of Brazilian music.
“Tom Jobim – Esse Seu Olhar” is an Arpoador Audiovisual and Urca Filmes production which is co-produced by Globo Filmes. Peregrino and Leonardo Edde are producing. Diana Vasconcellos co-wrote the doc’s screenplay along with Miguel Faria Jr. and also serves as the film’s editor.
“Miguel Faria Jr. conducted extensive archival research. He gathered interviews with Tom Jobim from television and other media and edited them in such a way that 70% to 80% of the documentary is narrated by Tom himself,” Peregrino said.

The Society for Cyberabad Security Council (SCSC) marked its 20th anniversary on Sunday, commemorating two decades of collaboration between the Cyberabad Police, industry and the community on safety and security issues.
SCSC, which was formally established on August 23, 2006, held its anniversary programme at AVASA Hotel in HITEC City under the theme ‘Celebrating Two Decades of Trustworthy Partnership, Security & Growth’. The SCSC@20 logo was unveiled and a commemorative book, ‘Enabling Enterprise – 2 Decades of SCSC’, was launched.
Cyberabad Police Commissioner M. Ramesh said the safety and security of IT professionals and the wider technology community remained an important priority for the police. He credited SCSC with supporting the police and strengthening the public-private partnership over the past two decades.
Recalling challenging periods, including the Telangana movement and the COVID-19 pandemic, Dr. Ramesh said close coordination between the police, industry and other stakeholders had helped address security, operational and community-related challenges. He said the partnership had evolved from responding to problems to developing proactive solutions to emerging challenges.
Former SCSC Secretary General Krishna Yedula recalled the organisation’s early days and said its formation followed discussions between the police and industry on creating a safe environment for the rapidly growing technology sector. Consultations on industry concerns and standard operating procedures eventually led to its formal establishment in 2006.
The anniversary programme featured four panel discussions on women’s and children’s safety, cybersecurity, road safety and community health.

Suresh Reddy.

DGP C.V. Anand, who earlier served as Cyberabad Commissioner, congratulated SCSC on completing 20 years. In a message, he said effective police-public engagement required the participation of citizens and private organisations.
