The reasons Siri may not work on CarPlay
Screaming "HEY SIRI!" even louder isn't fixing the problem, surprisingly.
CarPlay is happily running Maps and playing music, and then suddenly, Siri stops listening. Maybe it does hear you but won't answer. Or it responds in a subdued tone, and you begin to think the voice assistant has made the decision to mumble for the duration of the drive.
The thing is, Siri itself may not be the problem. A failure can begin with the settings on the iPhone or the CarPlay connection or the car's infotainment system, and finding out which one is misbehaving can save you from changing a dozen settings that were just fine to begin with.
You can activate Siri in CarPlay by holding the car's voice-command button or pressing and holding the CarPlay Home button on the display. Some cars also allow you to use "Hey Siri." If the button wakes Siri but the wake phrase does not, it may be that your car simply doesn't support voice activation.
Don't blame CarPlay if Siri doesn't work on the iPhone
Begin with the phone. It's the easier suspect to rule out.
Apple keeps Siri's voice activation controls under Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri (or Siri) > Talk & Type to Siri. Apple suggests turning "Siri" or "Hey Siri" off and on, and then repeating the voice-recognition setup if it's not working.
There are a couple of not-so-obvious settings that can cause problems as well. Siri can be disabled when the iPhone is locked, which is quite a pain when the phone remains untouched in a pocket, bag or cupholder for an entire drive. CarPlay can also be turned off under Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions > Allowed Apps.
Then there's connectivity. CarPlay can stay fully visible on the dashboard while Siri struggles to respond to requests because Siri needs an internet connection. Apple also says that some VPN profiles may prevent Siri from working, but doesn't detail which VPN configurations are likely to cause this issue.
The check is simple: just disconnect CarPlay and test Siri on the iPhone. If Siri still doesn't listen or respond, it's likely that poking around the car's infotainment menus won't work a miracle.
When Siri is working on the phone but not in the car
If Siri suddenly remembers how to do its job as soon as the phone leaves CarPlay, the connection becomes highly suspect.
For wired and wireless CarPlay, the potential connection problems are a little different. If you're using wired CarPlay, Apple suggests using a different USB cable or a compatible USB port. Wireless CarPlay requires both Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, with Auto-Join turned on for the CarPlay network, so either connection can cause odd behavior even if the CarPlay interface appears to be working normally.
Apple's troubleshooting list includes restarting the iPhone and the vehicle, forgetting the car under Settings > General > CarPlay and pairing it again. The company also suggests checking with the vehicle manufacturer for infotainment firmware updates (because restarting the car isn't enough anymore).
If the entire CarPlay connection is acting up rather than Siri alone, broader CarPlay connection problems such as cables, pairing and vehicle compatibility are worth checking before spending another afternoon buried in Siri settings.
One issue that can be confused with a broken Siri is volume. If Siri hears your command and responds but you can barely hear the response, adjust the car's volume while Siri is speaking or while you're holding the button to activate it. If Siri is not talking at all, then there is a Prefer Spoken Responses option you can enable in Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri > Siri Responses.

I tally the dead. I tally today’s dead. I seek a tally of the dead or seek
 yesterday’s dead. I try to count them, the dead. Reports tell me there are,
 today, more dead. I announce the dead—the house is quiet. I try to
 count. I seek numbers. I provide numbers. I wake trying. I cover
 myself in numbers, trying to keep still.
I seek some stillness beyond the dead—I try to just manage. I tally the dead,
 each pair of lungs, I wander through numbers, the daffodils nevertheless
 fly up. I hide the numbers, paper over what I know. The warm house fills.  
 What are you doing, he says. I say prayers for, try to put faces to the dead
as if to anchor the dead—I condemn the dead, their utter defenselessness.  
 Again I try to spare no numbers, the ones who have died, not the ones
 about to die, and when I wake they are there, counted and uncounted.  
 When life takes more away, I keep the dead inside me, the ones not
 injured but gone, although many are injured. My counting—
 what even matters? I don’t feel like going out. Soon I am counting.
At the gate of the house I feel the faint dusk resolve. I bless the dead,
 I forget the dead from last year, I lose more dead, I tally what I can.  
 I count through the morning. Light drifts across the thick rug. I move
 my hands as if I am counting the dead. As if I am altering the dead
 in my hands as I count.

Journalist Mariam Abu Dagga was killed in the 25 August 2025 double-tap attack on Nasser Hospital in Gaza. Based on dozens of witness testimonies, whistleblowers and visual analysis, this is the most comprehensive reconstruction yet into the strike
9.30am, 25 August 2025
Against the deadly drumbeat of Israeli tank fire, Mariam Abu Dagga is eking out the last of her precious coffee supplies with close friend, flatmate and journalist Baraa Lafi.
It's another Monday in this relentless slaughter.
The 33-year-old journalist, who works for Independent Arabia and the Associated Press, is sitting in the partially destroyed building she shares with other female reporters in Khan Younis, south Gaza. Israeli military bulldozers had, at some point earlier in this war, punched through the side of the wall, which the owners had patched up with rubble, cement and rocks. And so the room is "crushed and deformed", Baraa says. But it is home - for now.
Together the two women, who bonded over their passion for work, are discussing their latest joint report about overcrowding in Nasser Hospital, located just across the street. They had interviewed their friend, Canadian-Palestinian emergency nurse and international volunteer Amanda, whose surname is coincidentally Nasser.
They are interrupted by Baraa's mother calling to check on them. They reassure her they are both fine.
Truthfully, Mariam hasn't been good for weeks. She deeply misses her only child: 14-year-old Ghaith she had managed to send out of Gaza to the UAE last year. She is still grieving the loss of her mother, who in the middle of the bombing in May 2024 died of cancer, in part due to a lack of treatment. Her father, to whom she had donated one of her kidneys before the war, wasn’t doing well either. The family had, like so many in Gaza, lost their home in Khan Younis, been forcibly displaced multiple times and survived starvation.
Surrounded by death, she had secretly left a will for her son with Baraa. Three days earlier, she had also sent a voice note to Hadi Torfi, her editor at Independent Arabia, warning that she might be forced to flee for the fourth time. The staff at Nasser Hospital had told journalists, following a well-worn pattern of Israel striking, encircling and laying siege to hospitals, that Nasser and the surrounding area would be next.
"I hope you are still tracking me, right?" she says in the voicenote, breaking off into deep, chest-wracking coughs. "I don't know where to go. I have nowhere to go," she trails off.
Inside the hospital, Amanda Nasser, who is volunteering with the Canadian medical charity GLIA, is frustrated that she has to leave her work to get in a convoy. All the international medics at Nasser had been told the night before that they must attend mandatory World Health Organisation (WHO) training about gender-based violence (GBV), off campus.
The stifling wards, thick with the smell of death and decay, are over capacity, and so any medic leaving the hospital seems excessive. "Usually we can get [training] through some sort of lesson we can do remotely online," she recalls. "GBV is a problem happening as well. But obviously we're in the middle of a genocide."
Another international GLIA volunteer, anaesthetist Dr Travis Melin, is equally bemused. Today is his last day in Gaza: why would he need to do this training now?
"They usually plan things in advance. What felt funny to us was that all of a sudden, they said, 'Hey, there's mandatory training now,'" he remembers.
Outside, the courtyard of the hospital, now a bustling tent city, is waking up in the blistering heat of the summer morning. Civilians who have fled their flattened homes across the 40km-long enclave have set up camp in the grounds of a complex that, under international law, is supposed to be protected. An ecosystem has sprung up: by the main gate there are people selling what meagre supplies are available; among them is Ali Abu Latifa.
The biggest tent within the courtyard is long, topped with bright blue tarpaulin, and stretches alongside the eastern side of the compound. It is reserved for the journalists, also displaced, who effectively live here too.
9.45am
Inside this tent, freelance journalist Abdallah al-Attar, 27, and videographer Moaz Abu Taha, are resting between reports. Abdallah is drifting in and out of sleep against the persistent whine of Israeli surveillance drones overhead.
Also sheltering from the heat is veteran Ghad TV correspondent Ibrahim Qannan who, at 53, is widely seen as a father figure among the younger correspondents.
He is speaking to Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri, 49, a father-of-four, who is worried about the harsh sun overheating his camera and interrupting the live feed on the external stairwell on the eastern side of the hospital. Hussam leaves to go and adjust it, while Ibrahim prepares for his 10am live broadcast just opposite. The friends bid one another farewell.
Hussam makes his way across the street to the eastern external concrete "emergency" stairwell, which, capped by a wooden shelter, has become the known hangout spot for reporters to do their live stand-ups, have a cigarette or get mobile phone signal during the frequent power blackouts. A week and a half prior, a photo taken and posted by Mariam shows Hussam standing next to his camera which is draped in a green-and-white prayer rug to shield it from the heat. Mariam also spent most days there, checking her social media posts and filing her reports.
In fact it is Mariam who apparently appears in Israeli surveillance footage, taken four days beforehand, according to screenshots obtained by The Independent. Head bent, she is seen hunched over her phone sitting next to the tripod and camera. Rafael Hayun, an Israeli civilian who says he monitors the situation in Gaza, provided an image to The Independent, declining to give its source and saying it showed the Hamas camera endangering troops. The Israeli military did not reply to a request for comment.
But Reuters later confirmed the camera was their live feed of Khan Younis and that the Israeli military knew they had teams working in Nasser Hospital. The British news agency says in the days prior to the strike the feed had been capturing footage of Israeli military bulldozers demolishing parts of southern Gaza.
10.09am
Samaher, 39, Hussam al-Masri's wife, calls her husband as he stands next to his camera on the stairwell. She has just managed to locate and buy some vegetables at an extortionate price, so needs him to transfer funds into their account. Hussam sounds tired and worn out. Recently, Samaher, who is fighting ovarian cancer in the besieged territory where there is no treatment, has been worried her husband is becoming too morbid.
"I just want to rest. I want to be martyred so I can finally rest," he tells her again in despair.
Their conversation is cut short. A massive explosion erupts and the line goes dead.
Ghad TV correspondent Ibrahim Qannan is standing by the eastern entrance to the complex, preparing to go live, when two deafening blasts rip open the skies.
One projectile crashes into the northern side of the hospital, tearing through what has been nicknamed "the Titanic": a communal area, flanked by large windows, near the operating room, where medics rest between surgeries.
The second smashes through the eastern external stairwell on the fourth floor.
Through his viewfinder, Ibrahim can see a metre-wide hole clawed out of the stairwell exactly where his friend Hussam had been standing moments before. In his place is a cloud of ash and dust.
Ibrahim immediately messages the Ghad TV main studio in Cairo to come to him now. "The hospital is being bombed," he repeats in shock.
Journalists Abdallah al-Attar and Moaz Abu Taha are shaken awake inside the journalist tent. Abdallah doesn't even have time to put on proper shoes as, together with Moaz, he runs in the direction of the explosion. Ibrahim asks them what is happening as they run past. "Hussam, Hussam, Hussam," is all Moaz can reply.
The explosions also rock the buildings opposite. Baraa grabs her press jacket and, quicker than Mariam, rushes out of the flat still in slippers. Just as she is leaving, she calls back to her friend who is still getting her things together, "I'm heading out ahead of you, ok?"
Hatem Omar, another Reuters contractor, is also sprinting to the scene of the explosion, filming the crowds going both towards and away from the bomb site. Ahmed Abu Aziz, a stringer for Middle East Eye, in a black bucket hat, crosses in front of him in the melee. He too is filming on his mobile.
In the chaos, the journalists unwittingly split into two groups. Hatem, Ahmed, Moaz, Mariam, as well as Palestine TV cameraman Jamal Badah and Mohamed Salama, who works with Al Jazeera, start to ascend the stairwell towards Hussam's body. Others, including Mohamed Salama's younger brother Ibrahim, also a journalist, and Baraa, are filming the ground-floor entrance to the ER.
From his stall by the entrance, Ali Abu Latifa sees a group of displaced civilians living in the complex have made it to the fourth floor shouting: "There are martyrs, there are martyrs!” He instinctively joins them to ferry down the wounded, a well-worn practice all in Gaza have learned to do.
When he gets there, a man in a sleeveless vest and flip-flops is holding out to the crowds below the remains of what appears to be Hussam’s destroyed camera and live-feed devices.
In the confusion, people begin to notice an Israeli quadcopter overhead and someone shouts, "There is another plane, they might bomb, go down!” Terrified of another imminent strike, Ali rushes down the stairwell, crossing paths with his neighbour and friend Mariam, who is intensely focused on reporting. She is wearing a white headscarf and black coat.
Mariam is, as usual, one of the first on the scene.
10.10am to 10.16am
Dr Mohamed Sakr, the director of nursing at Nasser, had just been shaken out of a reverie by this enormous boom that he describes as "an earthquake". He looks out of the window of his office in a different block, to see smoke billowing from the northern and eastern side of the Yassin Building. It houses three of the most critical departments in the whole hospital: the ER, the operating room and the ICU. He scrambles to check on his staff.
On his way into the ground-floor reception, he runs into Saja, one of his medical students, drenched in blood and staggering down from the fourth floor. On the northern side, one of the projectiles had punched through the walls, injuring medics as they worked.
Saja has been injured in the head; she hands her blood-stained scrubs to the nursing director, who takes them downstairs to show the waiting journalists and the world.
Baraa and others are filming with their mobiles as Dr Sakr steps into frame, holding the scrubs. "This belonged to a nurse waiting inside the operating department. She was targeted," he says in horror.
A few hundred metres away, at the local civil defence HQ, the team is starting its 24-hour shift. In charge is the unflappable veteran first responder and fire department chief, Major Raed Saqr. He arrives at the scene with ambulance drivers Ahmed Siam, Bassem Abu Nimr, and Osama Musbah, as well as Imad Al-Shaer who was just finishing his shift but joins in to help anyway. The group reaches the fourth floor stairwell less than five minutes after the strike. Apart from Imad, all of them are in distinctive high-visibility orange vests. They start retrieving body parts, which, Ahmed explains later, are "scattered everywhere" in a pool of blood.
There is now confusion with well over 20 people on different levels of the stairwell and more still on the ground floor. It is being filmed live, and from multiple angles, with journalists reporting for some of the biggest news agencies in the world. A rescue operation is clearly in full swing.
Reuters’ Hatem Omar (known professionally as Hatem Khaled), in a red T-shirt and jeans, is at the very top of the stairwell next to Mohamed Salama. The walls behind them are etched with the high-velocity impact pattern of shrapnel, emanating out from the epicentre like a mandala of teardrops. With his stills camera around his neck, Hatem deftly moves between photographing what is happening and filming the bloody scenes on his mobile. His camera picks up Mohamed as he begins walking down the stairwell towards Mariam, Ahmed Abu Aziz, Moaz Abu Taha, and civil defence worker Osama Musbah, in a hardhat, who are one level below.
Switching back to his mobile, he starts carefully walking down towards the rescuers to get a closer shot.
Major Saqr calls down to his team on the ground for more body bags.
10.17am
Two deafening explosions - so close together they meld into a single deadly heartbeat - crack open the sky, the air, sound and light itself.
Ibrahim's live stream is engulfed in a fist of dust, concrete, splintered metal and wood. In shock, he screams incomplete sentences live on air. "Oh God. The civil defence, gone. They killed people. Civil defence, gone."
Hatem's mobile phone, which keeps rolling, is swallowed into the explosion. The ghost of an arm in an orange visibility vest appears to the left of the screen. The audio is chillingly silent.
It is now seven to eight minutes after the first blast: just long enough for medics, first responders and journalists to gather en masse at the site.
Jamal Badah comes to but can't hear or see anything for 30 seconds. The pain is so blindingly intense he is convinced his legs have been blown off. When he can finally open his eyes, he sees Mariam lying motionless at his feet. Mohamed Salama has been struck on the back of his head and is vomiting. On one side Ahmed Abu Aziz is bleeding out. Nearby, Moaz Abu Taha has lost half his head.
Jamal begs anyone for help.
First responder Ahmed Siam, disorientated and unable to see or hear properly, can't understand where his teammates have gone.
"I saw pitch darkness, heard the noise, smelled explosives, wood, concrete, the scent of corpses, the smell of blood," he says.
Confused, he crawls over what he later finds out is the dead body of his colleague Imad, thinking he is dragging himself to safety.
In fact, as the dust clears, he is filmed live on air reaching through the destroyed side of the stairwell and inching out into a four-storey void.
"I was on the verge of falling from the top of the stairs, had it not been for the crowd below shouting for me to take a step back.”
He has shrapnel embedded in his eyes and so cannot see; the pain is unbearable. He calls out to his colleagues using their nicknames: "Abu Mahmoud, Abu Ahmed, where are you? Abu Ahmed, are you okay?"
He only hears a journalist who was slightly above him reply, "I'm here, I hear you."
"Then the sound vanished. I asked him, 'Where are you?' But the sound had cut out."
Downstairs on the ground floor, journalist Ibrahim Salama is in shock and injured. Chunks of concrete and shrapnel showered down on the emergency department, killing people above and below; body parts were scattered across the area. His first and only thought is of his brother, Mohamed, whom he had just seen on the now-destroyed stairwell.
Blind, Ahmed Siam stumbles down the stairs with a young man beside him.
"I asked him, 'What are we walking on?' He replied, 'Nothing at all.' But I realised quickly we were stepping over body parts, over dead people.”
There were over a dozen bodies in this narrow space. Major Saqr is also filmed staggering down the stairwell, administering first aid to himself. Rescue teams are too afraid to go back up in case Israel strikes again.
Mohamad Ghadour, another of Mariam's editors at Independent Arabia, is on annual leave when the news of the double-tap strike on Nasser Hospital bleeps up on his phone.
He is in Lebanon looking after family members, because Israel, locked in another war with Lebanese militant group Hezbollah, has destroyed his childhood home in the south of the country. A few days before, Mariam had messaged him to check with him: she profoundly understands the unique pressure of caring for a family under decades of Israeli fire.
Nasser Hospital is where Mariam lives, Mohamad realises, with growing panic.
"I started sending her messages but there was no response. I'm sending messages but there is no connection," he explains.
With Mariam unreachable, and no confirmed information, Hadi, the assistant editor-in-chief, is also furiously calling her. He sends another correspondent from Gaza City to try to work out what happened.
Both pray for a miracle.
The emergency rooms are packed, with bleeding, wounded people staggering in, calling for help.
Panicked family members are desperate to find their loved ones. Ibrahim is looking for his brother Mohamed Salama, certain he must have been killed in the attack. But he is not in the ER or the morgue.
Baraa, whose trousers are soaked in her own blood, is looking for Mariam with Mariam’s brother. Despite people warning of Israeli quadcopters hovering “unnaturally close”, sparking fears of a third strike, Baraa climbs the stairwell to find out.
The side of it has been completely obliterated, the slats of the wooden canopy blasted open.
"The stairs were covered in blood, body parts and scattered flesh lying everywhere. When I reached the fourth floor, I met two young men. One of them looked at me and said, 'Are you looking for your friend? We just brought her down as a martyr.'
"I completely collapsed."
At his live camera position opposite the hospital, Ibrahim Qannan begs the Ghad TV studio to let him go and look after the younger journalists he feels responsible for.
"I could not hold myself together, I was the oldest, most experienced."
Inside the emergency department, he finds Baraa and others weeping uncontrollably, still unable to find Mariam. In one corner, Hatem Omar is drenched in blood, in shock. Jamal Badah has had a foot amputated and is being taken out of the ICU.
There are bodies everywhere. The room is "a scene from the day of judgement," one eyewitness later describes.
In the north-west corner, Ibrahim sees one unattended body, covered by a hospital sheet.
"I asked one of the doctors, is the person under the sheet a woman?"
Ibrahim’s stomach drops as the doctor nods, and he asks for permission to uncover her face.
It is Mariam.
"Imagine a person who you have been talking to 24 hours a day, a friend, someone who was standing in front of you just minutes ago ... dead."
At the gender-based violence training about a 20 minute drive away, news reaches the international medics that Nasser Hospital has come under attack shortly after they were all required to leave. As many as 22 people are dead including five journalists and five first responders and medics.
"When I heard Mariam was one of them I lost it. I kept saying, 'No, we have to go back to the hospital now,'" says Amanda.
But the organisers of the training ruled it was too dangerous for the foreigners to return that night, perhaps worried about another strike, perhaps worried the local community might think the internationals knew in advance and had deliberately left.
"I was crying for an hour straight. I was so overwhelmed with emotions, fear, anger.
“It’s very clear what happened, why we were lured out so the hospital could get hit. It felt like a warning: they could do whatever they want.”
The movement of international volunteers should have been coordinated with the Israeli military as part of deconfliction protocol, she adds. The military must have known, she says.
"They follow our every move."
The world had watched in real time as Israel carried out a double-tap attack on journalists, first responders and doctors, at a hospital, in broad daylight. Even if the international community had become indifferent to slaughter in Gaza, there was uproar.
The Israeli military initially put out a statement claiming it was launching yet another investigation, adding it "regrets any harm to uninvolved individuals" and that it "does not target journalists as such”.
The Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu - who has an ICC arrest warrant against him for war crimes, including the crime against humanity of murder - called it a "tragic mishap", claiming Israel “values the work of journalists, medical staff, and all civilians”. (Netanyahu denies the charges against him).
But as Ibrahim Qannan put it, Mariam was killed "in an execution carried out live on air, witnessed by the entire planet”.
And the evidence gathered by The Independent tells a different story to that offered by Israel. The Israeli military later said that the Golani Brigade, one of Israel’s elite infantry brigades, identified a camera "that was positioned by Hamas" to observe troops.
But again Reuters had confirmed it was their live position - which was also corroborated by half a dozen journalists, two members of the local community and international medics working at the hospital who spoke to The Independent. An image of the camera, covered in a prayer blanket, was taken and posted by Mariam herself in the days before. Reuters said the Israeli military knew they had teams inside the hospital.
Dr Sakr, head of nursing, told The Independent that Israel was in direct contact with the hospital staff and could have easily raised any issue they had with any camera.
"They know our numbers. If they had reservations about anything, they would have contacted us as they usually do, and we would have dealt with any problem that bothered them."
The Israeli military released the names of six men whom it said were "terrorists" killed in the strikes on the hospital.
Among the names released by the military was “Omar Abu Teim”. But Ismail Al-Thawabta, the head of the Hamas-run government media office in Gaza told Reuters that he was not killed in 25 August 2025 attack on Nasser Hospital. The Independent reached out to Al-Thawabta but has not received a reply.
The Israeli military also listed Imad al-Shaer, who was named by multiple members of the civil defence team as operating at the scene, as part of their rescue team. The Independent also visually identified him in multiple videos clearly assisting the emergency response. After the second strike, footage shows his body hanging off the ledge on the fourth floor where he had been working.
Nasser Hospital's own Facebook page identified a third individual named by Israel as a hospital worker.
Reuters said it spoke to the family members of two of the other men listed, who said they were visiting patients at the hospital and were taking part in rescue efforts when they were killed in the second strike. The Independent was unable to locate the family members.
The Independent spoke to seven witnesses at the scene of the attack who had registered seeing surveillance drones flying over the area immediately after the first attack. Khaled Shaath, a freelance journalist The Independent interviewed, filmed one just a few minutes after the first attack. Everyone The Independent spoke to felt that they were being closely watched as the groups gathered on the stairwell to help and report.
The Independent spoke to two Israeli whistleblowers, both reservists who served in south Gaza. One who served in a tank unit told The Independent that the nature of the attack showed it was not only "deliberate" but that "this looks like something very planned”.
Both said that taking out a camera was "standard protocol", and it did not require additional authorisation. But shooting a hospital multiple times would have required sign-off at battalion level or higher from the Southern Command. "So many people would need to be involved in the decision-making process to choose this target and this particular firing method,” the first whistleblower said .
The individual said the "special fire method of two tank shells" around 10 minutes after the first attack, meant "they definitely saw the crowd", bolstering the belief it was an intentional double-tap.
"One shell is supposed to break the shelter, the second one kills the people," the individual added: standard protocol to cause maximum human damage. When tanks fire, the whistleblower continued, they are looking directly at their target through the gunner’s sight.
This whistleblower concluded that this all came as part of a "culture" to encourage “the most lethal outcome”.
"It's not a mistake, the whole environment is not a mistake. It's a deliberate method that is used by our government … that blurred everything, made it very confusing, more chaotic and more lethal,” the individual said.
That was particularly the case in Khan Younis where this tank officer served and felt that the Israeli military kept them there without a clear mission “for so long just to make this kind of chaos”.
The other whistleblower said not only is there a “light finger on the trigger” but “there is no accountability whatsoever”.
A freeze-frame from one of the wide camera shots of the strike shows two projectiles hitting in quick succession, too close together for it to be a single tank fire. Again suggesting coordination.
Earshot, an NGO that conducts audio investigations for human rights advocacy, carried out an in-depth acoustic analysis, triangulating the footage from at least five cameras filming the second round which killed Mariam.
Lawrence Abu Hamdan, Earshot’s founder, told The Independent they believe it was likely a 120mm M329 tank shell, made by Elbit Systems, and that one of them was set to anti-personnel mode with six submunitions or bomblets, “creating a kind of lethal blast zone”.
Analysis of the sound, the flight path of the projectiles, and the distance between impact and the sound of the muzzle blast meant they were able to estimate the distance and location of the tank that fired it: 2.5km north east of the hospital.
The Independent examined satellite imagery provided by Planet Labs on 25 August 2025, which showed the presence of a tank base, complete with berms, 2.5km north of the hospital. There are multiple tanks positioned there.
The Independent also interviewed two other weapons experts, Chris Cobb-Smith and N.R. Jenzen-Jones, the director of arms munitions consultancy Armament Research Services. Both identified fragments found at the scene, which were pictured by Associated Press, and concluded they were parts of an Israeli 120mm tank shell. N.R. Jenzen-Jones said the footage at the scene “also indicates the use of high explosive or ‘multi-purpose’ projectiles, as would be expected by tank gunfire targeting personnel in buildings.”
Kevin Jon Heller, a professor of international law at the University of Copenhagen's Centre for Military Studies, told The Independent after examining all the evidence, a prosecutor could "reasonably conclude” that the perpetrators had committed the war crimes “of intentionally attacking civilians and of launching a disproportionate attack, particularly with regard to the second attack".
“There was, for example, no attempt to warn the hospital at all,” he continued. “There's absolutely a duty in International Humanitarian Law to give a warning to the hospital, to give the reasonable time to address whatever the alleged problem is.”
Proportionality was an issue given the small military advantage of Israel’s claimed aim of taking out a camera compared to the huge collateral civilian damage in a double-tap attack. “ Do you really need two high explosive tank shells to take out a camera?” he asked.
And this does not happen in a vacuum.
The Committee to Project Journalists (CPJ) has said Israel has killed more than 200 Palestinian media workers since 2023: more journalists than any other government since it began collecting data in 1992. Previously the CPJ has that warned the Israeli military has launched smear campaigns against journalists, accusing them of being militants - like Al-Jazeera journalist Anas Al Sharif who was killed in a targeted assassination a few weeks before the Nasser attack - to "manufacture consent to kill them”.
“By silencing the press, Israel is silencing those who document and bear witness to what human rights groups and UN experts agree is a genocide,” the CPJ said.
In multiple statements to The Independent over the years, the Israeli military has repeatedly denied it targets journalists or that its troops have committed war crimes or that its actions amount to genocide. The Israeli government has made similar denials.
But UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, who is currently investigating attacks on Palestinian journalists, said the Nasser Hospital double-tap killings came within the pattern of "targeting and killing journalists that suggests a clear intention to silence Palestinian journalists in all possible ways."
"The investigations I have conducted for my upcoming report strongly suggest that journalists have been intentionally targeted so that they will not report on the crimes committed against the Palestinians in the context of the ongoing genocide,” she told The Independent.
"There are statements of Israeli leaders and soldiers, referring to the voice of journalists as a weapon, as a threat."
"Journalists have to be protected during conflict. But Palestinian journalists in Gaza feel that for them wearing the press vest makes them a deliberate target."
The Independent shared all its findings with the Israeli military and asked for comments on each point. The military declined to respond, adding only “the review is still ongoing under the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism.”
One year on and there has been no justice for Mariam or the others whose lives were taken.
There has been no one held accountable for what the CPJ has classified as the murders of the journalists - no answers for Mariam’s family and no end to the slaughter which continues in Gaza despite a nominal ceasefire.
And no guarantees that those journalists who survive in Gaza won’t be the next.
“For anyone who didn't know her, she was deeply, genuinely human—not just a journalist,” says Baraa, Mariam’s friend, who had to deliver Mariam’s will to her shattered teenage son.
“Every story Mariam went to film, she felt the pain of the people living it.
“She was someone beyond description. Everyone who knew her - young or old - loved her. She was the best of us.”
*Additional reporting by Matan Cohen and Doaa Alshaikh Eid

CJP's Saurav Das rejects Mohandas Pai's suggestion on inspecting schools: ‘Boring, unconnected from reality'
The war of words between Mohandas Pai and CJP's Saurav Das began after CJP alleged that the volunteers were attacked in Jaipur on their way to inspect a school.
Amid Cockroach Janta Party's ‘School Thik Karo’ campaign, the youth-led movement's chief spokesperson Saurav Das was engaged in a war of words with Mohandas Pai, chairman of Aarin Capital, after the later suggested how the CJP should move ahead with its campaign.
Pai had a bunch of suggestions for the CJP's campaign to highlight the infrastructural issues of government-run schools in India. But Das rejected them as ‘slow, boring, unconnected to reality’.
What set off the war of words
It all began with Pai's comment after CJP co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka highlighted how the volunteers came under attack in Jaipur while they were on their way to ‘inspect’ a school, reportedly functioning from a cow shelter.
Pai called his allegations rubbish and said that the CJP volunteers should have not gone as a ‘mob’ to the school.
Das reacted sharply to Pai's remarks and said, “Sir, please come along with us next time and show us how to do it best. You lead, we follow. Deal?”
On this, Pai offered a bunch of suggestions, which included forming two groups of volunteers in all states and inspect schools after getting permission ‘respectfully’.
"Prepare a report on the status on the ground by Taluk and give it to the state government Then demand change armed with full data. Publish a quarterly report and talk to citizens. Now you have data on your side and citizens will respect you for your work. You will know which state is behind,” Pai wrote.
However, Das noted that all of this was already being done by the NITI Aayog and independent NGOs. “Yet you see what you see. Groups of two in unruly states, take permission and what not? Respectfully sir, your suggestion is slow, boring, unconnected to reality. Much like the present system!” Das wrote.
CJP volunteers allege attack in Jaipur
CJP volunteers, led by co-convener Ranka, were allegedly assaulted by a group of people on Friday while they were on their way to inspect a government school in Jaipur’s Bagru assembly constituency.
One of the volunteers suffered a fractured arm in the attack, Ranka said.
The incident occurred near Rampura Kanwarpura village, where Ranka and his team planned to visit a government school to assess its infrastructure and facilities.
The CJP team had planned to visit two government schools in Jaipur, one at Rampura Kanwarpura and the other at Bhatta Wala on Vatika Road.
According to the party, the visits were aimed at assessing the condition of school buildings, the education system and facilities available to students.
Ranka had earlier posted on social media about the condition of the primary school at Rampura Kanwarpura. According to him, the main school building has become unsafe and has been closed after portions of the roof and beams deteriorated. The structure is being supported with iron angles.
Students have consequently been shifted to a shed around 50 metres from the main building, where they are studying under a tin roof, Ranka alleged. He also claimed that animal fodder was lying inside the shed and that bricks had fallen from portions of the structure.

MPs call for UK to hold Israeli government to account for killing of journalists following Independent investigation
A joint investigation has uncovered evidence of possible war crimes committed by the Israeli military in an August 2025 attack that killed Independent Arabia’s Gaza correspondent Mariam Abu Dagga
MPs have urged Britain to “take the strongest measures” against the Israeli government in the wake of an investigation by The Independent into the killing of journalists, first responders and medics in a double-tap attack on one of the last functioning hospitals in Gaza.
They want Downing Street to increase sanctions and cease all trade with Israel rather than “accept weak justifications” for apparent war crimes and breaches of international humanitarian law.
It follows revelations by this publication along with Independent Arabia into the 25 August, 2025 incident that killed Gaza correspondent Mariam Abu Dagga and at least 19 others.
The investigation and reconstruction was based on 17 eyewitness accounts as well as the testimony of two Israeli whistleblowers, three weapons experts and international law experts.
Mariam was one of more than 20 people, including five journalists, killed by Israeli tank fire as she rushed to report on an earlier strike. The initial attack had taken place just eight minutes beforehand, killing Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri as he manned his live position at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis.
The Independent and Independent Arabia’s investigation and reconstruction uncovered evidence that, according to international law experts, would point to the war crimes of intentionally attacking civilians and of launching a disproportionate attack, particularly with regard to the second attack.
The Israeli military said at the time it “regrets any harm to uninvolved individuals” and that it “does not target journalists as such”.
It later claimed the Golani Brigade, one of Israel’s elite infantry brigades, identified a camera “that was positioned by Hamas” to observe troops and identified six “terrorists” who were killed in the attack. The Israeli military has repeatedly denied committing any war crimes in Gaza.
But the investigation shows the camera in question was the Reuters live feed, placed on the fourth floor of an external stairwell that hundreds of journalists, including Mariam, regularly used to take videos, report live and access internet and mobile phone connections.
Mariam herself took a photo of the camera in the weeks before the attack, with Hussam al-Masri, and appeared in apparent Israeli military surveillance footage three days before.
The investigation found the military did not contact the hospital about the issue they had with the camera, despite having staffers’ phone numbers, or warn them of impending strikes, which they are obliged to do, according to international law experts spoken to by The Independent.
The investigation further found that in the first round of strikes there were likely two tank projectiles, one of which killed Hussam al-Masri, and destroyed his camera on the eastern stairwell.
Another hit an entirely different area within the hospital, near the operating theatre, called the “Titanic” where medics would rest.
Eight minutes later as journalists, medics, first responders and displaced civilians gathered on the stairwell to help and report – in full view of live-streamed cameras – two more tank projectiles were fired, killing more than 20 people.
Seven eyewitnesses we spoke to also reported seeing Israeli surveillance drones closely monitoring that stairwell and the activity of first responders between the attacks.
The Independent identified two of the six people labelled as “terrorists” killed in the attack as actually being a hospital worker and a member of the civil defence assisting in the rescue operation.
At the time, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu – who has an ICC arrest warrant out against him – called it a “tragic mishap”.
But whistleblowers said that an attack of this size on a hospital – a protected building under international law – would have required sign-off from at least battalion level and planning.
Kevin Jon Heller, a professor of international law at the University of Copenhagen's Centre for Military Studies, told The Independent after examining all the evidence, a prosecutor could "reasonably conclude” that the perpetrators had committed the war crimes “of intentionally attacking civilians and of launching a disproportionate attack, particularly with regard to the second attack".
The Independent shared all its findings with the Israeli military and asked for comments on each point. The military declined to respond, adding only “the review is still ongoing under the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism.”
In response to the investigation, International Development Committee chair and Labour MP Sarah Champion called on the government to ensure the Geneva Convention is upheld.
“Where is our outrage over journalists seemingly becoming a legitimate target? Is this the new reality; that killing civilians, medics, and humanitarian workers no longer has consequences?” she told The Independent.
“The Geneva Convention was written 77 years ago to provide some order and agreed responsibilities during the chaos of conflict. It is the international communities’ responsibility to make sure those conventions are upheld.
“Sadly, in the case of Gaza, it seems we are choosing to accept weak justifications rather than uphold international humanitarian law.”
Liberal Democrat MP Layla Moran said the investigation marked “yet another example of the reasons why we need the criminal case against Netanyahu and his ministers to go ahead at the International Criminal Court”.
“The targeting of the hospitals, but also the targeting of journalists has unfortunately become all too common. The lack of proportionality in the actions of the IDF is now well documented,” she said.
“This investigation is yet another example of the reasons why we need the criminal case against Netanyahu and his ministers to go ahead at the International Criminal Court, and for the International Court of Justice to move forward with its investigation into war crimes and genocide,” she continued. “It is right that it is ultimately decided in international courts.
“The moral case to end this war has never been clearer. And while there is a so-called ceasefire in place, we know attacks still continue to this day.”
She added she was concerned Britain could be “sitting on evidence that they haven’t put forward”, and called for reassurance from foreign secretary Ed Miliband and defence secretary Wes Streeting that there be “a no-questions-asked threshold if information is requested”.
“They should hand it over willingly and be proactive in making sure that that information gets to the right people so that it can be properly considered at the right level,” she said.
Baroness Helena Kennedy KC said there is “serious alarm” about the “failure to protect journalists” around the world and in the Middle East.
The Labour peer and chair of the High Level Legal Panel of the Media Freedom Coalition told The Independent there should be an international inquiry into the deaths of journalists in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank.
“What had happened in the Middle East is seriously alarming,” she said. “I firmly take the view that there should be an International Inquiry into the huge numbers of deaths of journalists in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank.
“The closure of Gaza to international news agencies was unconscionable. The world needs to be able to see and judge the conduct of a war. I support all steps to investigate what has taken place.”
Labour MP Rachael Maskell said the IDF must be held accountable through the international courts, and said the the UK government “must take the strongest measures” against the Israeli government.
“Having spoken to medics working in Gaza, they have reported to MPs that they have identified targeted war crimes, with precision targeting humanitarian workers including with sniper fire and drone use,” she said.
“The UK Government must take the strongest measures, including ceasing all trade and increasing sanctions against the Israeli government to hold it to account for the actions of the IDF.
“The evidence continues to mount of the war crimes that have been committed, and justice must be served through the international courts.”
A government spokesperson said: “Israel’s attack on Nasser hospital a year ago was horrific. It is vital that civilians are protected, and that journalists and humanitarian workers be able to carry out their essential work in safety.
“The Government of Israel must uphold its obligations under international law and ensure that it investigates any potential breaches when such incidents occur and ensures that those who are responsible are held to account.
“This government's record on Gaza is clear. We have recognised the state of Palestine, suspended the negotiations on a trade deal with Israel and the foreign secretary raised concerns over the humanitarian situation last week in a call with the Israeli foreign minister.”

Tributes are being paid to two police officers who died on Teesside when a car travelling the wrong way along the A66 crashed head on into their vehicle, also killing five young men.
PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed when the marked armed response vehicle they were in was struck by a Volkswagen Passat in the early hours of Saturday morning.
On Sunday, Anna Turley, a Home Office minister and local Redcar MP, said that it was “devastating” to think about the grief of the families of everyone who lost their lives on Saturday morning. The whole community was “reeling”, she said.
“All of us in the community here are sending our heartfelt thoughts and sympathies to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives so tragically,” she told BBC Breakfast.
Turley said it was important to avoid speculation about what might have happened and allow families the privacy to grieve.
“I do want to place on record my tribute to PC Blades and PC Clough. The bravery that we see from our police officers every day, every night is incredible. No one should not come home to their families at the end of their shift.”
She also said it was important to thank the emergency services who attended at the scene during “a really horrific incident”.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he was “devastated” to hear that two police officers lost their lives on duty, as well as five members of the public.
“My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland police. Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”
Cleveland police chief constable, Victoria Fuller, said she and her deputy had on Saturday visited the families of the two officers to offer condolences and support.
“This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland,” she said. “This loss is being felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies.
“These were brave officers, protecting our communities and serving our residents, who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift.”
Lauren Somerville, the chair of Cleveland police federation, said the grief among officers was “all-consuming, overwhelming”. She said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland police family are feeling.
The Tees Valley mayor, Ben Houchen, said in a statement on Facebook: “A horrible and tragic incident in South Bank this morning and my thoughts are with those affected, their families and the emergency services who attended the scene.
“Our police officers are heroes who put everything on the line to protect us, and I know all of Teesside will want to pay tribute to the officers and other emergency service workers involved for the bravery they have shown in responding to this incident.”
The five young men in the VW Passat have not been named by the authorities, although they have been named on social media. The Independent Office for Police Conduct has opened an investigation into the circumstances leading to the crash at 3.39am in South Bank after a mandatory referral from Cleveland police.
Police vehicles had been pursuing the car before it joined the A66 although it is understood the pursuit had ended before the fatal crash. Ring doorbell footage published by several websites minutes before the crash shows a car being driven at speed down a residential road and being followed by police cars.
Ellie Westerman, who lives locally, told the Sun: “The noise woke me and I shot out of bed. You could feel the vibration in the house as the car went past and the police vehicles followed with their lights and sirens going. It was frightening that cars were being driven at that speed through a residential area.”

Guinea rubbish landfill collapse kills 30
- Published
At least 30 people have been killed after a mound of rubbish at a major waste site collapsed on to nearby homes in Guinea's capital Conakry, the government has said.
Another 22 people were injured, including six seriously, in the city's Dar-es-Salam area.
"Significant" resources and personnel - including the military - have been deployed to search for survivors after the collapse at about 02:00 local time following heavy rain overnight, the government added in a statement.
One woman told local media her five children had died in the disaster. There are fears that the death toll will rise further.
Rescuers were later seen using excavators to comb through a mountain of scattered rubbish at the site as local residents gathered nearby.
Guinea's Prime Minister Mamadou Oury Bah visited the scene to assess the situation and oversee the search efforts.
Neighbourhood leader Lancine Sylla had earlier told the AFP news agency he feared there would be a heavy death toll.
"We have pulled out 18 bodies that were taken to the morgue," he said.
Another landslide at the site killed 10 people in 2017.

Chinese robots tackle tennis, smash track records at World Humanoid Robot Games
Event highlights robots’ remaining weaknesses, including balance issues, limited autonomy and battery constraints, while underscoring need for faster networks
A tennis ball flew across the net. On the other side, a humanoid robot crouched, shuffled sideways in a series of quick steps, adjusted its position and swung its racquet to send the ball back.
The robot traded forehands and backhands with human players during singles and mixed-doubles demonstrations. At one point, while chasing a ball, it lost its balance and toppled backwards, drawing gasps from the crowd. It then rolled over, pushed itself back to its feet and resumed playing.
The robot was developed by Beijing-based Galbot and took part in what the company described as the world’s first human-robot tennis match.
The demonstration took place as the second World Humanoid Robot Games opened on Saturday night at Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, the speed-skating venue used for the 2022 Winter Olympics. The five-day event brings humanoid robots together to compete in sports ranging from running and football to table tennis and combat events.
This year’s games feature 51 events and 1,301 matches involving more than 600 teams and 2,056 humanoid robots, according to the organiser. New competitions include table tennis and kickboxing, while scenario-based events have been expanded to cover tasks in industrial production, hotels, homes and logistics.
Tennis presents a demanding challenge for humanoid robots. The tennis robot had to track an incoming ball, predict where it would land, move to the right position, and coordinate its torso and arms to return the shot, all within a matter of seconds.

Gurugram Police have registered a case against ecommerce platform Meesho and one of its sellers over the alleged sale of highly toxic ‘Sulfas’, the consumption of which allegedly led to the death of a minor. The FIR was registered following a complaint by Anuradha Mehra, a resident of Gurugram’s Tikli village and the mother of the deceased, PTI reported. According to the complaint, her 17-year-old son, who had recently appeared for his Class 12 examinations, consumed the poisonous substance on April 28 and subsequently died. During the investigation, police found that the minor allegedly ordered ‘Sulfas’ through the Meesho app on April 11. His mother discovered the order while checking his mobile phone following his death, police said. Inc42 has reached out to Meesho for comments on the development. The story will be updated on receiving a response. According to the police, the invoice named Pankaj Bharatbhai Parmar, the operator of Surat-based Evergreen Agro and Gardening Mall, as the seller. Mehra subsequently approached a court, alleging that regulations governing the sale of the substance had been violated and that her son died after consuming it. On the court’s direction, an FIR was registered at the Badshahpur police station on August 19 under Sections 106 and 286 of the BNS, according to a Times of India report. The provisions pertain to causing death by negligence and negligent conduct involving poisonous substances, respectively. “An FIR has been registered and an investigation launched into the matter. Police are now investigating the online sale of Sulfas, the ordering process, and the role of the concerned seller,” PTI quoted investigating officer ASI Sanjeev Kumar as saying. “Meesho and firm representatives will be questioned soon and action will be taken as per the law after verifying the facts,” he added. Police had earlier initiated inquest proceedings under Section 194 of the BNSS after the minor’s father filed a report following his death. The minor’s viscera and blood samples were sent to the forensic science laboratory in Bhondsi, and the reports are awaited, police said. No arrests have been made so far. This is not the first time Meesho has come under the authorities’ radar over products sold on its platform. In 2022, the Maharashtra FDA filed an FIR against the ecommerce platform for allegedly selling MTP kits without prescriptions or pharmacy bills. The action followed a drug inspector posing as a customer and ordering an ‘Unwanted Kit’, containing mifepristone and misoprostol, from a Meesho seller. Meesho also faced legal scrutiny in 2021 when an FIR was registered against its founders, Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Barnwal, over allegations that counterfeit Rolex watches and Gucci apparel were sold through the platform. Separately, the Delhi High Court sought the Centre’s response to a petition alleging that Meesho and other ecommerce platforms were not complying with certain product disclosure requirements.

Chinese, Southeast Asian ride-hailing firms eye Hong Kong amid licensing roll-out
Transport chief Mable Chan says more than 7,500 people have applied for new combined taxi and ride-hailing vehicle written test
More ride-hailing platform operators from mainland China and Southeast Asia have approached the Hong Kong government about entering the city’s market ahead of the launch of licensed operations, the transport minister has revealed.
Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also said on Sunday that more than 7,500 people applied for the new combined taxi and ride-hailing vehicle written test, calling the number a “very good and positive” sign.
“We hope there will be more competition and greater diversity, which will provide more choices for residents and future ride-hailing drivers,” she said on a television programme.
Hong Kong officially legalised ride-hailing services earlier this year, requiring platforms, vehicles, and drivers to obtain separate licences or permits.
Although the new regulatory regime took effect on August 3, the first licensed services are not expected to launch until later this year.
Chan said the overseas operators included established companies that Hongkongers might have encountered while visiting the mainland or Southeast Asia, but she did not identify them or disclose how many had made contact.

‘iPhone is not your identity’: Shehzad Poonawalla’s advice to youth after Maharashtra teen, family die in hill fall
His comments came after a 19-year-old boy died along with his parents at Khavdya Dongar in Maharashtra's Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district on Friday.
BJP leader Shehzad Poonawalla has commented on the deaths of a 19-year-old boy and his parents in Maharashtra following a dispute over a mobile phone bought on EMI, saying the tragedy should force society to reflect on the growing pressure to own expensive products and maintain lifestyles that may be beyond one's means.
“The topic is not about an iPhone. The topic is that is an iPhone, a brand, a possession, a product, a position, a status symbol, more than your identity?” Poonawalla said, reacting to the incident.
Also Read | A family ends over a phone: Gadget addiction gone too far? Experts weigh in
19-year old's death and an iphone
Deep Dive
His comments came after a 19-year-old boy, identified as Kunal, died along with his parents at Khavdya Dongar in Maharashtra's Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district on Friday.
According to multiple reports, Kunal had bought an iPhone on EMI and an argument broke out with his parents over money for the instalments.
Following the dispute, the teenager climbed the hill and threatened to take his own life.
Police, villagers and his family spent nearly three hours trying to persuade him to step away. However, when Kunal suddenly jumped, his father fell while attempting to save him. His mother, on seeing the two fall, also jumped from the hilltop. All three died.
‘Keep aspirations’ not ‘delusion’: Poonawalla
“No matter how much income he had, it is possible that he could not afford an iPhone. But because of EMI, the lifestyle of 1 lakh, 2 lakhs, 4 lakhs is a delusion for us. We get a delusion that we can afford it,” he said.
Poonawalla said aspiration was not inherently wrong, but warned against allowing possessions to become measures of self-worth.
“Upgrade your phones. Surely. But don't do it at the cost of downgrading your life,” he said. “The iPhone cannot become such a big status symbol. Or a car cannot become such a big status symbol that it is more important than your identity.”
He also urged young people to understand their family's financial circumstances and not treat being told “no” as an attack on their independence or an indication that they were missing out.
“Keep an aspiration. For sure, keep an aspiration. But the aspiration should be rooted in reality,” Poonawalla said. “Sometimes listening to no, understanding the reality of parents, understanding their challenges, this is not an ego issue.”
'Social media, consumerism to be blamed'
Poonawalla also linked the pressure to consumerism with the constant exposure to other people's lifestyles on social media.
“You are seeing your friends' possessions on social media. You are chasing likes. But when will you chase values? Chase values,” he said.
He argued that true wealth should not be defined simply by the ability to purchase expensive products.
“And the wealth, the richness, to be rich, does not come from acquiring these possessions,” Poonawalla said. “Richness is not the ability to buy everything. Richness is the ability to know whether you need something or you don't need that something.”
He further urged people not to let temporary financial limitations or feelings of missing out push them towards irreversible decisions.

Stepping up its protest demanding the resignation of Minister B. Nagendra, the Bharatiya Janata Party has decided to lay siege to the Vidhana Soudha on Monday.
Announcing this at a press conference in Bengaluru on Sunday, Leader of the Opposition in the Assembly R. Ashok said the BJP members will take out a protest march from Freedom Park before laying siege to the Vidhana Soudha.
All prominent leaders, including State president B.Y. Vijayendra, will participate in the protest, he said.
The BJP, which has been protesting in the legislature demanding the resignation of Mr. Nagendra who has been chargesheeted in the case of alleged embezzlement of funds meant for ST communities, will continue its protest inside the legislature, he said.
Janata Dal (Secular) leader and Union Minister for Heavy Industries and Steel H.D. Kumaraswamy had expressed a view that the protest should continue in the session, Mr. Ashok said.

‘Goondaism’
Meanwhile, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar launched a counter-attack on the Opposition by remarking that it was disrupting the legislature proceedings as it lacked the strength to face the Congress. He also accused them of resorting to goondaism.
Commenting on the Opposition’s plans to lay siege to the Vidhana Soudha, the Chief Minister said: “There is a law of the land here. There is provision to protest within the framework of the law.  Over a fortnight after the severed body parts of a Jagatsinghpur woman were found stuffed inside a suitcase aboard Chennai-Delhi Tamil Nadu Express near Agra in Uttar Pradesh, a team of Chennai police on Sunday launched extensive searches in different parts of Odisha in pursuit of a couple suspected of the murder and disposing of the mutilated remains.
The severed body parts of victim Hayathun Nisha (38) of Odisha’s Jagatsinghpur district were first found on Aug 5. Follow‑up searches by Agra Govt Railway Police led investigators to her rented residence at Guduvanchery in Chennai, where more body parts were recovered last Friday.
A senior state police officer said the woman was employed at a private firm in Chennai and lived in a rented house with a couple — Manik Uddin Laskar from Assam and Bhagabati Majhi from Odisha. “Believing they may have fled to Odisha, Chennai police have sought our cooperation to track them down,” the senior police officer said.
The probe started after the railway staff at Agra station discovered a red trolley bag containing the decomposed and beheaded body parts in the rear general compartment of Train no. 12621 on Aug 5. The Agra railway police registered a case, later confirming that the remains were of Nisha.
Acting on leads from Agra, the Govt Railway Police at Chennai Central station and Crime Intelligence Branch of the 
Railway Protection Force
 scanned CCTV camera footage from Platform 4. The footage showed a man and a woman boarding the Tamil Nadu Express on Aug 3 around 10 pm, carrying a trolley bag resembling the one in which the body parts were found. The suspects later got down from the train.
On Friday, investigators traced the suspects’ rented accommodation on Masuthi Street in Chennai’s Guduvanchery and alerted the local police. A search of the premises allegedly uncovered more body parts stored inside a large box.
“Guduvanchery police are probing to determine the circumstances of Nisha’s death and establish the motive behind the gruesome killing,” the police officer said.

This summer, and this year, further shows the importance of protecting the theatrical window as the domestic annual box office has crossed the $7 billion mark according to Rentrak.
Those are the best numbers we’ve seen post Covid, +20% above the same period a year ago (Jan. 1-Aug. 23 which was at $5.86B with the year ending at $8.87B) and it’s 7% behind where we were in 2019 ($7.6B, that year ending at $11.4B). Best annual year post Covid was 2023 with $9B.
If we maintain a +20% pace ahead of last year, we’ll wind up at $10.6B, but don’t count your chickens before they hatch as we’re heading into the fall, which will have varying results between Zach Cregger’s reboot of Resident Evil (expected to do quite well) and DC’s Clayface (a lower budget comic book movie with a different set of box office forecasts than say Superman). Warner/Legendary’s Dune: Part Three and Disney/Marvel’s Avengers: Doomsday at Christmas will certainly assist in taking us to another atmospheric level at the B.O.
It’s been a year where we’re about to see the second-highest grossing movie ever at the domestic box office with Spider-Man: Brand New Day (set to overtake Avengers: Endgame at $858.3M), a record title for Christopher Nolan in The Odyssey ($539M), the continued affecting powers of Pixar in Toy Story 5 ($478M), the power of Nintendo at the B.O. with Super Mario Galaxy Movie ($429.8M), Lionsgate’s highest grossing movie ever with Michael ($372.3M), Amazon’s commitment to theatrical in Project Hail Mary ($344M) and the rise of the YouTube filmmakers in Focus Features’ highest grossing title ever, Obsession ($263.4M) in addition to A24’s all-time record, Backrooms ($197.5M).
Watch on Deadline
Summer stands at $4.4B, +26% ahead of last summer, 6% ahead of 2019’s at this point, and just -2% behind 2013 which remains the best summer ever at the domestic B.O. with $4.755B. If this summer is going to be a record, then it needs to gross $311.8M per Rentrak in the next 15 days, potentially a high bar. Next weekend there’s 20th Century Studios’ Ridley Scott directed Jacob Elordi title Dog Stars, Ketchup Entertainment’s Coyote vs. Acme, while over Labor Day there’s Paramount’s Mark Wahlberg mob title By Any Means and A24’s Adam Wingard directed Onslaught.

Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 introduced some powerful items to the loot pool, including the God Mode Llama. It allows you to enter ‘God Mode’ and go full ‘Override’ on your opponents. That said, here’s how to get the God Mode Llama in Fortnite.
Where to Find God Mode Llama in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4
There’s only one way to get the God Mode Llama in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4: using a Llama Supply Drop Gizmo. It is one of the many new Gizmos added to Override, which you can read more about in our Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 patch notes.

How to Use God Mode Llama in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4
To use the God Mode Llama in Fortnite, you’ll need to equip it in your inventory first. When you’re ready, press the “Fire” button to activate it. Once it’s active, you will get speed and jump boosts, unlimited stamina, and also invincibility for a short period of time. However, this invincibility will last for only 15 seconds.

You will also be able to run through structures and break them with ease. In a way, you gain the powers of the Sonic Power Sneakers in Fortnite, but with added benefits.

- You’ll be invincible for 15 seconds.
- You will gain speed and jump boosts.
- You will have unlimited stamina.
- You will not take damage from any source.
- You will be able to run through structures effortlessly.
Looking at the buffs you’ll receive for 15 seconds, it’s easy to understand why the God Mode Llama is an overpowered item in Fortnite. If you manage to also obtain a 1-Up Token in Fortnite, you can use them together in a single match to get yourself out of any situation.

The God Mode Llama item in Fortnite provides invincibility for 15 seconds, gives unlimited stamina, and boosts speed and jump height. It also allows you to run through structures and removes incoming damage from all sources, at the cost of removing your ability to use weapons.

Yes, the God Mode Llama takes up one inventory slot, which means it can be dropped or given to another Fortnite player.

Women and child healthcare were among the key priorities in the announcements made by Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj in the Legislative Assembly on Monday (August 17, 2026). In a first, the State government will formulate a ‘Peri-Menopausal Care Policy’ to enable early identification of the physical and mental health needs of women in the peri-menopausal age group, along with screening, counselling and treatment services.
Bluetooth-enabled blood pressure (BP) monitors will be introduced to track BP in pregnant women, with real-time transmission of data to facilitate timely intervention, while children under 18 with type 1 diabetes will receive free year-round insulin supply in government hospitals at a cost of ₹9.94 crore.
In the first phase, the BP apparatus will be provided to nearly 10,000 pregnant women in 14 districts, including Kallakurichi, Nilgiris, Tirupattur, Dharmapuri, Dindigul and Namakkal.
According to the announcement, under the peri-menopausal policy, camps would be conducted on a specific day every week at all primary health centres (PHC) and urban PHCs for symptomatic assessment, basic tests, counselling and referrals for treatment at district headquarters hospitals and government medical college hospitals.
“Irumbu Kanmani” - School Anaemia Prevention will be rolled out at a cost of ₹6.37 crore. Haemoglobin estimation will be done for nearly 16.5 lakh adolescents studying in classes VI, IX and XI in government and government-aided schools and appropriate treatment and monitoring will be done.
The department will launch rare genetic disease screening for newborns. Nearly 4.5 lakh babies delivered in all government hospitals in the State will be screened for seven rare genetic diseases in a hub-and-spoke model. This will include congenital hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, galactosemia and biotinidase deficiency.
Neo Genesis Unit for extreme low birth weight babies will be set up at a cost of ₹16.81 crore. The intrauterine/womb-like environments will be set up at the Institute of Obstetrics and Gynaecology in Chennai and government medical college hospitals in Madurai, Coimbatore, Tirunelveli, Chengalpattu and Tiruchi.
An Autism Early Detection Programme will be launched to screen children for autism spectrum disorder. For this, 12,456 village health nurses and 5,000 doctors will be trained. A Childhood Obesity Prevention Programme will be launched in schools, while a School Orthodontic Treatment programme will be rolled out in five districts — Cuddalore, Nagapattinam, Kancheepuram, Kallakurichi and Virudhunagar — covering 1,500 children at a cost of ₹1.80 crore.
Newborn hearing screening facilities such as Otoacoustic Emission and Sound Proof Room will be established. The monthly financial assistance for children affected by or living with HIV/AIDS will be increased and additional funds to the tune of ₹1.21 crore will be allotted.
Transport ventilators for newborns, modern equipment for human milk banks, mother and newborn care units, administration of ferric carboxy maltose injections for pregnant women with moderate anaemia and adolescent girls with severe anaemia and strengthening maternal and child care infrastructure were among other announcements.

Ajit Doval to visit China for boundary talks ahead of Xi’s India trip
Doval’s visit assumes greater significance as it comes ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected trip to India next month
National security adviser Ajit Doval is expected to visit China on Monday for a meeting of the Special Representatives on the boundary issue, which is part of efforts by the two sides to normalise ties, people familiar with the matter said on Sunday.
Doval is expected to meet his counterpart for the Special Representatives mechanism, Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi, on Tuesday, the people said on condition of anonymity. This will be the 25th round of talks under the mechanism, established in 2003 to work out a framework for resolving the dispute over the 3,488-km border.
Doval’s visit assumes greater significance as it comes ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected trip to India next month to participate in the BRICS Summit in New Delhi. Though both sides have not made an official announcement in this regard, Xi is expected to join the summit to be held during September 12-13, the people said.
This will be Xi’s first visit to India in seven years. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Xi last met in August 2025 on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in China.
The talks between the Special Representatives is being held against the backdrop of a recent standoff between Indian and Chinese troops in the Arunachal Pradesh sector of the Line of Actual Control (LAC). External affairs minister S Jaishankar reiterated at a media conclave on Saturday that the state of the border will determine the course of the overall India-China relationship.
“I think we went through a particularly bad patch between the summer of 2020 and the autumn of 2024, and that was primarily an outcome of the situation in the border areas,” Jaishankar said, referring to a military face-off in the Ladakh sector of the LAC that lasted more than four years and took bilateral ties to a six-decade low.
After the two sides reached an understanding on ending the face-off in Ladakh in October 2024, Xi and Modi met in Russia and agreed on measures to normalise ties and address the border dispute. Though the two sides have taken steps such as reviving the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, resuming direct flights and easing visa restrictions for Chinese nationals, there has been no forward movement on de-escalation on the LAC.
At the last round of Special Representatives’ talks in New Delhi a year ago, the two sides reiterated the “importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity” on the border to promote the overall development of ties.
According to an Indian readout issued at the time, the Special Representatives agreed on the need for a “political perspective” while working on a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable framework for settling the boundary question in line with the Agreement on Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for Settlement of the India-China Boundary Question of 2005.
They also agreed to set up an expert group under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (WMCC) on India-China Border Affairs to “explore early harvest in boundary delimitation”, and a working group under the WMCC to advance effective border management.
They further agreed to create general-level mechanisms in the eastern and middle sectors of the border, in addition to the existing general-level mechanism in the western sector.
There has been no word from both sides on what, if any, progress has been made on these matters.
The latest meeting of the WMCC, held in New Delhi on August 6, saw the two sides having detailed exchanges on “boundary delimitation, border management, mechanism‑building and trans‑border cooperation” as a follow-up to the last round of talks between the Special Representatives, according to an Indian readout.
