Trautman - who has treated child stars - said they often have "adult access" to drugs and alcohol without adult protection.
"We aren't equipped at a young age to be able to say no to it, to manage it, to correctly stay away from it altogether," he said.
Other child stars have talked about being exposed to drugs at an early age, including Drew Barrymore, who went to rehab at 12, and Demi Lovato, a Disney Channel star.
"I got into a car accident and they prescribed me opiates. My mum didn't think she would have to lock up the opiates from her 13-year-old daughter, but I was already drinking at that point," the singer told podcast Call Her Daddy in 2022.
Actress Michelle Rodriguez, who once hosted the World Music Awards with Panettiere, said this week that the number of child actors who had passed away at a young age was strange.
"I just can't stand how many young people are leaving us lately. It's disheartening, and it's making me think, 'What's going on?' It's not normal," she told Variety.
Panettiere's death comes just a year after the death of Michelle Trachtenberg and months after Daveigh Chase, two child stars who both struggled with drugs and alcohol.
In an essay she wrote after Panettiere's death, former Disney star Christy Carlson Romano compared early fame to a traumatic brain disease.
"[W]e have almost no language for what happens when stress, scrutiny, rejection, adult pressure, and the collapse of privacy become the architecture of a childhood," she wrote.
And when a child actor's career changes or comes to an end, they are left without the dopamine of fame and money that came with their identity as an actor, cautioned Trautman.
"At the same time many of them self medicated... so their brain is still reliant on that, and it's really really hard to stop using," he said.
Many child stars also have professional relationships with their parents, which can blur boundaries and leave them vulnerable, Trautman said.
In her book and in the media, Panettiere has discussed the pressure her mother placed on her to excel as an actress from an early age. She appeared in her first commercial when she was just 11-months-old.
"You always want to think the best of your parents and see them in the brightest light," the actress told the New York Times in May. "But there were a lot of things done with an approach that was not about my mental health or what was emotionally or mentally safe for me to do."
Substance abuse also puts people at risk for a host of medical conditions, including heart disease and liver and other organ damage.
Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition, and Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother was using heroin and cocaine leading up to his death.
But after he died, the actress told People Magazine in 2024 she was committed to staying sober, telling the outlet her addiction was "in the rear view mirror".
She said in her book that at one point a doctor told her that if she did not stop drinking, she would be "dead within five years".
For Moyers and other substance abuse experts, addiction is a chronic illness, meaning that relapses still happen even while treatment saves lives.
"Living in recovery means doing the best we can, but doing it imperfectly," he said.

Thank You for Your Inattention to This Matter
The good news is that the world has stopped responding breathlessly to Donald Trump’s every empty provocation. That’s also the bad news.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
One of Donald Trump’s current favorite riffs is to contrast how (in his opinion) the United States was seen under his predecessor, Joe Biden, and how it’s seen now.
“They didn’t respect us two years ago. They laughed at us. NATO laughed at us. Everybody laughed at us,” Trump said at a summit in Turkey with allies last month. “They don’t laugh anymore. There’s no more laughing.”
He’s right. It’s worse than laughing—they’re ignoring the president of the United States altogether. Trump styles himself as an heir to Theodore Roosevelt, but where Roosevelt said that America should speak softly and carry a big stick, Trump speaks loudly and carries a small one. Roosevelt’s bully pulpit has been reduced to a bullshit pulpit.
This week, Trump made two announcements that, in the past, would have shaken the globe. Speaking to Fox News’s Trey Yingst about negotiations with Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, Trump said, “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them.” In an ordinary world, such a threat would be a huge news event. Oman is not a hostile nation: It is one of the oldest U.S. allies in the Gulf region and has been a key intermediary in negotiations with Iran for years.
Yet the news drew little governmental response. Neither Oman nor other U.S. allies in the region issued official comments or took any other action that suggested that they found the threat realistic. One possible reason for their muted response is that Trump has actually made this threat before: He said in May that if Oman didn’t cooperate with Americans’ plans for the strait, “we’ll have to blow them up.”
Trump’s credibility has been undercut by his own capriciousness. Back then, he was threatening Oman over any negotiations that would imperil the neutrality of the Strait of Hormuz. On Tuesday, however, he posted a graphic on Truth Social that declared the strait a “NEW U.S. Territory.” (He’d previously said that he would soon declare it U.S. territory.) American annexation of an international waterway would represent a major shift in maritime legal precedent and require an enormous U.S.-military presence, but everyone knew that the pronouncement was nonsense. Trump has no means of controlling the strait, and The Washington Post reports that the Defense Department is actually considering a reduced regional footprint. Trump has also repeatedly promised that a deal with Iran is near completion, but after multiple false starts, these announcements fool only the markets.
This is a big shift. During his first term, Trump garnered outsized attention for outrageous statements. In August 2017, for example, he created an international incident by threatening North Korea with “fire, fury, and frankly power, the likes of which this world has never seen before.” Trump clearly delighted in how the press and global leaders would scramble to respond to these provocations, and some people argued that he was pursuing Richard Nixon’s “madman theory” of keeping adversaries off balance. One can draw a direct connection between the fire-and-fury threat in 2017 and Trump’s friendly statements about North Korea’s Kim Jong Un in the past week. But over time, the world has grown jaundiced about Trump’s threats.
The good news is that few world leaders and observers feel the need to take Trump’s outbursts seriously anymore. Fire drills driven by Trump’s idle talk fatigue the media, the public, and geopolitical systems, and they distract from more important stories. But that’s also the bad news. First, some of the things that Trump says are very dangerous. His favoritism toward North Korea could destabilize the region and encourage South Korea and Japan—to say nothing of Iran and other rogue states—to pursue nuclear-weapons programs. Second, he does occasionally follow through; Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro may have thought that Trump was bluffing before he was arrested during an American incursion in January.
Third, Trump needs credibility to enact his agenda, including to try to end the quagmire in Iran. On Wednesday, he said that he was “announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY!” All-caps notwithstanding, this declaration didn’t receive a great deal of attention. (“They have no clear plan, unfortunately,” one Middle Eastern diplomat told NOTUS.) In order for the sanctions regime he envisions to have its greatest effect, Trump will need the cooperation of allies as well as rival powers such as China. But years of empty boasts and months of feints on Iran mean that other world leaders don’t really heed Trump’s statements. He’s failed to enlist key allies in the war effort, and China has declined to take any concrete action in the strait, despite Trump traveling to Beijing in May to pressure Xi Jinping.
This diminished respect given to presidential statements is self-evidently bad for Trump, and it does nothing to make America great again. But it’s also bad for the world. Even now, no other country has the power the U.S. has to maintain order, and the closest challengers, Russia and China, pursue systems that are repressive and dangerous. The U.S. can regain credibility only by using its rhetoric more carefully and matching its actions to its words—two things that are unlikely to happen under Trump. If he wants to be believed, the president needs to either surrender some American influence or show that his threats are real, and neither option is appealing. The costs of not being taken seriously are very serious indeed.

Ossoff’s ‘Natalie’ Moment
The Georgia senator’s latest viral moment reveals much about Trump—and plenty about Ossoff himself.
How many words does it take to trigger MAGA world? Three, it turns out.
When Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia said at a rally on Sunday that President Trump wants to “travel with Natalie”—implying an untoward relationship between the 80-year-old grandfather and his 35-year-old special assistant, Natalie Harp—the outrage from Trump allies was as loud as it was predictable: Megyn Kelly, Newt Gingrich, and Laura Ingraham, among others, accused Ossoff of misogyny, despite having previously defended Trump’s own sexist comments. (The word hypocrisy feels inadequate here.)
But as this debate over propriety unfolds, a dedicated swath of the Democratic base is delighted. Since Trump’s reelection, these voters have been hankering to see their leaders show, well, a little more fight. So far, most of that fight seems to have come from midterm candidates on the far left, who often target the Democratic Party itself or the so-called establishment. To hear Ossoff, a more moderate Democrat in a reddish-purple state, direct a sharp—albeit petty—jab directly at the president thrilled such voters.
Some, in fact, found it almost cathartic. “Someone finally said something,” a 52-year-old woman named Rebecca, who attended Ossoff’s Atlanta rally, told me, sounding delighted. Bring on the “smoke,” Aaron Whitely, the chair of the Democratic Party of Chatham County, in Georgia, told me. “The younger folks are looking for it. The older folks are loving it.”
Ossoff appears to know this. It’s why viral clips of the senator, who is running for reelection, seem to pop up every few weeks like zinnias in summer. It’s also why you can’t have a conversation about the 2028 presidential race without mentioning his name. But just because the base loves the smoke doesn’t mean every other Georgia voter will.
Throughout Ossoff’s reelection campaign, Democratic talking heads have credited the senator for succinctly calling out the Trump administration’s alleged self-dealing. His speech at the Center Stage Theater in Atlanta on Sunday afternoon contained his usual anti-corruption message: “They made you pay more for everything and took us to war on lies and spent most of last year trying to cover up for the world’s most famous pedophile,” he told the crowd, “while the crook president and his crook family raked in billions.”
But this time, about 10 minutes into the speech, Ossoff threw in the comment that lit up social media and group chats. “The president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks,” he said. “See, he doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.”
The rowdy crowd laughed and groaned. Ossoff’s speeches are typically so dense with current-affairs references that only the most plugged-in rally-goers fully understand them. In those few lines alone, the senator nodded to the ongoing Iran war, to viral footage of Trump appearing to nap in public, to the controversial gift of a plane that Trump was forced to abandon because of security concerns, and, ultimately, to Trump’s intense closeness with Harp, the aide whose obsession with the president reportedly alarmed the Secret Service. Attendees understood him immediately. “He didn’t have to make any reference to their relationship; it’s very well known,” Rebecca, who declined to share her last name for fear of being targeted by the administration, said. “It’s in the public consciousness.”
People who have scrolled Facebook or tuned in to MS NOW during the past two years—and plenty of engaged Democrats of a certain age have done both, obsessively—are quite familiar with Harp. In 2024, reporting from Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan identified her as Trump’s closest aide, one who keeps the president updated on positive press coverage and social-media buzz and who once gushed to Trump in a letter, “You are all that matters to me.” This week, CNN reported that Harp had once hunkered down in the trunk of an SUV to avoid being separated from the president. Another report revealed that Harp had worked in the White House for more than a year without an active security clearance.
It’s obvious that Ossoff’s comment about Harp found its target in the West Wing, because, as that awful saying goes, a hit dog really does tend to holler. “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, posted. When the CNN reporter Kristen Holmes asked Trump about Ossoff’s remark, the White House Rapid Response X account called her a “disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession” and said that one day, her children would be “sickened and embarrassed” by her. Soon, it was as though a private memo had gone out—and perhaps one did—to MAGA talking heads instructing them to frame Ossoff’s words as a misogynistic smear on a woman simply doing her job. “I feel bad for your staff if this is what you think of women,” Representative Anna Paulina Luna of Florida wrote on X. “Donald Trump has done more to elevate women in politics than any other President,” CNN’s Scott Jennings, who might be auditioning to replace Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary, offered on X.
Some Democrats were irked with Ossoff too. The comments about Natalie “distracted and detracted from the power” of his otherwise effective message, the former Barack Obama adviser David Axelrod wrote on X. On the whole, “Ossoff has gone after Trump in a tough, fair, and pointed way,” Axelrod told me on a phone call yesterday. “This just seemed a little unnecessary and a bit gratuitous.”
Axelrod’s response was dismissed by the voters and local party leaders I spoke with as too sensitive. They pointed out that Ossoff had made only a light reference to Harp—one that a listener could interpret as they pleased. He didn’t actually accuse them of having an affair! Even if he had, those Democrats said, isn’t it time for party leaders to take a break from the high road? When I read Axelrod’s quote over the phone to Wanda Townes, the chair of the Democrats of Camden County, in Georgia, she was instantly annoyed. “That softness is the reason that Trump is in office. Stop being soft,” she told me. (“There’s no doubt it was chum in the water” for people “who feel like Trump has pushed Democrats around,” Axelrod said when I asked for his response.)
Earlier this summer, I wrote about the Democrats’ frustration that their party leaders still haven’t seemed to match their voters’ rage. “We’re still pissed that we lost the election in 2024—and we’re pissed at them for not doing a better job of standing up to the Republicans and to Trump,” Susan Polakoff Shaw, a leader of an Ohio grassroots Democratic group, told me then. It makes sense that she loved Ossoff’s comment this week about Harp. “If nothing else, Ossoff shed light on who this young woman is, what her job is, and the twisted relationship the two of them have,” she texted me. “I mean, who writes love letters to an 80 year old!??”
Pissed is certainly the operative word. And Ossoff has been successful lately because he sounds about as ticked off as voters are and channels that anger into clippable sound bites for social media. California Governor Gavin Newsom similarly attempts to provoke Trump in an aggressive, Trumpian style. But from Ossoff, who cuts a more wholesome figure and doesn’t imitate the president, the attacks are more surprising—and therefore perhaps more effective. Videos of the senator that have gone viral this year include Ossoff referring to Trump as a “failed president and a national disgrace” and using the phrases “Mar-a-Lago mafia” and “the Epstein class” to describe the president’s allies. Last month, Ossoff repeatedly asked Jay Clayton, Trump’s nominee for director of national intelligence, who had won the 2020 presidential election and called it “humiliating” when Clayton would not answer.
This kind of assertiveness is refreshing to Democrats, the party members I spoke with said. “Older white ladies, older Black ladies—they’re loving it,” Whitely said. Townes described her ideal future for the Democrats: “We need more Ossoffs; we need more Jasmine Crocketts,” she said, referring to the Texas representative whose own MAGA jabs have gone viral.
There is, of course, a downside to jabbing in politics: Not every voter relishes the melee. Crockett, to use Townes’s example, lost a primary for Senate in Texas this year, at least in part because even the Democrats who loved her pugnacity did not believe that she would be able to persuade independent and moderate Texans to vote for a Democrat. Similarly, success for Ossoff will be measured not by how much he delights his party’s most loyal supporters but by how many Georgians he can win over in November.
Madison Hahamy contributed research to this report.

Newcastle and Liverpool united in tribute to legend Keegan
- Published
Kevin Keegan's family were in attendance as Newcastle United and Liverpool supporters came together to pay tribute to the former England captain.
Keegan, who played for both clubs, before going on to manage Newcastle, died at the age of 75 last month following a battle with cancer.
As the teams met for the first time since his death, in their Premier League season opener at St James' Park on Sunday, members of Keegan's family were present in the directors' box.
A number of Keegan's former players from this memorable first spell in charge of Newcastle, between 1992 and 1997, were also at the game.
These included Alan Shearer, Rob Lee, Peter Beardsley, Tino Asprilla, Warren Barton, Shaka Hislop, Lee Clark, Darren Peacock, Steve Watson, Ruel Fox, Steve Howey and Liam O'Brien.
In the warm-up, players from both sides wore Keegan 7 on the back of their shirts while a centre circle mosaic made up of more than 500 shirts left outside St James' Park following Keegan's death was unfurled in the centre circle a few minutes later.
A tribute video to Keegan was then played on the big screen before supporters' group Wor Flags unveiled a huge display, which involved every seat in the ground, including Liverpool supporters.
Keegan 7 was spelt out in the Leazes End, there was a massive tifo of 'King Kev' in the East Stand and, in the Gallowgate End, there was a memorable quote from the most transformational figure in Newcastle's history.
"I want people to dream about their football club," the banner read. "They should. We should all be dreamers at heart. Some people are the opposite and say, 'We can't do that'. But when you ask them why, they can't give a reason. Well, I say, 'Why not?'"
The teams and fans then joined together in an emotional minute's applause before the match as "one Kevin Keegan" rang out from the stands.
Keegan's family wrote an open letter in advance of the game to thank supporters for "filling us with so much comfort during these difficult days" after they previously saw the huge number of tributes left outside the stadium.
"The sea of black and white shirts and scarves, alongside colours from so many other clubs, reminded us how much Kevin meant to the footballing world," they said.
"It was a sombre moment that reminded us of our pain and loss, yet matched with immense pride and love as we read so many personal and heartfelt messages.
"Kevin always shared his love for Newcastle United, Geordies, and the city, captivating us with stories told with his infectious smile.
"Seeing these tributes brought those stories to life for Kevin's grandchildren, showing them how deeply their grandfather was loved in return."

Our phones have become do-it-all gadgets. They enable us to keep in touch with one another, track how many steps we're taking each day, snap photos of everything, and access the collective knowledge of humanity. All that universal functionality extends across both our work and personal lives.
The gadget that pings you on Slack when your colleague has a question is the same one that alerts you when your friend has just outscored you at Wordle. That blurring of boundaries can be a problem.
There is actually a solution to this, at least if you're using an Android phone. Android supports the use of multiple profiles (based on Google accounts), so you can switch between two different ones as needed. The most obvious use case for this is to split up your work and personal usage.
It's essentially like having two phones on the same physical device: The profile that's active dictates the apps you can use, the notifications you see, the browsing history you can dig into, and the files you've got access to, all dictated by the Google account.
Note that while this feature has been around in Android for a long time and is available on many handsets (including Pixel phones), not every Android manufacturer has implemented it. It's not available on Galaxy phones, for example, though Samsung does offer something similar with the Secure Folder.
Get Started
To begin with, you're going to need two Google accounts, but many of us already have a Google account managed by work anyway. If not, you can set up a new Google account, free of charge, to use as the basis of the work profile on your phone: Head to the Google account portal on the web, then click Create an account.
The details you'll need to provide include a first name, your birthday, and a Gmail address you'd like to register to use with the account—this is what you'll use to sign in to this account on your phone and on the web. You get some suggestions for an available address based on your name, but you can also come up with something custom as long as no one else has taken it first.
Once you've got a second account you can use, open Settings, then choose System > Users. Tap Add user, then Next, and you're able to give a name to the second user account. With that done, select it from the Users screen, choose the Switch to... option, and you'll be taken through the process of signing in to your secondary Google account.
The setup process that follows is very similar to the one for setting up your phone in the first place. You can set a PIN code, a fingerprint scan, or a face scan (depending on the options your phone offers) to stop other people from accessing your account, and you will be asked to work through the various Android terms-and-conditions screens.
Using Your Second Profile
After you've set up a second profile, you'll be taken straight to it. It will make your phone look like a brand-new device, with the default home screen layout and wallpaper in place. Any configuration changes you've made to Android on your main account will have to be done on this secondary one too.
There are a couple of ways to switch between profiles. You can head to Settings > System > Users and pick an account from the list, or you can do a two-finger swipe down from the top of the screen to open Quick Settings and tap the user account icon underneath the widgets (it's just to the left of the settings cog icon).
You'll need to configure all of your apps again on this secondary account—which is the point of the extra profile, after all. Open up Google Photos, for example, and you'll be prompted to go through the process of choosing your backup options again. You'll also need to install the apps you need on this secondary account, which can be a different set from those on your other profile.
Some parts of the Android experience are shared between profiles, including Wi-Fi network information. However, you won't be able to see saved files or apps in your second profile from your original one (or vice versa). You might want to install a third-party cloud storage app if you need to share files between accounts regularly.
On the Settings > System > Users screen for your primary account, you'll see an Allow user switch option: You can turn this off if you want to temporarily disable user switching (it removes the icon on Quick Settings, for example), but it won't remove the second account from your phone. To do that, select it on the Users screen and pick Delete user.

President Trump Has a Pet-Project Docket at the National Parks
The National Park Service changed the way it prioritizes projects so that the president’s requests are quickly approved.
President Trump gets what he wants, when he wants it, from the National Park Service. One and a half million dollars to replace brick pavers in Lafayette Park, across from the White House? Contracting officials at the NPS Washington headquarters found the money within five days last month. A $170,000 request to remove a fence around the Hains Point golf course, preparing the ground for a new “championship-quality” layout? Six days this summer. And the more–than–$5 million project to gild equine statues along the nearby Memorial Bridge? That took 12 days.
The rapid-approval system is specific to projects Trump wants, thanks to a reorganization at the Interior Department led by Secretary Doug Burgum. Trump issued an executive order to make the District of Columbia “safe and beautiful,” justifying the creation of an NPS docket of “White House priorities” that is handled separately from other park projects and is prioritized both for funding and contracting resources, according to documents I obtained and interviews with five current or former NPS officials. Meanwhile, many other projects throughout the nationwide system of parks are languishing.
The list I received includes Trump’s well-known projects on the National Mall and the refurbishment of the White House, along with several lesser-known efforts: The hiring and equipping of 450 new U.S. Park Police officers in the Washington region, and more than $12.8 million—some of which came from the Department of Justice—for police equipment, including new Flock license-plate-reading cameras, radios, tasers, laptops, body cameras, and body armor. Internal documentation for park projects typically includes “Consequences of Failure to Act,” which scores the urgency based on health and safety measures. When work began in January on fountains near the White House, officials described the need for the work in this way: “Such failure will disappoint visitors, as well as residents and employees of the White House.”
The new project-funding system was described by a contracting officer during an April meeting with NPS officials. “There’s three different lists: White House priorities, high priorities, and low priorities,” the official told colleagues on the virtual call, according to a written account that was provided to me. Those on the call, who do not work on White House priorities, were advised that projects on the low-priority list likely would not be completed, so they should attempt to get their needs moved to the high-priority list. White House priorities, meanwhile, were nonnegotiable. As Washington is beautified at great expense, officials told me, vital needs at dozens of national parks are not being filled.
I obtained copies of the high- and low-priority lists that circulated this summer inside the NPS. As of mid-July, that low-priority list included 1,573 projects, including many that officials told me would have been funded under prior administrations. Projects that have not yet been funded from that list, according to a separate national-park database, include requests for new wildlife-resistant dumpsters in Bryce Canyon National Park, snow machines to provide fire remediation in Alaska’s remote Yukon–Charley Rivers National Preserve, and an archaeological survey of recently acquired land at Camp Nelson National Monument, a major Union supply base during the Civil War that trained Black soldiers.
The Interior Department dismissed the concerns over this approach when I reached out for comment and told me that the low-priority list I had obtained included items that had been “mis-prioritized and were corrected.” Interior leaders have also boasted about new funding streams, including revenue from more expensive national-park passes for foreign visitors. “In any year, the National Park Service must prioritize projects most in need,” the press office said in an unsigned statement. “The National Park Service has not only been focused on beautifying the district for the 250th celebrations in our nation’s capital but has also been working on many deferred maintenance projects throughout the country.”
But those working in the parks say that it is not just money holding these projects back. It’s also a lack of staff, after rounds of workforce reductions, who are able to handle contracts, a problem that the contracting official on the April call referred to as “capacity.” When Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency targeted the department last year, many contracting managers at the NPS took buyouts, and many of those who remained found themselves reassigned within the larger department. The NPS had 179 full-time administrative officers in June, a 21 percent decrease from the month Trump took office, according to Office of Management and Budget records. The result is a growing backlog of unfinished projects in far-flung parks, as government employees try to jury-rig temporary fixes, the officials said. “There is very little acquisition support,” one of the NPS employees told me. “This is going to get exponentially worse.”
Spencer Morgan, the site superintendent of the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site, in Buffalo, New York, told me that his facility is still waiting on this fiscal year’s promised operating-support funding, which needs to arrive before the end of September, or he will have to institute major cuts. He has been told that an additional stream of routine-maintenance funding he was expecting will never arrive. Because the site is run in conjunction with a local nonprofit that pays Morgan’s salary, he said that he was comfortable speaking openly about the struggles his staff faces as funding and resources are instead directed to the White House list. “I am not beholden to hold my tongue at this point,” he said.
Inside the NPS, Morgan said, the staff has been decimated. “I started in this role in April of 2024, and the number of people who are not there since I started is gut-wrenching,” he told me. “There is a whole loss of institutional knowledge.”
Other NPS employees requested anonymity to speak with me because they fear retaliation from their supervisors. One employee told me that their park can’t hire employees to fill vacant slots but also can’t contract out work, because it’s difficult to get on the high-priority list. “We keep being told to be creative,” this employee said. “And we are running into dead ends every time we try to pivot.”
This reduction in spending showed up in budgetary documents I reported on in June. The documents showed a decrease of $854 million, or 68 percent, in spending on projects in park regions outside the Washington area in the first eight and a half months of fiscal year 2026, compared with the full prior fiscal year. During that same period, spending around Washington increased by about $100 million, not counting about $310 million in donations that the NPS received from allies of the president, most of which is going to fund a new White House ballroom.
The frustration over these shifting priorities has been a frequent topic of conversation among park superintendents, who are struggling to maintain services this summer. At another NPS meeting in early July, an employee presented a list of 133 projects, totaling $35.8 million, that they said were ready to go but lacked contracting staff to make them happen, according to a person on the call.
It’s not clear whether all of the projects on the White House priority list will receive funding this fiscal year. The list also includes a $25 million plan to replace the Eagle One helicopter used by the U.S. Park Police (and at least once by Burgum when he was running late for an Air Force One flight), $475,000 to clean and repaint the White House exterior, drones “to support law enforcement” in the Washington region, a new park-police substation for Rock Creek Park, and streetlight replacement along the National Mall. The priority list also includes improvements for parts of the country where Trump is known to travel. The document shows a $77,300 expense to clear brush and plant new trees around Camp David, the presidential retreat in Maryland, as part of a much larger effort to plant 3,000 trees and provide a “security benefit” to the facility.
 
 And Trump continues to add more projects to the list—or expand projects already on it. Take, for example, the brick pavers in Lafayette Park outside the White House gates. In May, Trump said that the park renovation would be funded by “a contribution that I made,” even though internal documentation shows public funds being used. After the Fourth of July celebrations, the NPS agreed to pay an additional $1.5 million to replace more of the brick pavers in that park. Then, in August, the president told reporters in the Oval Office that he was still deliberating on whether the brick pavers were good enough.
“Now we have a big decision to make,” he said. “Do we take the pavers that are red—you know, the red-brick pavers—and do we change them into a granite, to gray granite? They’re beautiful, but they’re not the original. So we’re gonna have to make that decision.” The National Park Service, no doubt, will be ready to follow the president’s lead if he pivots.

My colleague Paresh Dave and I each spent a day in federal court in Oakland, California, this week, monitoring the latest Meta child safety trial.
In case you missed it in the spring, Meta (along with YouTube) lost a landmark social media case in California, in which a jury found the companies liable for harming a young user with certain design features in their apps. Then, earlier this month, Meta was ordered to pay more than $940 million in the state of New Mexico for being a public nuisance and causing psychological harm to children.
Now Meta is defending itself in a federal civil trial taking place in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. The plaintiffs in this case are 29 state attorneys general. They’re claiming that Meta violated a federal privacy law protecting children, known as COPPA, by improperly collecting personal information about children under 13 without parental consent. The lead AGs, which span four states—California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey—also say that Meta made deceptive statements about its platform that were likely to mislead consumers.
Two specific Meta apps are in focus in this trial: Facebook and Instagram.
Meta maintains that it satisfied COPPA law requirements in those states, and denies that its statements about how its apps work were deceptive or misleading. It also insists it is protected from liability by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996, which essentially says that platforms like Meta aren’t responsible for the content posted on their apps by users.
I was in the packed courtroom Tuesday to hear opening arguments from both sides, presided over by chief district judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. Per usual, Meta was represented by an army of well-heeled lawyers, who quite ironically kept experiencing technical difficulties with the mic. Megan O’Neill, the deputy attorney general at the California Department of Justice, kicked off the opening statements, laying out how the state AGs believe Meta deliberately hooked kids on its apps and harvested their data.
O’Neill emphasized that throughout the trial, the jury would be shown just “how many features work both individually and together to keep people in the apps. To draw them in and keep them in for longer. Meta has used these features to draw kids onto the apps, and to keep them coming back.”
Meta lead attorney Paul Schmidt then laid out the dozens of safety features that have been built into Meta’s apps over the past several years, and he said the company is committed to improving its apps. He also shifted some responsibility onto users, saying there’s no dispute that some kids find their way onto Meta’s apps and that some teens “struggle to manage their time.” And inevitably some people will post negative content on social media apps, Schmidt said.
Later on Tuesday and then again on Wednesday, the courtroom heard from Arturo Bejar, a former Meta employee and key witness in earlier trials. His main point: Mark Zuckerberg didn’t prioritize youth safety. It was part of company culture during Bejar’s time there that if you had an inkling of an idea for a feature that would spur growth, “you could just test it,” he said. At the same time, he described a culture in which it was “near impossible” to screen products and features for potential harms.
(On Thursday, the trial was put on pause due to a sick juror.)
Meta has been embroiled in a remarkable number of scandals over the past decade, many of which have faded from public memory, been chalked up to the cost of doing business, or were settled out of court. The company’s platforms have played a role in stoking violence and swaying elections. It has regularly siphoned personal data from users in purposefully opaque ways. Not to mention the amount of internal workplace dysfunction at Meta that’s been revealed through depositions, books, and news reports like these.
All the while, Meta’s formidable technology—the AI that underpins its apps—has successfully kept people hooked. And Meta has monetized its business by keeping their feeds lined with uncannily targeted ads. No amount of scandal can seem to keep Meta’s users away for very long.
But these recent social media trials have, shall we say, ominous vibes for Meta. So far, Meta’s legal strategy hasn’t proved to be a winning one. Other companies in Meta’s social media cohort, like Snap, TikTok, and YouTube, have opted this year to settle some suits that allege their platforms have harmed kids’ mental health. Meta instead chose to go to trial, only to very publicly lose and pay massive fines.
It’s not just billions of dollars at stake for Meta in this case (the state AGs are seeking some $200 billion in damages). Meta faces the possibility of having to make changes to core features of its platforms. Those include stricter age-gating and enforcement of existing safety features for younger users, like time limits. Meta might also be compelled to eliminate “likes” and the “endless scroll” for younger users, and offer more algorithmic transparency about how a user’s feed is tuned.
My colleague Paresh told me after reporting from the courthouse on Wednesday that while a lot of the jurors or potential jurors indicated they barely use Facebook for anything besides Marketplace (relatable!), “they do use Instagram, and many have concerns about their own use or their children’s.” At the same time, Paresh got the sense that the jurors want or expect “parents to have a role in oversight, and not just quickly blame everything on the company.”
“So there’s something about this trial that could really represent the voice of the zeitgeist around social media usage,” Paresh told me.
We both agreed that there’s probably no scandal that will make people quit Instagram en masse if they’re already hooked. But if the judge rules in favor of the AGs, based on the evidence presented, then Meta could be held accountable—not for the content it serves on its platform but for how that content is served to younger, more impressionable users. It could force small changes in the company’s growth-at-all-costs ethos and the algorithmic witchcraft with which it juices its apps. And it could change the outcomes for a generation of iPad babies who ostensibly wouldn’t grow up as hooked on Meta’s apps. Maybe.
Paresh Dave contributed to this story.

A US judge on Monday dismissed criminal charges against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, after the justice department said it had decided to abandon the fraud and bribery case.
The Brooklyn-based district judge Nicholas Garaufis’s decision to grant federal prosecutors’ rare attempt to toss the case came after he inquired into their reasons for doing so, including by asking Adani whether anything was promised in exchange for the dropping of the case. In November 2024, before the charges were unsealed, Adani had promised to invest $10bn in the United States.
Adani was charged in 2024 with agreeing to bribe Indian government officials so a subsidiary of his Adani Group could win approval to develop a solar energy plant, then misleading US investors by providing reassuring information about his company’s anti-corruption practices.
Adani Group has consistently denied wrongdoing. Adani himself has not appeared in US court to respond to the charges. On 18 May, the justice department announced it would no longer pursue the case. That marked the latest instance in which federal prosecutors had sought to drop a high-profile white-collar criminal prosecution during Donald Trump’s second term in the White House.
Legal experts say US judges have little discretion to compel prosecutors to continue with criminal cases they no longer wish to pursue, but the charges cannot be formally dismissed without a judge’s approval.
Garaufis asked the justice department to justify its decision to drop the charges, writing that its “bland and conclusory” announcement did not give him enough information.
In a 4 July court filing, Trent McCotter, a senior justice department official, said the case was primarily foreign, hard to prove and inconsistent with the agency’s current priorities.
In the filing, McCotter also denied as false what he called media stories suggesting he sought to dismiss the case in part because of a promise by Adani to invest money in the United States.
In response, Garaufis asked Adani whether he was “aware of any agreement exchanging anything for the dismissal of the indictment”.
In a sworn declaration filed in court on 15 July, Adani said he was not aware of any such agreement. He acknowledged having previously promised to invest $10bn in the US and said his lawyers told the justice department in meetings that the pledge “might be part of a resolution of these matters”. Robert Giuffra, a lawyer for Adani, said in a 15 July court filing that the justice department had told him that it would not consider the Adani Group’s willingness to invest in the US as part of any resolution.

Gujarat spurious liquor case death toll rises to 13; three remain hospitalised
The Bhavnagar spurious liquor death toll has risen to 13, with 61 people affected and 14 arrested in the Gujarat methanol poisoning case.
The death toll in the Bhavnagar spurious liquor case rose to 13 on Sunday after two more people died during treatment, while three others remained hospitalised in stable condition, officials said.
Bhavnagar collector Manish Bansal said two more people had died during treatment since Saturday evening. Bhargavbhai Upadhyay, 42, died on Sunday, while Mukeshbhai Manilal Damor, 36, died on Saturday. Both were residents of Bhavnagar.
Three people remain under treatment — two at Sir T Hospital and one at Pulse Hospital. All three are stable, officials added.
A total of 61 people have been affected in the incident, officials said.
Gujarat is a dry state, where the manufacture, sale and consumption of liquor are prohibited under the state’s prohibition law.
The liquor was first consumed at a party at a farmhouse in Kharakadi village on the night of August 16, according to the FIR. Yadav fell ill after consuming the liquor and was admitted to a hospital in Bhavnagar on August 17. He died during treatment on August 18.
Also Read: Gujarat SMC arrests 13, detains MP-based key suspect for toxic liquor that killed 7
The case was initially registered at Vartej police station as an accidental death case on August 18. During the investigation, police found that more people had died and suffered serious injuries after consuming spurious liquor. Gujarat DGP GS Malik then handed the investigation to the SMC.
Key accused Raees was arrested on Friday and remanded in police custody for nine days, taking the total number of arrests to 14, officials said. Police have registered cases against 21 accused.
The FIR alleges that Raees, Gautam Virambhai Solanki (24) of Vartej, and Zuber of Ujjain travelled to Ahmedabad to procure methanol, bottles, caps and liquor stickers. They allegedly prepared spurious liquor at Solanki’s house.
According to the FIR, the accused first prepared around 51 cases of spurious liquor and sold them. They destroyed a second batch, after which Raees allegedly brought Narendra Singh Yadav from Madhya Pradesh because of his expertise in preparing liquor. The group then allegedly prepared around 25 more cases and supplied them to bootleggers and consumers in Bhavnagar.
Yadav was admitted to a Bhavnagar hospital on August 17 after consuming the liquor and died during treatment on August 18, according to the FIR.
The FIR alleges that methanol was used to prepare the spurious liquor. A seized bottle contained 38.59% methanol and 0.94% ethanol, while methanol was detected in blood samples collected from victims.
Two police inspectors and five other police personnel were suspended after a preliminary investigation found negligence.

The Asus PG27UCWM brings a new sub-pixel layout to the world of OLED gaming monitors, and in my testing, I appreciated the improvements it brings to the table.
Top-notch contrast. Outstanding color performance. Crisp motion clarity. Absolutely loaded with extra features.
TIRED
Mirror-like display finish isn’t for everyone. Stand takes up a lot of space on the desk. Expensive at full price.
RGB Stripe OLED panels are the new hotness in 2026. The new OLED panel technology is designed to improve text clarity and color performance, which potentially give a monitor like the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM a broader appeal beyond just a typical gaming monitor.
That is, perhaps, why Asus takes the everything-and-the-kitchen-sink approach. At a glance, it might seem like a typical 4K OLED gaming monitor. It has a 26.5-inch tandem 4K RGB Stripe OLED panel, a 240Hz refresh rate, and HDR support with VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black certification. But it's also rounded out with tons of features, which helps make the higher price of $1,200 easier to swallow.
Super Glossy, Superior Contrast
The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM has the company’s unique TrueBlack display finish, which is designed to deliver an ultrahigh-contrast experience in a wide variety of lighting conditions. It does so with a high-gloss coat that minimizes the impact of ambient light across the display.
It’s not just marketing drivel. The TrueBlack finish provides noticeably deeper black levels in a bright room. The matte OLED finish on Samsung’s OLEDs looks positively hazy by comparison. Glossy OLED monitors from competing brands also look less contrast-rich, though the difference is most noticeable in a very bright room—brighter, I suspect, than most PC gaming dens.
I also feel it comes across in how colors present. Technically, the monitor’s results are modest for an OLED monitor: It has a color gamut that spanned 94 percent of DCI-P3 and 89 percent of AdobeRGB. That’s a tad more narrow than top QD-OLED monitors, which can hit up to 98 percent and 95 percent, respectively. However, the ultra-clear, high-contrast look of the panel amplifies the sense of impact. I’m not saying it’s better than the best competitors, but the PG27UCWM’s overall image quality is in the upper tier. That's at least partially due to the fact that RGB Stripe OLED also improves “color volume," which is a display's ability to maintain color that gamut had max brightness.
Unfortunately, the vivid and contrast-rich image is paired with mirror-like reflections. I could likely use the monitor to shave. It’s not a problem in a dark room, but it’s noticeable when even modest ambient light is present.
This is an important, and divisive, point. Many OLED purists adore an ultra-gloss finish because it highlights the rich contrast and color the technology can provide. Others, myself included, prefer matte displays that reduce or eliminate discernible reflections.
There’s no right answer to this question, but you’ll need to decide your preference before you make a purchase.
Great for Sharpness, Great HDR
Beneath the PG27UCWM’s glossy coat you’ll find a tandem RGB Stripe OLED panel with a native resolution of 3840 x 2160. It’s crisp. Earlier OLED monitors have used an unusual sub-pixel arrangement that could hurt image clarity, but the PG27UCWM has a more conventional RGB sub-pixel layout that eliminates the issue. You'll sometimes see this marketed as “5th-Gen QD-OLED," and it initially launched in 34-inch monitors like the Alienware AW3426DW. But finally, the PG27UCWM is bringing it to the more standard 27-inch size.
Text clarity, in particular, has always been one of the chief issues about those shopping for OLED monitors, and I no longer have complaints in that regard. The resolution helps, too, providing a pixel density of about 165 pixels per inch across the 26.5-inch panel. The panel’s sharpness was excellent with the monitor connected to both my Windows 11 desktop and my MacBook Air M4.
HDR is where the PG27UCWM’s tandem OLED panel really begins to earn its keep. My testing found it can hit up to 800 nits of brightness. While that’s not a record-setting result, it’s in line with other premium OLED monitors, which typically offer 800 to 900 nits in my testing (the best barely clear 1,000 nits). The monitor also supports Dolby Vision HDR, which is rare.
The PG27UCWM’s brightness, contrast, and resolution combine to deliver real impact in HDR games. It’s so bright that it can at times feel overwhelming. Fortunately, Asus includes HDR brightness adjustment options that let you tone down the brightness if you’d prefer.
Asus’ PG27UCWM isn’t uniquely bright in HDR though. The Alienware AW3426DW, Acer Predator X27 X1, and MSI MPG 32URXW are among the monitors I’ve tested that deliver similar HDR brightness (and some of which are significantly cheaper). Still, the PG27UCWM performs much better than least expensive OLED monitors like the entry-level Alienware AW2726DM, which can only deliver roughly 400 nits in HDR.
Motion Clarity Checks the Boxes
The PG27UCWM can reach a refresh rate of up to 240 Hz at 4K resolution. That’s standard for a high-end 4K OLED in 2026. It also provides a dual-mode feature that can reduce the resolution to 1080p in exchange for a refresh rate of up to 480 Hz. That’s less common, though many OLED monitors now offer a similar feature.
I think the 1080p/480Hz mode will prove niche, as the monitor’s motion clarity is already excellent at 4K and 240 Hz. Motion blur is minimal and small objects are easy to make out. Though perhaps most useful in games, the monitor’s motion clarity is also noticeable on a Windows 11 or macOS desktop. Scrolling text is readable and OS animations look ultrasmooth.
Still, the 480 Hz mode has uses. It’s ideal for people who like to play competitively in esports titles, yet also want to enjoy maximum image quality in single-player games. The PG27UCWM can handle both without compromise.
The PG27UCWM lists compatibility with AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, Nvidia G-Sync, and VESA Adaptive Sync. In practice, many monitors that list support for only one of these can work with all three, as they are based on the same core technology. However, I always prefer to see official support listed, so you don’t have to guess whether adaptive sync will work with your PC or game console.
Features Galore
The PG27UCWM is more than just excellent image quality though. Asus has packed it full with a treasure trove of features to sweeten the deal.
The monitor’s design is top-notch. It includes attractive transparent plastic elements on the rear of the display and an RGB-LED logo that can be synced to other RGB-LED devices with Asus’ Aura Sync. An ergonomic stand is included and offers the usual range of adjustment for height, tilt, swivel, and pivot; VESA mounting for third-party arms and stands is possible with a provided adapter.
There’s also an 1/4-inch screw mount on the top of the stand neck. This is a common type of mount for camera and streaming equipment. You can use the mount to place a webcam or ring light above the monitor. It’s an uncommon but useful feature.
I do have one nitpick with the stand, and that’s the stand base. Asus opts for a wide base that takes up a lot of desk space. It’s not the largest I’ve seen, but I prefer the more compact stand base found with competitors like the MSI MPG 272URX and Alienware AW2725Q. On the plus side, though, the stand is remarkably solid. Most monitor stands allow a hint of wobble if I purposefully jostle my desk, but the PG27UCWM is unbothered.
Image-quality purists will be happy to see the monitor is packed with adjustments. These include multiple color space presets, color temperature and gamma modes that target precise values, and six-axis color saturation adjustment.
The monitor even has a built-in sensor that can detect ambient light and the user’s presence. This is used primarily to enable the monitor’s OLED burn-in reduction features, which can turn off the monitor automatically when you step away (if it’s not on, it won’t burn in).
Connectivity is great, too. The monitor has two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 2.1, and one USB-C port with DisplayPort input for a total of four video inputs. All of the inputs can reach 4K at 240 Hz, and the DisplayPort 2.1 port offers UHBR20 data rates of up to 80Gbps, which means it can hit the 4K/240 Hz target without display stream compression.
The USB-C port offers 90 watts of power delivery for charging a connected laptop or tablet. A USB-C hub is included, as well, and provides three downstream USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 ports. The USB-A ports are accessible through the USB-C input or a USB-B input. A KVM switch is present as well. As if that wasn't all, Asus even throws in a three-year warranty for good measure.
What’s the Catch?
The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM is a great gaming monitor with a long list of features. It has a beautiful, sharp image, smooth-motion clarity, good HDR, lots of display inputs, and a USB hub. It even looks nice on a desk. The super-vivid, super-reflective TrueBlack coat won’t be to everyone’s taste, but it delivers on its promise to improve perceived contrast.
Which brings us to the only serious issue with the PG27UCWM: the price.
The monitor will set you back $1,200 at retail price. That’s a lot of clams for a 27-inch 4K OLED monitor. The PG27UCWM does a lot to justify a higher price, but I can’t broadly recommend the PG27UCWM over less expensive options like the PG27UCDM (currently $950) or MSI MPG 272URX (currently $800). Neither of those have the newer RGB Stripe OLED, of course, but that might not be enough for the average gamer to full appreciate given the hundreds of dollars of difference in price.
Still, the PG27UCWM is worth consideration if you want a flagship 27-inch 4K OLED monitor with the latest panel technology and a boatload of features when it becomes available in October. A 32-inch model will also be launched alongside it.

Salah scores twice as Trabzonspor beat Basaksehir 2-1
Aug 23 : Mohamed Salah opened his account in the Turkish Super Lig with a double as Trabzonspor beat Istanbul Basaksehir 2-1 to clinch their first win of the season on Sunday.
Salah, who joined Trabzonspor on a free transfer after leaving Liverpool following a trophy-laden nine-year spell, also had two goals disallowed in a standout performance.
Making his first league start after appearing as a substitute in Trabzonspor's season opener, Salah put his side ahead in the eighth minute, capitalising after Basaksehir goalkeeper Muhammed Sengezer failed to hold onto the ball.
Basaksehir's Eldor Shomurodov equalised from the penalty spot in the 19th minute, but Salah restored Trabzonspor's lead three minutes into the second half, bursting down the right, exchanging passes with Ernest Muci and slotting the ball into the far corner.
The 34-year-old winger had a stoppage-time effort chalked off for a foul in the build-up and another ruled out for offside when he found the empty net from long range with the goalkeeper up-field for a corner.
He will now turn his attention to Thursday's Europa League playoff second leg away to Ferencvaros after his side suffered a 1-0 home defeat in the first leg.

Travel just two hours west of Beijing by train, and you’ll find yourself surrounded by the rolling grasslands and ancient cinder cones of Inner Mongolia. This vast, arid land has long been China’s capital of sheep farming and coal mining, but over the last few years, it has become the hottest place in the country to build an AI data center.
In Ulanqab, a city in Inner Mongolia home to about 1.5 million people, nearly 100 data centers have been opened or begun construction since 2016. Chinese companies have pledged to build projects with a combined estimated capacity of 12.5 gigawatts in the city, and over 70 percent of the total commitments have been announced in just the last year, making it one of the fastest growing compute clusters in Asia, according to a research note published by Goldman Sachs last week. For comparison, OpenAI’s $500 billion Stargate Project is set to reach only 10 gigawatts of total capacity when it’s complete.
Chinese companies are flocking to Ulanqab for a number of reasons. The city sits at high elevation on the Inner Mongolian Plateau and has long, cold winters, which means data centers there don’t need to use as much energy to stay cool. It’s also relatively close to Beijing, so data can be transmitted to China’s populous regions with minimum latency. But the most enticing factor has to do with costs. Electricity is cheaper in Inner Mongolia than almost anywhere else in China, driven by both the strong growth of wind and solar energy and an abundant supply of coal.
What’s also interesting is who is building these data centers. For the first time, Chinese AI companies are making big investments in their own infrastructure, rather than renting compute from cloud companies. DeepSeek is reportedly building a massive AI data center in Ulanqab, as are ByteDance, Alibaba, and Xiaohongshu. For years, Chinese AI companies have spent far less on building physical infrastructure than their American peers, despite developing a number of popular AI models with impressive capabilities. The Ulanqab data center boom signals that now they are finally starting to catch up.
There’s just one problem: finding enough water. Ulanqab is about as dry as Denver, getting only roughly 14 inches of rain each year. The local government is already struggling to provide enough water to meet resident demand—before many of the planned data center projects are even up and running. Last month, the local water company in Ulanqab was forced to turn off several waterworks for seven hours each night to mitigate peak demand. The data centers being built in the city will need less water in the winter—weather data from the local government of Ulanqab shows they only require additional water for cooling during two months out of the year—but all of the new infrastructure could still pose a significant environmental challenge for the region.
The Boonies
Inner Mongolia has been a data center hot spot for at least a decade, long before the current AI boom. Huawei built its first one in Ulanqab in 2016, and Apple followed suit three years later. In 2021, the area was designated as one of the main hubs of a country-wide government project dubbed “Eastern Data, Western Compute,” which aims to build data centers in the Western hinterlands of China.
There was one major drawback, though. Because they are located far from China’s populous eastern coast, these data centers initially faced high latency rates when transferring data to the majority of users. As a result, they were initially largely relegated to backup storage—until AI gave them a new purpose. “With the rise of AI in 2022, there was the realization that actually, those remote data centers could be well-utilized for model training,” says Andrew Stokols, a professor at Singapore Management University who studies China’s compute infrastructure. A training run for an AI model can take months and doesn’t require much real-time tinkering, so latency is less of an issue.
Relatively speaking, Ulanqab is also not really that far away. Inner Mongolia is much closer to Beijing and other major metropolitan areas in China than any Western data center hub is. And it’s now connected by two dedicated fiber optics cables built in 2017 and 2019 that reduced average latency speeds to less than five milliseconds, fast enough to support real-time data exchanges like AI inference.
Compared to other data center hubs in China, Ulanqab’s growth seems to have been driven more by commercial demand than government-led investment, Stokols says. As Chinese AI startups like DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and Zhiput AI have begun attracting more paying users at home, they have found a viable business case for inference data centers close enough to serve them without excessive latency.
Powered by Renewables
The Chinese government is excited about building data centers in Inner Mongolia for another reason: It could help absorb the country’s excess capacity of renewable energy. Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, a Singapore-based research center, says there’s a positive correlation between regions in China with the most unused renewable energy and those that have built the most data centers.
In the eyes of the government, this is a win-win strategy. China can catch up to pace of data center construction in the US, while simultaneously increasing demand for renewable energy. So it should come as no surprise that Envision, one of the largest Chinese manufacturers of wind turbines, announced this month that it will build a 2 gigawatt AI data center in Ulanqab connected directly to the company’s own clean power supply.
But experts caution that looking at AI data centers and renewable energy in China as a match made in heaven is too simple of a story. Stokols found in his research that about 37 percent of electricity in Ulanqab still comes from coal. And since data centers need to run around the clock, operators have traditionally favored fossil fuels for their reliability.
“Inner Mongolia has long been the West Virginia of China. It’s a coal country,” says Ma. The region is now racing to replace coal with wind and solar, but it remains unclear how fast that transition will happen or how far it will go. For now, the data centers popping up in China’s remote highlands will have to keep relying on coal to some extent. But “in three years, maybe it will be completely powered by renewables,” Ma says.

Humanoid robots have beaten Usain Bolt's 100-meter dash record
And they looked absolutely ridiculous doing it.
Usain Bolt's 2009 world record for the 100-meter dash still remains unbroken at 9.58 seconds, but only if we're talking about humans. During the second annual World Humanoid Robot Games that kicked off in Beijing on Saturday, the Tiangong Ultra humanoid robot completed the 100-meter dash in 9.39 seconds during a preliminary heat. Developed by Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, the record-holding robot overtook Honor's Lightning robot, which completed the sprint in 9.47 seconds.
Despite the impressive finish times, don't expect these humanoid robots to be used for any commercial purposes yet. After their sprints, they slammed directly into pads and some even required human assistance to be stretchered off the course. However, it's still a major improvement from last year's inaugural World Humanoid Robot Games, where the Tiangong Ultra won the 100-meter dash in 21.5 seconds.
Aside from this Robot Olympics event, Beijing hosted a half-marathon for Chinese companies to show off the capabilities of their humanoid robots. The event had its fair share of crashes too, but Honor's Lightning robot managed to secure the gold medal with a finish time of 50 minutes and 26 seconds, which also surpassed another human record. The World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing kicked off August 22 and will run until the 26, hosting thousands of robot participants competing in more than just track and field events, including soccer, table tennis and boxing.

A24’s Tony landed at no. 7 in a big expansion to 1,642 runs (from just under 40). It’s cooking with a $5 million weekend and $6.6 million cume in week 3 for the Matt Johnson film starring Dominic Sessa as a young Anthony Bourdain and Antonio Banderas as an early mentor.
The coming-of-age story imagines a Cape Cod summer working at a lobster restaurant that helped shape the beloved late chef and TV host into the icon he ultimately became. The film is Certified Fresh at 95% on Rotten Tomatoes with a 92% audience score, excellent exits and great word of mouth across age demos.
Black Bear’s ensemble company Spa Weekend, at no. 9, opened to an estimated $3 million on just over 2,00 screens. Three childhood besties embark on a much-needed spa getaway that descends into chaos when their trainwreck friend joins. Stars Leslie Mann, Isla Fisher, Michelle Buteau and Anna Faris.
Watch on Deadline
With a B+ CinemaScore, it played strongest in the South, Midwest, and West Coast and reached an older audience who often continue to turn out for films later in their theatrical run.

Limited releases: Neon horror It Ends opened on 5 screens to $60k.

Greenwich opened French hit The Marching Band in NYC at the Angelika Film Center for an estimated 3-day weekend gross of $12.2k.

A man has received threats from the Taliban after his work for the Afghan police was revealed by a Ministry of Defence leak and the UK refused his application for resettlement.
Hamid* worked for the Afghan national police special unit and received certificates for his work signed by senior British figures praising his “dedication, unparalleled service and leadership”. His details were also included in an accidental 2022 leak by an MoD official that identified 18,700 Afghans who had worked with or for the British government.
Hamid said he had received a number of threats from the Taliban, including a video he shared with the Guardian in which a man cradling a rifle and sitting below a Taliban flag threatens to pursue him and cites knowledge of his previous movements.
The MoD, however, has rejected his application for resettlement under the Afghan relocations and assistance policy (Arap) scheme. His most recent rejection, received on 31 July, stated that Hamid had not provided evidence of “working alongside, in partnership with or closely supporting a UK government department”. It gave him 28 days to appeal.
Hamid said: “This is extremely painful because I have already submitted every document available to me proving my service. Furthermore, many of my former colleagues who served in exactly the same department and performed the same duties have already been relocated to the UK through the Arap scheme.
“Despite this evidence, my case continues to be refused. I believe my case raises serious questions about how some former Afghan partners of the UK continue to be treated despite years of loyal service.”
Hamid’s plea for help comes five years after the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on 15 August 2021 after the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. The UK government launched the Arap scheme on 1 April 2021 and closed it to new applications on 1 July last year. Pre-existing applications continue to be processed.
Under Arap, high risk of death or serious injury are only taken into account if the rest of the criteria are deemed to have been met, which they have not in Hamid’s case. “Must I wait until I am captured, tortured or killed by the Taliban before my service and the danger I face are finally recognised?” he said.
“Following the Ministry of Defence data breach, my personal information was exposed, placing me at even greater risk. Since then, my life has changed completely. I cannot safely leave my home to work. I live in constant fear of being recognised or targeted.”
After the leak, the then defence secretary, John Healey, said the dataset included people who had made speculative applications under Arap and had not worked with British forces. He said being included in the leak “doesn’t give them a right to claim access to Britain”.
“It doesn’t give them a right to claim asylum. It doesn’t make them eligible for the special [Arap] scheme that Britain put in place for those who’d worked alongside or served with our forces,” he said.
Hamid said that because he was in hiding he had no reliable income and relied on his wife, who supports the family by doing small jobs from home. “This is our family’s only source of income, and even then we struggle simply to survive,” he said.
“The emotional impact has been devastating. My wife and I have become deeply exhausted, depressed and hopeless after years of fear, uncertainty, repeated refusals and financial hardship.
“I am not asking for special treatment. I am only asking for a fair review based on the evidence I have already provided.”
An MoD spokesperson said: “Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis, assessed against the evidence provided, such as how they supported the UK mission in Afghanistan, and in line with the publicly available eligibility criteria.
“Since the Taliban takeover, the UK has resettled almost 39,000 Afghan men, women and children through Afghan resettlement schemes.”

  Russia has begun importing fuel, its government has confirmed, as a shipload of gasoline arrived from India. A fuel exporter in peacetime, Russia has been forced to turn to imports after Ukrainian strikes on its refineries and depots in response to the Russian invasion. The campaign by Kyiv’s military has been a major success, causing fuel shortages across Russia and in illegally occupied Crimea. At least one cargo of gasoline from India has just entered Russia’s domestic market, three industry sources told Reuters and shipping data showed. Russia is also arranging rail imports of gasoline from Belarus and Kazakhstan, and has placed a ban on fuel exports. Reuters reported last week that Russia had also begun shipping in diesel from Asia.
- 
  An Oman-flagged tanker loaded about 68,000 tonnes of gasoline at the Port Said anchorage in a ship-to-ship transfer from the tanker Agni, which had been loaded at India’s Vadinar port, sources told Reuters. The tanker unloaded at Russia’s Arctic port of Vitino in early August, shipping data showed. India has been one of the keenest customers of Russian oil held at low prices by war sanctions.
- 
  The importation of refined Indian products is a reversal of the flow that speaks to the toll of the war on Russia’s own processing capabilities. According to industry data, at least two more gasoline cargoes from India are expected to arrive at Russian ports within the next two weeks. Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak acknowledged on Wednesday that imports had begun but did not give details on the volumes or sources. Fuel stations in Moscow have reimposed purchasing limits, according to Reuters witnesses and fuel suppliers. State-owned Rosneft, Russia’s biggest oil company, said petrol purchases were restricted to 30 litres at all its stations across the country.
